chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Point or displacement? One drone lifts off from the rooftop R=(2,1); a second drone lifts off from a different rooftop S=(7,3). Both receive the same instruction, the displacement (4,4). Without computing either landing point, decide two things and say why: do the drones end at the same place, and does the pair (4,4) on its own tell you where either drone is? In one sentence, what does a displacement record, and what does it deliberately leave out? Ask what question each ordered pair answers. A point answers where?; a displacement answers which way, and how far? Try applying the same instruction at two different starting points and notice whether the change depends on where you began.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: One number or one arrow? On the same weather map, the temperature reading T(x,y) and the wind \mathbf F(x,y) are both functions of position. Yet only one of them is called a vector field. Without writing any formulas, explain what the wind output carries at each point that the temperature output does not, and why that difference is exactly what earns the wind the name vector field. Picture standing at one spot and asking, What does this map hand me here? The thermometer hands you a single number; the wind hands you something you could draw as an arrow. Think about what an arrow records that a number alone cannot.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Why one slope is not enough? On a single-variable graph, asking how steep is it here? has one answer. On a hillside, the same question feels incomplete until you add something. What is the missing piece of information that the hiker must supply before how steep? becomes a sensible question, and why did that piece never come up on the number line? On a line there were only two ways to move, so the answer was forced. On a hill the hiker gets to choose a way to step. Think about what changes between facing uphill and facing along the slope at the same spot.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: What does a negative scalar do? You scale a nonzero vector \mathbf u by some number c. For which values of c does c\mathbf u still point the same way as \mathbf u, and for which does it point the opposite way? What single value of c collapses the arrow to no displacement at all? Try a few cases like c=2, c=\tfrac12, and c=-1, and watch only the direction of the arrow, not its length. Where does the dividing line between same way and opposite way sit on the number line?

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Why is the origin always in a span? No matter which vectors \mathbf u and \mathbf v you start with, the zero vector \mathbf 0 always belongs to \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u,\mathbf v\}. Why must this be true for every span? A span is the set of all linear combinations a\mathbf u+b\mathbf v. Is there a choice of the coefficients a and b that is always allowed and that always lands you back at \mathbf 0?

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: When is an affine line a line through the origin? An affine line has the form P+\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\}. Geometrically, how is it different from the plain line \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\} through the origin? Under what condition on the point P do the two lines actually coincide? Think of the affine line as the origin line slid over so that it passes through P instead of through \mathbf 0. What if P already lies on the original line? Use P=t_0\mathbf u to compare the sets of points.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: What does a coordinate tell you to do? We wrote (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)=x_1\mathbf e_1+x_2\mathbf e_2+\cdots+x_n\mathbf e_n and called the coordinates instructions. In your own words, what instruction does a single coordinate, say x_2, give, and why does the basis vector \mathbf e_2 make that instruction precise? Think of each \mathbf e_j as a single step in one pure direction. What role does the number x_2 play once you know which direction \mathbf e_2 points?

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Why keep two descriptions of one line? The same line was written both as (x,y)=(2,1)+t(3,2) and as 2x-3y=1. If both describe the very same set of points, why might you reach for one form rather than the other? Give a task that the parametric form handles easily and a task that the equation handles easily. One form is good at producing points on the line; the other is good at checking whether a given point belongs. Which is which?

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Computing in \mathbb R^4 with no picture? We cannot draw the greenhouse reading (T,p,h,c) as an arrow in four perpendicular directions, yet we still added \Delta\mathbf s to it and compared components. What is it about the way addition and scaling are defined that lets the algebra keep working even after the picture disappears? Look back at how a sum or a scalar multiple is actually computed. Does any step require you to see the vectors, or does each step only touch the coordinates one at a time?

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Why can the zero vector never join an independent list? Suppose a list of vectors includes the zero vector \mathbf 0. Explain in your own words why such a list can never be linearly independent, no matter what the other vectors are. What happens if you take a nonzero multiple of \mathbf 0 and zero times every other vector? Is that combination forced to be trivial?

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: What does uniqueness of coordinates really say? A basis gives every vector exactly one coordinate list. In plain language, what would go wrong if a vector had two different coordinate lists relative to the same basis? Why is having a single, unambiguous list the whole point of a coordinate system? Think of coordinates as an address. If one location had two different addresses, could you trust the address to name the location? Connect this to the two conditions in the definition of a basis.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Why does dimension count directions, not vectors? Someone writes down four vectors in \mathbb R^3 and concludes that they span a four-dimensional space. Without doing any computation, explain why this conclusion must be wrong, and what the number of vectors actually tells you here. Dimension is the number of vectors in a basis, and a basis must be independent. Could four vectors in \mathbb R^3 ever stay independent? What does the standard basis suggest about the most genuine directions available?

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: A preview of tangent spaces The language of spans, bases, and dimension will return in a new form when we study curves and surfaces. A curve has one direction of motion at each point, as long as it is not stopped there. For example, the curve \mathbf r(t)=(t,t^2) passes through \mathbf r(1)=(1,1). Its image is the familiar graph y=x^2. Single-variable calculus gives slope 2 at x=1, so (1,2) is a direction vector for the tangent. The tangent line at (1,1) has the form (1,1)+s(1,2). That is an affine line: a point plus the span of one direction. A surface usually has two independent tangent directions at each point. Those two directions span a tangent plane. Later, when we differentiate parametrized surfaces, this idea will become concrete: \text{tangent plane}=\text{point}+\operatorname{span}\{\text{two tangent directions}\}. This is the first glimpse of a theme that will follow us through the book. Geometry near a point often becomes linear. A curve becomes a tangent line. A surface becomes a tangent plane. A nonlinear function becomes its best linear approximation. Linear independence tells us when directions can serve as coordinates. But it does not yet tell us how long a direction is. In standard coordinates the vector (3,4) has length 5, but in a diagonal or slanted basis the coordinate pair (3,4) may represent a very different geometric arrow. To talk about speed, distance, spheres, and unit directions, we need a way to measure length itself.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: A sphere with no thickness? We just saw that the sphere of radius r=0 centered at C is the single point C. Explain, without computing, why that has to be so. What is the only point X whose distance from C can equal 0? Remember that \|X-C\| is a distance, and a distance is 0 only when there is nothing to travel. When does a vector have length 0?

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: When is the detour no detour? The triangle inequality \|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|\leq \|\mathbf u\|+\|\mathbf v\| becomes an equality exactly when \mathbf u and \mathbf v point the same way. Using the hiker who walks cabin to lake to lookout, describe in words what the three stops look like when the direct path is exactly as long as the broken path. Picture the triangle formed by \mathbf u, \mathbf v, and \mathbf u+\mathbf v. What happens to that triangle when there is no real bend at the lake? Think about a triangle that has been flattened.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Why can't we normalize zero? Suppose a stubborn friend insists on normalizing the zero vector by computing \mathbf 0/\|\mathbf 0\|. Point to two separate things that go wrong: one purely arithmetic, and one about what a unit vector is supposed to mean. Why does the geometric problem run deeper than the arithmetic one? For the arithmetic issue, look at the denominator \|\mathbf 0\|. For the geometric issue, ask yourself: if someone asked you which way \mathbf 0 points, what could you possibly answer?

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Why so many descriptions? The same geometric line can be written as X=P+t\mathbf u in infinitely many ways. Without computing anything, explain what you are free to change about P and \mathbf u while still tracing out exactly the same set of points. Ask yourself two questions: which starting points P already lie on the line, and which directions \mathbf u point along it? Think about what scaling or reversing \mathbf u does to the path versus the set of points it covers.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: What does the normal vector know? A normal vector \mathbf n=(A,B,C) records the coefficients of the plane Ax+By+Cz=D. Explain, in your own words, why directions that lie inside the plane leave the value of Ax+By+Cz unchanged, while moving along \mathbf n changes it. What does this tell you about the relationship between \mathbf n and the plane? Imagine taking a tiny step (\Delta x,\Delta y,\Delta z) and watching the number Ax+By+Cz. Staying on the plane means that number must not move. You do not need the dot product yet, just the idea of which steps keep the value fixed.

chapter.title: Points, Vectors, and Space

text: Why exactly one dimension? A single linear equation in \mathbb R^n produces a hyperplane of dimension n-1, not n-2 and not n. Explain why one honest linear constraint removes exactly one free direction. What goes wrong with the counting if all the coefficients a_i were zero? Count the choices: before the equation you may pick all n coordinates freely. The equation lets you solve for one coordinate in terms of the rest. How many remain free? Then ask what the equation even says when no a_i can be used to solve for anything.

text: A multiplication that measures agreement in direction should be symmetric: \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u. A multiplication that measures oriented area should change sign when the order is swapped. Why might one product not be enough?

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why does multiplying by i turn the plane a quarter turn? You just saw that i sends (a,b) to (-b,a). Without computing any example, explain in your own words why this single algebraic rule i^2=-1 forces multiplication by i to be a quarter-turn rotation rather than, say, a stretch or a reflection. Apply multiplication by i twice. Where does 1 land after one step, and after two? A quarter turn done twice should be a half turn — and a half turn is exactly multiplication by -1.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: What makes complex multiplication the natural product of the plane? A nonzero plane vector carries exactly two pieces of geometric data: a length and an angle. Why does this fact make multiply the lengths, add the angles the most natural rule for combining two such vectors, rather than something we simply chose to define? Ask what operation on positive numbers is most natural, and what operation on angles stacks one turn on top of another. Multiplication already does both jobs separately — the plane just lets you do them at the same time.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why did Hamilton's three-dimensional dream run into trouble? In the plane, one imaginary unit i was enough to capture rotation. Hamilton hoped to multiply triples x+yi+zj in space the same way. What is the conceptual obstacle that makes a single extra imaginary unit not enough in three dimensions? Count the directions perpendicular to a given axis. In the plane there is essentially one; in space there is a whole circle of them. If multiplication must respect all of those perpendicular directions at once, can one unit speak for all of them?

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: What does one rule force? Hamilton packed everything into the single line i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1. Take the piece ijk=-1 and ask: if you already know i^2=-1, what must the product ij equal? Try to deduce the value of ij from ijk=-1 alone, without peeking at the table. Multiply both sides of ijk=-1 on the right by k, and remember that k^2=-1. One short rearrangement reveals ij.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: A feature, not a defect? It is tempting to read ij=-ji as a flaw, as if the algebra simply failed to be tidy. But think about turning a book around two different axes in space, first one order and then the reversed order. Why is it actually desirable that ij\neq ji if these symbols are meant to describe three-dimensional rotation? Ask what would go wrong if order did not matter. If ij equalled ji, could the algebra ever tell two opposite spatial orientations apart?

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why call them vectors at all? We keep writing (x,y,z)\leftrightarrow xi+yj+zk as if a pure imaginary quaternion simply is a vector in \mathbb R^3. What earns that identification? Name a couple of features of pure imaginary quaternions that line up exactly with how vectors in space already behave. Think about addition, scalar multiplication, and especially the quantity V^2. Which familiar measurement of the vector (x,y,z) is hiding inside V^2?

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why does the scalar part carry the dot product? When you multiply two pure imaginary quaternions, the scalar part of the product turns out to be -\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v. Without computing anything, can you explain where that minus sign comes from, and why a quantity built from a product of directions ends up measuring how much the two vectors point the same way? Think about what happens when a single direction multiplies itself. What is i^2, j^2, or k^2? Those self-products are exactly the terms that survive in the scalar part when \mathbf u and \mathbf v line up.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why does the vector part carry the cross product? The vector part of UV is \mathbf u\times\mathbf v, and swapping the order of the two quaternions flips its sign. Why is it natural that the vector part of a product should reverse direction when you reverse the order, while the scalar part does not? What feature of an oriented area is the quaternion product faithfully recording? Compare ij=k with ji=-k. Picture the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors and ask what should happen to its orientation when you trace its edges in the opposite order.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: What do the two halves of a product measure? Any product UV can be split into a symmetric piece \tfrac{1}{2}(UV+VU) and an antisymmetric piece \tfrac{1}{2}(UV-VU). In plain words, what does each half measure about the relationship between \mathbf u and \mathbf v, and why does it make sense that the symmetric half ignores order while the antisymmetric half depends on it? One half survives a swap unchanged; the other flips sign. Match each half to a quantity you have already met in this section, and ask which of those quantities cares about which vector comes first.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why does a zero dot product mean perpendicular? The angle formula says \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=\|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|\cos\theta. Using this, explain in your own words why \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v=0 forces two nonzero vectors to be perpendicular. Then say what goes wrong with this reasoning if one of the vectors is \mathbf 0. Both lengths are positive when the vectors are nonzero, so look at which factor in the product is allowed to vanish. What angle in [0,\pi] has that cosine?

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text:
Projection onto a line The dot product tells us how much one vector lies along another. Suppose a narrow trail runs in the direction \mathbf u=(3,4). A gust of wind pushes a hiker by the displacement \mathbf v=(7,1). Part of this displacement is along the trail. Part is sideways. The dot product finds the along-trail part: \mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u=7\cdot3+1\cdot4=25. Also, \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u=3^2+4^2=25. So the coefficient of \mathbf u in the along-trail part is  rac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}= rac{25}{25}=1. Thus the projection of \mathbf v onto the trail direction is 1\cdot \mathbf u=(3,4). The sideways leftover is \mathbf v-\mathbf u=(7,1)-(3,4)=(4,-3). Check that it is perpendicular to the trail: (4,-3)\cdot(3,4)=12-12=0. A vector splits into an along-line projection and a perpendicular leftover.  egin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.75, >=stealth] \draw[->] (-0.5,0) -- (8.5,0) node[right] {\(x\)}; \draw[->] (0,-3.5) -- (0,5.5) node[above] {\(y\)}; \coordinate (O) at (0,0); \coordinate (U) at (3,4); \coordinate (V) at (7,1); \coordinate (R) at (4,-3); \draw[thick, gray!70] (-1,-1.333) -- (4.2,5.6) node[above] {\(\operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\}\)}; \draw[->, very thick] (O) -- (V) node[midway, above right] {\(\mathbf v=(7,1)\)}; \draw[->, very thick] (O) -- (U) node[midway, left] {\(\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v=(3,4)\)}; \draw[->, thick, dashed] (U) -- (V) node[midway, right] {\((4,-3)\)}; \draw (2.76, 3.68) -- (3.08, 3.44) -- (3.32, 3.76);  ill (O) circle (2pt);  ill (U) circle (2pt);  ill (V) circle (2pt); \end{tikzpicture} Projection onto a line Let \mathbf u
eq \mathbf 0. The projection of \mathbf v onto the line spanned by \mathbf u is  oxed{\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v= rac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}\,\mathbf u.} The scalar component of \mathbf v in the direction of \mathbf u is  rac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\|\mathbf u\|}. The condition \mathbf u
eq\mathbf 0 is necessary. The zero vector does not determine a line direction, and the formula would divide by \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u=0. For example, asking for the projection of (1,2) onto the direction (0,0) has no geometric meaning. There is no direction to project onto. Projection is not only a formula. It is a closest approximation. What is the projection, and why subtract it? Describe geometrically what \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v represents: where does it sit relative to \mathbf v and the line through \mathbf u? Then explain why the leftover \mathbf v-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v is exactly the perpendicular part of \mathbf v, rather than just whatever is left. Picture the shadow \mathbf v casts onto the line. Then dot the leftover with \mathbf u: what value would confirm it points straight across the line? Projection is the closest vector on the line Let \mathbf u
eq\mathbf 0, and let \mathbf p=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v. Then \mathbf p is the vector on the line \operatorname{span}\{\mathbf u\} closest to \mathbf v. The vector \mathbf p has the form \mathbf p=c\mathbf u,\qquad c= rac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}. The leftover \mathbf r=\mathbf v-\mathbf p is perpendicular to \mathbf u, because \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf u \amp= (\mathbf v-c\mathbf u)\cdot\mathbf u \amp= \mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u-c(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u) \amp= \mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u- rac{\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf u}{\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u}(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf u) \amp= 0. Now take any other vector t\mathbf u on the same line. Then \mathbf v-t\mathbf u=(\mathbf v-\mathbf p)+(\mathbf p-t\mathbf u). The first vector is perpendicular to the line, and the second vector lies on the line. So by the Pythagorean theorem, \|\mathbf v-t\mathbf u\|^2=\|\mathbf v-\mathbf p\|^2+\|\mathbf p-t\mathbf u\|^2. This is smallest when \|\mathbf p-t\mathbf u\|^2=0, which happens only when t\mathbf u=\mathbf p. This theorem is the first glimpse of a large idea: dot products allow us to turn geometry into approximation. Later, the same idea will become least squares, tangent planes, and orthogonal projections in higher-dimensional spaces.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: What is the projection, and why subtract it? Describe geometrically what \operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v represents: where does it sit relative to \mathbf v and the line through \mathbf u? Then explain why the leftover \mathbf v-\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbf u}\mathbf v is exactly the perpendicular part of \mathbf v, rather than just whatever is left. Picture the shadow \mathbf v casts onto the line. Then dot the leftover with \mathbf u: what value would confirm it points straight across the line?

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: What does Cauchy–Schwarz say about the angle? Cauchy–Schwarz says |\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v|\leq \|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\|. Reading this through the angle formula, what does the inequality tell you about \cos\theta? And in geometric terms, what has to be true about \mathbf u and \mathbf v for the inequality to become an equality? Divide both sides by \|\mathbf u\|\,\|\mathbf v\| (for nonzero vectors) and compare with |\cos\theta|. Equality forces |\cos\theta| to its largest possible value, which pins down the angle.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why perpendicular to both? We checked by computation that \mathbf u\times\mathbf v is perpendicular to both \mathbf u and \mathbf v. Thinking of \mathbf u\times\mathbf v as the oriented area vector of the parallelogram spanned by \mathbf u and \mathbf v, explain in words why it has to point perpendicular to both, rather than slanting off in some other direction. The parallelogram lives flat inside one plane. If a single vector is going to stand in for that flat sheet, which direction is the only one that does not favor \mathbf u over \mathbf v or lean back into the sheet?

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: What do length and direction each measure? The vector \mathbf u\times\mathbf v carries two pieces of information at once: its length and its direction. In your own words, what does the length \|\mathbf u\times\mathbf v\| measure, and what does its direction encode? What changes about each piece if you swap the order to \mathbf v\times\mathbf u? One piece is a size that cannot be negative; the other is an orientation that the right-hand rule decides. Swapping the order leaves the parallelogram unchanged but reverses how you walk around it.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why only in three dimensions? The dot product \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v makes sense for vectors in any dimension, yet the cross product \mathbf u\times\mathbf v lives only in three. Explain why a plane in \mathbb R^3 can hand its oriented area to a single normal vector, while the same trick fails both in \mathbb R^2 and in \mathbb R^4. Count the directions perpendicular to a plane. In \mathbb R^2 there are none to spare; in \mathbb R^4 there are too many to choose from. Only one dimension leaves exactly one perpendicular line.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: What is the sign telling you? You compute two 2\times2 determinants and get +7 for one pair of vectors and -7 for another. The two parallelograms have exactly the same area. So what difference is the sign actually recording? Describe, in words, what the sign of \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v] tells you about how \mathbf u and \mathbf v sit relative to each other. Picture sweeping from \mathbf u toward \mathbf v through the parallelogram. Which way does that turn go? Think about what changes when you read the two vectors in the opposite order.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why does one swap flip the sign? Swapping just two vectors in an ordered basis turned \det=+1 into \det=-1, even though the same box was described both times. Why should interchanging two of the vectors reverse the orientation rather than leave it unchanged? Explain why a single swap must flip the sign, and predict what happens to the orientation if you then perform a second swap. A determinant is built so that two identical columns force it to be zero. Imagine slowly sliding one vector until it coincides with another: the signed volume must pass through 0. What does that forced passage through zero say about the sign on the two sides of the swap?

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why does one number rescale every rectangle? A rectangle has edge vectors (h,0) and (0,k), where h,k>0. Under T(x,y)=x(2,1)+y(1,3), what are the two image edge vectors? Compute their determinant and explain why the ratio of image area to original area is always 5, independent of h and k. The image edges are (2h,h) and (k,3k). Their determinant is (2h)(3k)-hk; the original rectangle has area hk.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why do repeated vector inputs give zero? The word alternating means that swapping the two inputs reverses the sign: B(\mathbf v,\mathbf u)=-B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v). Think about what this says geometrically for a parallelogram's signed area, and then explain why feeding the same vector into both slots of this real-valued measurement must give zero. Put \mathbf u=\mathbf v into the swap rule. You get B(\mathbf u,\mathbf u)=-B(\mathbf u,\mathbf u). What is the only number equal to its own negative? Geometrically, a vector and itself span no area.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why isn't dx\wedge dy ordinary multiplication? Ordinary multiplication is commutative: ab=ba. But the definition gives dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx. Using the idea that dx\wedge dy measures the signed area of the parallelogram built from two ordered vectors, explain in your own words why reversing the order of dx and dy should flip the sign rather than leave it unchanged. Evaluate both dx\wedge dy and dy\wedge dx on the same ordered pair (\mathbf u,\mathbf v). Their two scalar products occur with opposite signs. Compare this with the effect of swapping the vector inputs.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why does an ordered pair carry a sign? The vectors \mathbf u=(3,1) and \mathbf v=(1,2) span a parallelogram. Evaluate (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) and (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf v,\mathbf u). Explain why reversing the ordered pair changes signed area but leaves ordinary area unchanged. Use u_1v_2-u_2v_1, then interchange \mathbf u and \mathbf v. Ordinary area is the absolute value of the signed result.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Follow the two basis arrows Compute (c+si)1 and (c+si)i. Draw their images when \phi=\pi/6. What angle has each arrow turned? Use distributivity to find (c+si)(x+yi). Write the resulting coordinates, and check that their squared length is x^2+y^2. Write x+yi=r(\cos\alpha+i\sin\alpha). Use the angle-addition identities to show that multiplication replaces \alpha by \alpha+\phi. Why does this establish a rotation for every arrow? The basis images are c+si and -s+ci. In the length calculation, the mixed terms cancel and c^2+s^2=1.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Multiply every basis direction on the left Define L_{q_i}(X)=q_iX, and similarly for q_j,q_k. Here X can be any quaternion. Verify the first row of the table and fill every question mark in the other two rows. Keep the multiplier on the left. Images of the four basis directions under left multiplication. Multiplier1ijk q_ic+si-s+cicj+sk-sj+ck q_j???? q_k???? For L_{q_i}, recognize the rotation pattern in the ordered planes (1,i) and (j,k). Sketch these as two separate ordinary planes. Mark the angle \phi in each. For L_{q_j}, use the ordered planes (1,j) and (k,i). For L_{q_k}, use (1,k) and (i,j). Check that both planes in each pair turn by +\phi. Why would writing (i,k) in place of (k,i) reverse the reported sign? Use the two perpendicular planes to explain why each map preserves |X|^2, the sum of the four squared real coordinates. For example, q_jk=ck+s(jk)=ck+si, while q_ji=ci+s(ji)=ci-sk. Read these as images of the ordered pair (k,i). The squared lengths of the two plane components add to the squared length in four dimensions.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Why is one multiplication not yet our spatial rotation? Compute the real part of q_i(xi+yj+zk). Then set \phi=\pi/2 and follow the input i. Does its image still represent a vector in three-dimensional space? Explain why preserving length in four dimensions does not by itself give a rotation of the pure imaginary subspace. The real part is -sx. In particular, ii=-1 points along the real coordinate direction.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Find an inverse without guessing Write q=a_0+V, where V=a_1i+a_2j+a_3k, and use V^2=-(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2) to prove q\overline q=\overline q q=|q|^2. Deduce that q^{-1}=\overline q/|q|^2 for q\ne0. Check that q_i,q_j,q_k are unit quaternions. What is q_i^{-1}? Expand (a_0+V)(a_0-V). Real numbers commute with every quaternion, so the mixed terms cancel. For q_i, the inverse is c-si.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Which plane reverses its turn? Compute 1(c-si), i(c-si), j(c-si), and k(c-si). Compare each with the first row of . Show that right multiplication by q_i^{-1} turns the ordered plane (1,i) through -\phi, but turns (j,k) through +\phi. Predict what happens if you first apply L_{q_i} and then R_{q_i^{-1}}. Which plane should stop turning? Which angle should add? The crucial sign is ji=-k, so j(c-si)=cj-sji=cj+sk. On the other hand, i(c-si)=s+ci.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Check the prediction on all four directions Compute q_i1q_i^{-1} and q_iiq_i^{-1}. Explain why both 1 and i return to their starting positions. Complete this calculation without moving factors past one another: q_ijq_i^{-1}\amp=(cj+sk)(c-si) \amp=c^2j-csji+sck-s^2ki. Collect the j and k terms and use c^2-s^2=\cos(2\phi) and 2cs=\sin(2\phi). Compute q_ikq_i^{-1} in the same way. Use distributivity to find the image of xi+yj+zk. Does any real part remain? Use ji=-k and ki=j in the displayed expansion. For the final part, C_{q_i}(xi+yj+zk)=xC_{q_i}(i)+yC_{q_i}(j)+zC_{q_i}(k).

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Check your result against the coordinate rule (x,y,z)\longmapsto \bigl(x,\ y\cos(2\phi)-z\sin(2\phi),\ y\sin(2\phi)+z\cos(2\phi)\bigr). The x-coordinate stays fixed, and the yz-plane follows the complex rotation pattern. Thus the pure imaginary subspace stays pure imaginary. It rotates about the +i axis, with positive motion from j toward k. The angle is 2\phi: the two four-dimensional turns cancelled in (1,i) and added in (j,k).

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Choose the quaternion for a quarter turn To obtain a spatial angle \theta, what value of \phi should you use? Write the quaternion for a positive \pi/2 rotation about the x-axis. Use your quaternion to rotate V=i+2j+3k. Check your result geometrically in the yz-plane and compare the squared lengths. If someone uses q=i=e^{i\pi/2} in qVq^{-1}, what spatial angle do they actually get? Test the input j. Why would the analogous complex expression e^{i\phi}ze^{-i\phi} leave every complex number z unchanged? A spatial quarter turn needs q=(1+i)/\sqrt2 and gives i-3j+2k in the second part. Complex numbers commute, so their two multipliers can be brought together and cancelled.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Use cyclic order to keep the signs straight For q_j=c+sj, compute the four images under right multiplication by c-sj. Compare the turns in (1,j) and (k,i) with left multiplication. Then find all four images under X\longmapsto q_jXq_j^{-1}. Repeat for q_k=c+sk, using (1,k) and (i,j). Replace 2\phi by \theta. Write coordinate rules for rotating (x,y,z) about the y- and z-axes. Check positive quarter turns: about +j, k should move to i; about +k, i should move to j. Where do the other two coordinate directions go in each case? For the y-axis, the coordinate rule is (x,y,z)\longmapsto(x\cos\theta+z\sin\theta,\ y,\ -x\sin\theta+z\cos\theta). For the z-axis, it is (x,y,z)\longmapsto(x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta,\ x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta,\ z). In each case the coordinate along the axis stays fixed.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Make a basis suited to the chosen axis Choose any unit vector \mathbf b perpendicular to \mathbf u, write its pure imaginary quaternion as B, and set W=UB. Use the scalar-vector product identity UB=-\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf b+\mathbf u\times\mathbf b to explain why W is pure imaginary and corresponds to the unit vector \mathbf u\times\mathbf b. Why are 1,U,B,W four mutually perpendicular unit directions? Use the same product identity to prove BU=-UB=-W. Then use associativity to show UW=-B,\qquad WU=B. You have recovered the multiplication relations needed for two rotating planes. Compute the images of 1,U,B,W under left multiplication by c+sU and under right multiplication by c-sU. Identify the angles in the ordered planes (1,U) and (B,W). Combine the two maps. Show that conjugation fixes 1,U and sends B\amp\longmapsto\cos(2\phi)B+\sin(2\phi)W, W\amp\longmapsto-\sin(2\phi)B+\cos(2\phi)W. Why is positive motion from B toward W=UB the right-hand direction about \mathbf u? First, UW=U(UB)=U^2B=-B and WU=(UB)U=U(BU)=-U(UB)=B. Then qB=cB+sW, while Bq^{-1}=cB-sBU=cB+sW. Both operations turn the (B,W) plane in the same direction.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Recover a formula using dot and cross products Split the vector into components parallel and perpendicular to the axis: \mathbf v_{\parallel}=(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)\mathbf u,\qquad \mathbf v_{\perp}=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_{\parallel}. Check that \mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v_{\perp}=0. When \mathbf v_{\perp}\ne\mathbf0, choose \mathbf b=\mathbf v_{\perp}/\|\mathbf v_{\perp}\| in Step 6. Use the image of B to obtain \mathbf v'=\mathbf v_{\parallel}+\cos\theta\,\mathbf v_{\perp} +\sin\theta\,(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v_{\perp}). Explain separately why this also holds when \mathbf v_{\perp}=\mathbf0. Substitute the component formulas and use \mathbf u\times\mathbf v_{\parallel}=\mathbf0 to derive \mathbf v'\amp=\cos\theta\,\mathbf v +(1-\cos\theta)(\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v)\mathbf u \amp\qquad+\sin\theta\,(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v). This is called Rodrigues' rotation formula. Explain geometrically why the axis component and the length are preserved. The two perpendicular vectors \mathbf v_{\perp} and \mathbf u\times\mathbf v_{\perp} have equal length. Their sine-cosine combination is precisely the plane rotation already discovered.

chapter.title: Vector Products from Quaternions to Area and Volume

text: Three checks on your rotation rule Rotate through 2\pi/3 about \mathbf u=(1,1,1)/\sqrt3. Show that q=(1+i+j+k)/2, and compute the images of i,j,k by conjugation. Use them to rotate i+2j+3k. Check the length and the component along the axis. Show that q and -q give exactly the same map V\longmapsto qVq^{-1}. What quaternion does the half-angle rule produce for \theta=2\pi, and why is the resulting spatial map the identity? Let q_x=(1+i)/\sqrt2 and q_y=(1+j)/\sqrt2. Starting with k, apply the x-axis quarter turn and then the y-axis quarter turn. Reverse the order and compare. Use associativity to show that the first order is represented by q_yq_x: q_y(q_xVq_x^{-1})q_y^{-1}=(q_yq_x)V(q_x^{-1}q_y^{-1}). Verify that the last two factors form (q_yq_x)^{-1}. The first rotation cycles i\mapsto j\mapsto k\mapsto i. For the third part, the two orders send k to -j and i, respectively. A quaternion product encodes the first rotation in its rightmost factor.

Track \mathbf e_j step by step: A sends it to the column \mathbf a_j, and then B acts on that column. Which matrix has B\mathbf a_j as its columns?

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: Does the order of actions matter? The product BA means “first A, then B,” while AB means “first B, then A.” Without computing any numbers, explain why we should expect AB\neq BA in general. Picture a real pair of moves, like rotating a photo and cropping it: does swapping which one you do first usually land you in the same place? You only need one example where swapping the order changes the outcome. Try a move that throws information away (a projection) together with one that does not (a rotation), and ask what survives.

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: What does an inverse undo? Forget the formula A^{-1}A=I_n for a moment and think geometrically. What does it mean for a linear map to have an inverse, in terms of how it moves the grid? Why does collapsing space—like a projection flattening the plane onto a line—make an inverse impossible? An inverse must send every output back to exactly one input. If two different points get mapped to the same place, can any machine reliably tell them apart afterward?

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: Rotations, reflections, projections, and shears Many familiar geometric moves are linear transformations. Common linear transformations of the plane. Transformation Matrix Effect on (x,y) rotation by \theta \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta \end{pmatrix} (x\cos\theta-y\sin\theta,\;x\sin\theta+y\cos\theta) reflection across the x-axis \begin{pmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&-1 \end{pmatrix} (x,-y) projection onto the x-axis \begin{pmatrix} 1&0\\ 0&0 \end{pmatrix} (x,0) horizontal shear \begin{pmatrix} 1&k\\ 0&1 \end{pmatrix} (x+ky,y) The columns still tell the story. For a rotation by \theta, \mathbf e_1\longmapsto(\cos\theta,\sin\theta), and \mathbf e_2\longmapsto(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta). These are the two rotated coordinate directions. For a projection onto the x-axis, \mathbf e_1\longmapsto \mathbf e_1, \qquad \mathbf e_2\longmapsto \mathbf 0. The vertical direction is collapsed. For a shear, \mathbf e_1\longmapsto \mathbf e_1, \qquad \mathbf e_2\longmapsto(k,1). Vertical lines tilt, but horizontal lines stay horizontal. Composing rotations Let R_\alpha be rotation by angle \alpha, and let R_\beta be rotation by angle \beta. Rotating first by \alpha and then by \beta should be the same as rotating by \alpha+\beta: R_\beta R_\alpha=R_{\alpha+\beta}. Matrix multiplication turns this geometric fact into the angle-addition formulas: \begin{pmatrix} \cos\beta&-\sin\beta\\ \sin\beta&\cos\beta \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \cos\alpha&-\sin\alpha\\ \sin\alpha&\cos\alpha \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(\alpha+\beta)&-\sin(\alpha+\beta)\\ \sin(\alpha+\beta)&\cos(\alpha+\beta) \end{pmatrix}. Here a familiar trigonometric identity is really a statement about composing two linear transformations. Matrix multiplication lets us keep track of connected machines. But it does not yet tell us everything we want to know about those machines. A rotation turns a square without changing its area. A shear slants it without changing area. A projection flattens it to a line and destroys its area completely. Somewhere inside a square matrix there must be a single number that measures this area or volume effect. Chapter 2 already gave that number a name: the determinant.

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: What is a negative determinant telling you? A matrix A has \det A=-2. What does the size 2 tell you about areas, and what does the minus sign tell you about the picture? Describe in words what happens to the ordered pair (\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2). Think of the determinant as a signed area. The magnitude and the sign carry two separate pieces of news. The reflection example is a clean case of the sign on its own.

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: What does a zero determinant do to space? Suppose \det A=0 for a 2\times2 matrix A. Forget the formula for a moment and think only about the picture: what does A do to the whole plane? Why can no such map be undone? The determinant is the area of the image of the unit square. If that area is zero, the square has been squashed flat. Where could every output vector possibly live?

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: Why should determinants multiply? Apply A first, then B. If A scales every signed area by \det A and B then scales every signed area by \det B, explain in your own words why the combined map BA must scale signed area by \det(B)\det(A). Picture one area being stretched twice in a row. What do two successive scaling factors do to a single number? You are not asked to compute, only to chain the two stretches.

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: What is each equation saying? In the system 2x+y=7 and x+3y=8, what geometric object does each single equation describe? And in that picture, what does a solution of the whole system correspond to? Think about all the points (x,y) that make just one of the equations true. A solution must satisfy both equations at once, so where must it sit relative to the two objects you described?

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: Why are these moves safe? Adding a multiple of one equation to another changes how the system looks, yet it never changes which points (x,y,z) count as solutions. Why not? What is it about this operation that guarantees no solution is gained or lost? Ask yourself whether you could undo the move and get back exactly what you started with. If a point satisfies the old equations, does it satisfy the new ones, and the other way around too?

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: No, one, or infinitely many? Picture two lines in the plane drawn from a system of two equations in x and y. Describe the arrangement of those lines in each case: when does the system have no solution, when exactly one, and when infinitely many? A solution is a point shared by both lines. There are only a few ways two lines can sit together in a plane. How many points do they share when they cross, when they run parallel without meeting, and when they are secretly the same line?

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: Why symmetric? We just saw that a nonsymmetric matrix and its symmetric part give the very same quadratic form. So nothing forces us to pick the symmetric one. Why, then, do we agree to always represent a quadratic form q(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x by a symmetric matrix A? Think about uniqueness. Many matrices give the same form, but how many symmetric ones do? Choosing the symmetric representative gives each form a single, canonical matrix to call its own.

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: Ellipse or hyperbola? After rotating to good axes, one form became 6u^2+v^2 (an ellipse) while another became u^2-v^2 (a hyperbola). Looking only at the signs of the two squared coefficients, why does the level curve close up into an ellipse in one case but open out into a hyperbola in the other? Ask what values q can take. If both squared terms push the same way, can the sum ever stay bounded along a direction? Same signs versus opposite signs is the whole story.

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

text: What does positive definite say about the shape? Suppose q(\mathbf x)=\mathbf x^TA\mathbf x is positive definite. In plain words, what does that tell you about the shape of the graph z=q(x,y) near the origin, and what does it say about the origin itself? Positive definite means q(\mathbf x)>0 for every \mathbf x\neq\mathbf 0. So the origin is the only place the surface touches its lowest level. Picture which way every direction bends.

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

optional_markers.title: Preview: the Hessian matrix will classify critical points

text: Preview: the Hessian matrix will classify critical points Quadratic forms matter in calculus because a curved function often looks quadratic after its linear part disappears. Suppose a hiker stands at a point on a hill where the tangent plane is horizontal. There is no first-order uphill direction at that exact point. The next question is not Which way is the slope? The slope starts at zero. The next question is: \text{Does the surface bend up, bend down, or bend both ways?} That bending is measured by a quadratic form. Later, near a point (a,b), a function f(x,y) will have an approximation of the form f(a+h,b+k)\approx f(a,b)+\text{linear part}+\frac12\begin{pmatrix}h\amp k\end{pmatrix}H\begin{pmatrix}h\\k\end{pmatrix}. The matrix H=\begin{pmatrix}f_{xx}\amp f_{xy}\\f_{yx}\amp f_{yy}\end{pmatrix} is called the Hessian matrix. At a critical point, the linear part is zero. Then the Hessian's quadratic form becomes the first visible shape: The Hessian's sign pattern and the local shape at a critical point. Hessian type Local shape positive definite local minimum, like a bowl negative definite local maximum, like a dome indefinite saddle point degenerate the quadratic part is not enough This is only a preview. We do not yet have the derivative of a multivariable function. But the pattern is now visible: matrices describe the best linear part, and symmetric matrices describe the first curved part. The next step is to make the phrase best linear part precise. That phrase will become the multivariable derivative.

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

optional_markers.title: Linear approximation as a preview of the derivative

text: Why does zooming make a curve look straight? When we zoom in on a smooth graph near a point, it looks more and more like a straight line. Using the split H(4+h)-H(4)=2h-\frac12h^2, explain in your own words why the curved-looking piece fades from view faster than the straight piece as h shrinks. What is special about the size of h^2 compared with h when h is tiny? Compare the two terms at h=0.01: one is about 0.02, the other about 0.00005. Think about the ratio \frac{h^2}{h}=h and where it goes as h\to0.

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

optional_markers.title: Linear approximation as a preview of the derivative

text: Best, or merely linear? Many linear maps L can sit near a function and produce an error that goes to zero as \mathbf h\to\mathbf 0. Yet only one of them is called the derivative. What extra demand does best place on the error that ordinary smallness does not, and why does that demand single out a unique linear map? Re-read the phrase small compared with \|\mathbf h\|. For the map M(h)=7h on the zero function, the error has the same size as h, not smaller. Which comparison is the strict one?

chapter.title: Linear Functions, Linear Transformations, and Matrices

optional_markers.title: Linear approximation as a preview of the derivative

text: Why a matrix, and not a number? For a map F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m, the derivative at a point turns out to be a matrix rather than a single number. Thinking about what the derivative must do to a small input displacement (h,k), explain why one number could not carry enough information, and why an m\times n array is exactly the right size. The derivative is a linear map from \mathbb R^n to \mathbb R^m. How many numbers does it take to record where each of the n basic input directions lands in \mathbb R^m?

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: What does the motion add? The equation x^2+y^2=9 and the parametrization \mathbf r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t), 0\le t\le2\pi, describe the same circle. What does the parametrization capture about the ant's journey that the equation alone does not specify? Think about what changes as t increases: where the point begins, which way it heads, and how fast it sweeps around. Could a graph y=f(x) even represent a full circle?

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: What gets erased? Suppose you eliminate the parameter and arrive at a clean Cartesian equation such as y=x^2 or x^2+y^2=9. The equation is tidy, but something about the original moving point has been thrown away. What kind of information disappears when you trade \mathbf r(t) for an equation in x and y alone? An equation in x and y records which points belong to the curve. Does it remember the order in which they are visited, the starting point, the direction, or whether some points are passed more than once?

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Many clocks, one road? One curve can be described by many different parametrizations. Why is a single geometric shape able to support so many different rules \mathbf r(t), and what is the one thing all parametrizations of that curve must have in common? Two travelers can drive the same road using different speedometers and clocks. What do their trips necessarily agree on, and what are they free to choose differently?

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: What do the two numbers measure? In the polar pair (r,\theta), one number reports a length and the other reports a direction. Suppose a friend tells you only the angle \theta=\pi/6 but forgets to mention r. Have they pinned down a single point, or could they mean many different points? What does the missing number r contribute that the angle by itself cannot? Picture every point you could reach by walking outward from the origin along the direction \theta=\pi/6. The angle fixes the line of sight; ask yourself what is still free to change along that line.

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Why so many names for one point? Rectangular coordinates give each point exactly one address, yet a single point has infinitely many polar addresses. Where does this endless supply of names come from? And think about the pole itself: when r=0, why does every choice of \theta name the very same point? Turning the angle by a full revolution leaves a point unchanged. For the origin, ask what distance you travel once r=0 — does the direction you face still take you anywhere?

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Why are circles and spirals so simple here? A circle centered at the origin is the single equation r=3 in polar form, but becomes x^2+y^2=9 in rectangular form. A spiral is just r=\theta/4 in polar, yet has no tidy Cartesian formula at all. What is it about distance and angle that lets these curves be written so cleanly, when x and y struggle to keep up? Both a circle and a spiral are really statements about how far you are as the angle turns. Notice that polar coordinates measure exactly those two things directly, while x and y have to encode distance and direction together.

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Three kinds of level surface? In spherical coordinates, holding one coordinate fixed usually traces out a surface. Use \rho\gt0 and 0\lt\phi\lt\pi for the usual cases, and include the special plane at \phi=\pi/2. Without converting to rectangular coordinates, picture each of \rho=\text{const}, \phi=\text{const}, and \theta=\text{const}. What shape is each one, and why does fixing a distance behave so differently from fixing an angle? Read each coordinate's meaning out loud: \rho is distance from the origin, \phi is the angle down from the z-axis, and \theta is the angle around it. Let the words, not the formulas, suggest the surface.

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Pipe or ball? A long straight pipe and a solid ball each have round symmetry, yet we usually reach for cylindrical coordinates for the pipe and spherical coordinates for the ball. What is it about the shape of each object that makes one coordinate system speak more simply than the other? Ask what stays constant as you travel along each object. A pipe has a special axis; a ball has a special center. Which coordinate is held fixed by the surface in each case?

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Why isn't every little box the same? A spherical coordinate box with edges \Delta\rho, \Delta\phi, \Delta\theta uses the same three increments everywhere, yet the physical box it carves out is large in some places and tiny in others. Why does the same triple of increments not enclose the same amount of space everywhere? An angular increment sweeps out more length the farther you are from what you are turning around. Compare a step of \Delta\theta near the z-axis with one far from it, and observe that the radial edge stays \Delta\rho while the angular edges grow with their circle radii.

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Why do traces reveal the surface? For the given equation z=9-x^2-4y^2, describe the complete family of horizontal traces z=c. How does that family, together with the equation, identify a downward-opening elliptic paraboloid? Would a few isolated slices determine an arbitrary surface? Think about how each trace changes as you move the cutting plane. It is not one slice that identifies the surface. Here the formula describes every horizontal slice; a finite selection alone could miss changes between the selected planes.

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Level surface or graph? A graph z=g(x,y) and a level set f(x,y,z)=c describe sets in space in different ways. In z=g(x,y) one coordinate is singled out and expressed in terms of the other two; in f(x,y,z)=c all three coordinates appear on equal footing. How does this difference show up in the shapes each can describe, and why can a level surface represent something a graph cannot? Ask whether a vertical line can ever cross the surface more than once. A graph z=g(x,y) assigns exactly one height to each (x,y). Could a sphere, written as a level surface, ever be a graph of that kind?

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Equation versus motion A curve was described by motion: a single parameter t moves a point along, and you could ask how fast it travels. A surface, by contrast, is described by an equation that simply tests whether a point belongs. Why is it natural that a curve comes with a built-in sense of motion while a surface, given only by an equation like x^2+y^2+z^2=9, does not? Count the dimensions, or the degrees of freedom. A curve is one-dimensional, so one moving number can trace it out. How many independent numbers would you need to roam freely over a surface, and what does that suggest an equation alone is leaving out?

chapter.title: Curves, Coordinates, and Surfaces Before Calculus

text: Why two parameters? In the cylinder formula above, explain what changes when you vary only the angle, and what changes when you vary only the height. Why are two input numbers useful for specifying a point on this pipe? On the pipe you can change the angle and the height independently, so it takes two numbers to say where you are. How many independent ways can you move along a single curve?

Away from the seam, each point occurs once in the first domain and twice in the second.

text: Project: compare several parametrizations of a sphere For a>0, the sphere x^2+y^2+z^2=a^2 has many parametrizations. Compare the following three. 1. Spherical-coordinate parametrization \mathbf r_1(\theta,\phi) = (a\sin\phi\cos\theta,\, a\sin\phi\sin\theta,\, a\cos\phi), where 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi. 2. Upper and lower graph parametrizations The upper hemisphere is \mathbf r_2(u,v) = \left(u,v,\sqrt{a^2-u^2-v^2}\right), \qquad u^2+v^2\le a^2. The lower hemisphere is \mathbf r_3(u,v) = \left(u,v,-\sqrt{a^2-u^2-v^2}\right), \qquad u^2+v^2\le a^2. 3. Height-angle parametrization Use height z and angle \theta: \mathbf r_4(\theta,z) = \left( \sqrt{a^2-z^2}\cos\theta,\, \sqrt{a^2-z^2}\sin\theta,\, z \right), where 0\le\theta\le2\pi,\qquad -a\le z\le a. For each parametrization, answer: What is the parameter domain? Which parameter curves look like circles? Which parameter curves run from pole to pole? Where does the parametrization repeat points? Where does the parametrization collapse a whole edge or curve to one point? Which parametrization would you use to draw latitude and longitude? Which would you use to describe the sphere as two graphs? This project is not only about spheres. It teaches a larger lesson: a parametrization is a choice of coordinates on a surface, and different choices reveal different geometry.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why look at the pieces? Suppose a friend says, “If I understand each of the component functions x(t), y(t), and z(t) separately, then I understand the whole vector-valued function \mathbf r(t).” Why is that a reasonable thing to claim? What is it about how \mathbf r(t) is built that lets us study it one coordinate at a time? Look again at how \mathbf r(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)) is assembled. Knowing where the point is at time t means knowing each coordinate at that time, and nothing more.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why does the limit split apart? The theorem says \lim_{t\to a}\mathbf r(t) is just the vector whose entries are the limits of the components. Give an intuitive reason why this should be true. Why does asking the whole vector \mathbf r(t) to settle down to \mathbf L amount to asking every component to settle down on its own? Think about the distance \|\mathbf r(t)-\mathbf L\|. For that single distance to shrink to 0, what has to happen to each coordinate gap at once?

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: The map or the road? Two different functions \mathbf r_1(t) and \mathbf r_2(t) can have exactly the same image, yet we still treat them as different objects. In your own words, what does the function \mathbf r(t) know that the curve it traces does not? Give one piece of information carried by \mathbf r(t) that is invisible if you only look at the set of points. A curve is just a set of points sitting in space. The function also records a clock: when you arrive at each point, how fast you pass through, and how many times you return.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why does \mathbf r'(t) point along the path? Suppose \mathbf r'(t)\ne\mathbf0. The derivative is a limit of difference quotients \frac{\mathbf r(t+h)-\mathbf r(t)}{h}. Each numerator \mathbf r(t+h)-\mathbf r(t) is a displacement vector connecting two nearby points on the curve. As h\to 0^+, what happens to the direction of that displacement vector, and why does this explain that \mathbf r'(t) ends up pointing along the path rather than off in some other direction? Picture the two points \mathbf r(t) and \mathbf r(t+h) sliding toward each other as h shrinks. The chord between them is a secant of the curve; think about what a secant becomes in the limit. Dividing by the positive number h only rescales the vector, it does not turn it.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: What does the tangent vector's direction and length tell you? The tangent line at time a uses \mathbf r'(a) as its direction, so \mathbf r'(t) is tangent to the curve. Yet two motions can trace the very same curve while their velocity vectors differ in length, as the unit circle examples above showed. Explain in your own words why the direction of \mathbf r'(t) determines the tangent line to the curve, with its sign recording the chosen direction of travel, while the length \|\mathbf r'(t)\| is instead a feature of how the curve is being traced. Imagine driving along a fixed road. The road decides which way your car is pointing at each spot, but you choose how fast to go. Which of those two things is "direction" and which is "length"? Re-tracing the same circle twice as fast multiplies the velocity by a constant without rotating it.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: What does integrating velocity recover, and why a whole vector \mathbf C? When you integrate a velocity \mathbf v(t), the result is again a vector. In words, what quantity does this integral recover, and how does that meaning explain why the constant of integration must be a whole vector \mathbf C rather than a single number? Think about what kind of information you must supply to pin down the actual motion. Antidifferentiating each component leaves one unknown number per component, and there is a separate one in each coordinate direction. What single object do you get when you collect (C_1,C_2,C_3) together? Geometrically, knowing the velocity tells you the shape of the trip but not where it began.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Initial value problems for motion Often we know velocity or acceleration first, and we want position. A basketball is thrown across a gym. Let the x-axis point across the court, the y-axis point sideways, and the z-axis point upward. Suppose the ball starts at \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,1) meters and has initial velocity \mathbf v(0)=(8,3,10) meters per second. Ignore air resistance. Then acceleration is constant: \mathbf a(t)=(0,0,-9.8). Since \mathbf v'(t)=\mathbf a(t), we integrate acceleration: \mathbf v(t)=\int (0,0,-9.8)\,dt=(0,0,-9.8t)+\mathbf C. Use \mathbf v(0)=(8,3,10) to get \mathbf C=(8,3,10). Thus \mathbf v(t)=(8,3,10-9.8t). Now integrate velocity: \mathbf r(t)=\int (8,3,10-9.8t)\,dt=(8t,3t,10t-4.9t^2)+\mathbf D. Use \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,1) to get \mathbf D=(0,0,1). Therefore \boxed{\mathbf r(t)=(8t,\;3t,\;1+10t-4.9t^2).} The three coordinates tell three simpler stories: x(t)=8t, y(t)=3t, z(t)=1+10t-4.9t^2. The horizontal motion is linear. The vertical motion is the familiar falling-object parabola from single-variable calculus. Recovering position from velocity A small underwater robot has velocity \mathbf v(t)=(1+t,\;2,\;e^{-t}) and starts at \mathbf r(0)=(3,-1,0). Find \mathbf r(t). Since \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf v(t), we integrate: \mathbf r(t)=\left(t+\frac{t^2}{2},\;2t,\;-e^{-t}\right)+\mathbf C. Use the initial position: \mathbf r(0)=(0,0,-1)+\mathbf C=(3,-1,0). So \mathbf C=(3,-1,1). Therefore \boxed{\mathbf r(t)=\left(3+t+\frac{t^2}{2},\;-1+2t,\;1-e^{-t}\right).} This is an initial value problem. The derivative information gives a family of possible motions. The initial condition chooses the one motion that actually starts in the given place. Differentiation and integration now work for motion in space. But a subtle problem has appeared. The integral of velocity gives displacement, not distance traveled. A runner who completes one lap has \mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a)=\mathbf 0, but she certainly did not run zero meters. To measure distance traveled, we must add up tiny lengths \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. We return to this question in . First, the same curve derivatives let us revisit the surface grids from Chapter 4.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Choose an interior parameter pair (s_0,t_0), so that either parameter can vary a little in both directions. The two grid curves through P=\mathbf r(s_0,t_0) are \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=\mathbf r(s,t_0),\qquad \boldsymbol\beta(t)=\mathbf r(s_0,t). In the first curve t_0 is a constant; in the second s_0 is a constant. Their velocities at P are \boxed{\mathbf v=\boldsymbol\alpha'(s_0),\qquad \mathbf w=\boldsymbol\beta'(t_0).} A nonzero velocity is a tangent vector to its grid curve, based at P. The parameters need not measure physical time: velocity here means change of position per unit change of the parameter.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Freeze, differentiate, and compare For the bowl \mathbf r(s,t)=(s,t,s^2+t^2), write the two frozen-parameter grid curves through the parameter pair (1,-1). Find their velocities and a normal at the image point. Is the parametrization regular there? What happens to the normal if the two velocities are exchanged? In one curve set t=-1; in the other set s=1. Differentiate each curve in its remaining variable, then use the cross product. The curves are \boldsymbol\alpha(s)=(s,-1,s^2+1) and \boldsymbol\beta(t)=(1,t,1+t^2). At P=(1,-1,2) their velocities are (1,0,2) and (0,1,-2). Their cross product (-2,2,1) is nonzero, so the parameter point is regular and this vector is normal. Exchanging the velocities gives the opposite normal (2,-2,-1).

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why is the trip at least as long as the shortcut? Explain in your own words why the total distance traveled along a path is always at least as large as the magnitude of the displacement \|\mathbf r(b)-\mathbf r(a)\|. When are the two quantities equal? Think about the difference between the scalar integral \int_a^b\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt and the vector integral \int_a^b\mathbf r'(t)\,dt. The vector version lets backward steps cancel forward ones; the scalar version never does. What kind of path would have nothing to cancel?

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why does the clock not matter? When we sped up the clock so the same circle was traced over a shorter interval, the speed \|\mathbf r'\| grew but the arc length stayed 2\pi. Explain why changing how fast you traverse a curve never changes its length. Arc length is built from the product \|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt. A faster clock increases the speed but compresses the interval by the same factor. Picture walking and running along the same hallway: which one covers more floor?

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: What makes arc length the natural parameter? After reparametrizing a regular curve by arc length to get \mathbf R(s), what is its speed \|\mathbf R'(s)\|? Explain why that value is exactly what you should expect when the parameter s itself measures distance traveled. Speed is the rate at which distance is covered per unit of the parameter. If the parameter is distance, how much distance passes for each unit of s? You do not need to compute anything; reason from what s measures.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: What is curvature really measuring? In your own words, what does curvature \kappa measure about a curve? Using that description, explain why a straight line has curvature \kappa=0 no matter how fast a particle travels along it. Curvature watches the direction of \mathbf T, not its length, and it measures change per unit distance rather than per unit time. On a straight line, which way is \mathbf T pointing as you move along?

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why does \mathbf N point into the turn? The unit normal \mathbf N always points toward the inside of a turn, never toward the outside. Why should that be? Think about which way the tip of the unit tangent \mathbf T is being pulled as the curve bends. \mathbf N points in the direction of \mathbf T', the direction \mathbf T is changing. As you round a bend, the arrow \mathbf T swings toward the inside of the curve. Picture the circle \mathbf T' we computed: which way did it point relative to the center?

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why does acceleration split in two? Acceleration breaks neatly into a tangential part a_T\mathbf T and a normal part a_N\mathbf N. Explain conceptually why velocity can only change in these two ways, and which physical effect each part is responsible for. Velocity \mathbf r'=\sigma\mathbf T carries two pieces of information: a length \sigma (speed) and a direction \mathbf T. When you differentiate a product, what change in each factor does each resulting term record?

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why is the binormal perpendicular to the osculating plane? Explain why \mathbf B=\mathbf T\times\mathbf N is perpendicular to the osculating plane. Why does the order \mathbf T\times\mathbf N, rather than \mathbf N\times\mathbf T, matter? The osculating plane is spanned by \mathbf T and \mathbf N. Recall what the cross product does and how reversing its factors changes its sign.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Curvature versus torsion Curvature is always nonnegative, while torsion may be positive or negative. Explain what is different about the two definitions and what geometric information the sign of torsion records. Curvature is defined using a norm. Torsion is defined as a signed coefficient in d\mathbf B/ds=-\tau\mathbf N.

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why two pieces? In the boat example, the velocity has a radial part pointing away from the harbor and a transverse part pointing along a circle. Without computing anything, explain in words why two different motions of the boat are needed to account for its velocity. What does each piece describe about how the boat is moving? Picture holding the angle fixed and only letting r grow, then holding r fixed and only letting \theta grow. Where does the boat go in each case, and how could it ever move in just one of these ways alone?

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Constant speed, yet accelerating? A rider on the wheel moves at constant speed, so \omega never changes. Yet the acceleration -R\omega^2\mathbf e_r is not zero. How can something accelerate while its speed stays the same? What is actually changing from one instant to the next? Acceleration measures the change in the velocity vector, not just in the speed. Watch the direction of \mathbf e_\theta as the rider goes around: does the velocity vector ever stop turning?

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: Why equal areas? Under a central force the quantity r^2\theta' stays constant, so the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times. When the planet swings close to the sun and r shrinks, what must \theta' do to keep the swept-area rate \tfrac12 r^2\theta' unchanged? Use that to explain why a nearby planet races along and a distant one dawdles. Think of \tfrac12 r^2\theta' as a fixed budget. If r drops, the only way to keep the product the same is for \theta' to compensate. Which direction must it move?

chapter.title: Vector-Valued Functions and Motion

text: A complete review example Consider the helix \mathbf r(t)=(3\cos t,3\sin t,4t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. This is one turn around a cylinder of radius 3, rising 8\pi units in height. First, \mathbf r'(t)=(-3\sin t,3\cos t,4), so the speed is \|\mathbf r'(t)\|=\sqrt{9\sin^2t+9\cos^2t+16}=5. The length of one turn is L=\int_0^{2\pi}5\,dt=10\pi. The unit tangent vector is \mathbf T(t)=\frac15(-3\sin t,3\cos t,4). Since the speed is constant, the tangential acceleration is a_T=0. The acceleration is \mathbf r''(t)=(-3\cos t,-3\sin t,0). Its length is \|\mathbf r''(t)\|=3. Because the speed is constant, all acceleration is normal, so a_N=3. Now compute curvature: \mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)=(12\sin t,-12\cos t,9). Thus \|\mathbf r'(t)\times\mathbf r''(t)\|=\sqrt{144\sin^2t+144\cos^2t+81}=15. Therefore \kappa(t)=\frac{15}{5^3}=\frac{3}{25}. This agrees with a_N=\kappa\sigma^2, because \frac{3}{25}\cdot 25=3. The unit tangent is already in hand. The binormal is the unit vector in the direction of \mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'': \mathbf B(t) = \frac1{15}(12\sin t,-12\cos t,9) = \left(\frac45\sin t,-\frac45\cos t,\frac35\right). Then \mathbf N(t) = \mathbf B(t)\times\mathbf T(t) = (-\cos t,-\sin t,0). To obtain torsion, differentiate once more: \mathbf r'''(t)=(3\sin t,-3\cos t,0). The numerator of the torsion formula is (\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r'')\cdot\mathbf r'''=36, and the denominator is \|\mathbf r'\times\mathbf r''\|^2=225. Therefore \boxed{\tau=\frac{36}{225}=\frac4{25}.} This 3-4-5 helix has constant \kappa=\frac3{25},\qquad\tau=\frac4{25}. The same integers that made the speed equal to 5 now reappear in the curvature and torsion. The helix has constant speed, constant curvature, and constant torsion. It bends the same amount at every point, and it twists the same amount at every point.
