chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Scalar or vector? Two functions can both take a point of the plane as input, yet feel completely different. What single feature of the output tells you whether a function is a scalar field or a vector field, and why does it matter that the output of a vector field carries more than one number? Look at m in F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m. Ask what you would draw at a single point in each case: a temperature reading, or an arrow with a direction.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Why count the inputs? Suppose two friends both write down the rule z\mapsto z, but one is thinking of a function on the line and the other of a function on space. Why can the dimension of the domain change the meaning of a function just as much as the rule itself does? Think about how many independent variables you are free to vary, and what region the inputs sweep out. The same algebraic expression can live over a line, a plane, or all of space.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Why picture a field? A formula like \mathbf W(x,y)=(-y,x) already gives every value exactly. So why is it still useful to imagine the function as a whole field of values spread across its domain, rather than as one input-output computation at a time? A single value tells you about one point. A field lets you see how the values change from place to place, so patterns like swirling or flowing become visible at a glance.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Why does the graph need a third dimension? The domain of f(x,y) is a flat region in the plane, yet we draw its graph as a surface floating in three-dimensional space. Where does the extra dimension come from, and what does a single point (x,y,f(x,y)) of the graph record about the function? Two coordinates locate the input, but the output f(x,y) still has to go somewhere. Picture stacking that output as a height above the floor point (x,y).

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: How can a flat map hold a whole hill? A contour map is flat, yet its labels convey heights on a three-dimensional hill. Explain how. Why does a finite collection of contours leave some information between the curves undetermined? If neighboring contours have equal height increments, what does close spacing tell you about the average height change across them? Each curve carries a label c, so a height is attached to it even though the drawing is flat. Now think about moving across two nearby labels: if the labels differ by a lot but the curves are only a tiny distance apart, how fast must the height be changing?

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Reading steepness and shape from contours? You are handed a contour map you have never seen before, with no formula attached. Using both the labels and the spacing, how would you estimate where height changes most rapidly across neighboring contours? What happens to the function value if you travel along one level curve? Compare the change in labeled height with the distance between contours. Along a single contour the height is constant; the shape of one contour alone does not determine rates across it.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: How many ways in? In single-variable calculus, checking a limit means looking from just two sides: the left and the right. As a point (x,y) approaches (0,0) in the plane, how many genuinely different ways can it approach? Why does this make a two-variable limit harder to confirm than a one-variable limit? Picture every line, curve, spiral, and wandering path that ends at the point. On a line you have only two directions; in the plane you have a whole circle of directions, and curved paths beyond those. Think about how many of these the function must satisfy at once.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Why is disproving easier than proving? Finding two paths that approach (a,b) with different limiting values settles the matter: the limit does not exist. Yet finding two paths that agree tells us almost nothing about whether the limit exists. Why is there this asymmetry between the two situations? A limit must equal the same number along every approach. To break that, one conflict is enough. To confirm it, no finite collection of agreeing paths can speak for all the infinitely many paths you did not test — an untested path might still disagree.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: What does \varepsilon-\delta demand? Checking a few paths, or even infinitely many along one family, can never list every possible approach. What does the \varepsilon-\delta definition require that path-checking cannot guarantee? In particular, think about what the single number \delta must control. The condition 0\lt\|\mathbf x-\mathbf a\|\lt\delta describes a whole punctured disk around \mathbf a, not a curve. So one \delta must force \|F(\mathbf x)-\mathbf L\|\lt\varepsilon for all points in that disk at once — every path through it included.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: What does continuity really say? In your own words, what does it mean intuitively for a function f(x,y) to be continuous at a point \mathbf a? Try to describe it without writing the limit equation, using everyday language about nearby inputs and nearby outputs. Picture wiggling the input a tiny bit. If the output is only allowed to wiggle a tiny bit too, with no sudden jumps and no holes, what does that tell you about how nearby inputs and nearby outputs are related?

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Why does continuity survive composition? Suppose F is continuous and G is continuous. Explain, intuitively, why feeding the output of F into G should produce a continuous function G\circ F. What do you think could go wrong if one of the two pieces had a jump? Trace a small change in the input through both stages. The first function turns a small nudge into a small nudge; then think about what the second function does to that already small nudge. Where in this chain would a jump sneak in?

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Why both closed and bounded? A continuous function on a closed and bounded region is guaranteed to attain a maximum and a minimum. Intuitively, why are both words needed? Describe what can go wrong if the region is bounded but not closed, and separately what can go wrong if it is closed but not bounded. Think about a value the function keeps approaching but never reaches. Dropping closed lets the region leave out the very edge point where the best value would live; dropping bounded lets the region run off to infinity so the values never settle. Which missing word causes which kind of escape?

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Why aren't lines enough? Suppose you check every straight-line approach to a point and they all give the same value. Why isn't this enough to guarantee that the two-variable limit exists? What is it about approaching a point in the plane that straight lines simply cannot capture? Think about how many roads lead to the origin. Lines are not the only ones. Recall the parabola y=x^2 in the example above, and ask what other shapes a path could take.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Why isn't separate continuity enough? Being continuous in x alone and continuous in y alone only tests the function along horizontal and vertical lines through a point. Why doesn't passing both of these tests guarantee that the function is continuous as a function of both variables together? The two separate tests only walk you in along the coordinate directions. Picture all the other directions and curves you could slide in along, such as y=x, and ask whether the function has to agree with them too.

chapter.title: Functions of Several Variables, Limits, and Continuity

text: Can you trust the picture? A plotted graph or contour map near the origin can make it look as though M(x,y) settles down to a single value. Why can a picture fool you here, and when a drawing and a careful calculation seem to disagree about a limit, which one should you trust? A feature as thin as the strip 0\lt y\lt x^4 can be far too narrow to see at ordinary scale. Ask yourself what a finite-resolution picture can never show, and which tool gives an exact answer.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Why does a slice work? When we hold y fixed and let only x move, the surface z=H(x,y) becomes a single curve. Why does measuring the slope of that one curve with an ordinary one-variable derivative give us exactly the partial derivative we want, and what role does fixing y play in making this work? Think about what the graph looks like once y is frozen. You are walking along a single trail carved through the hillside, not wandering the whole surface.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: What does f_x freeze? When you compute f_x, which variable is held fixed, and which one is allowed to change? Explain why this makes f_x a rate of change in just one direction, rather than a measure of how f changes overall. Look back at the limit defining f_x(a,b): notice which input is nudged by h and which input never moves at all.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Why no diagonal slope? The two partials f_x and f_y report only the east and north slopes. Why is it that knowing these two numbers does not, by itself, tell you the slope you would feel walking in a diagonal direction such as northeast? A diagonal step changes x and y at the same time. The example above shows a surface whose coordinate slopes are both 0, yet which is far from flat along the line y=x.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Why does one dot product capture every direction? Assume the partial derivatives exist near \mathbf p and are continuous there. The gradient stores only the two coordinate slopes f_x(\mathbf p) and f_y(\mathbf p), yet the formula D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=\nabla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf u recovers the slope in every direction \mathbf u. Why should two numbers be enough to determine the rate of change along infinitely many directions? Write a unit direction as \mathbf u=u_1\mathbf i+u_2\mathbf j and think about how a small step t\mathbf u splits into an x-step and a y-step. What does continuity of the partials let you say about combining those two coordinate changes?

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text:
Why the gradient, and why its length? The steepest uphill direction turns out to be the gradient's own direction, and the steepest rate equals \|
abla f(\mathbf p)\|. Using D_{\mathbf u}f(\mathbf p)=
abla f(\mathbf p)\cdot\mathbf u, explain why pointing \mathbf u any other way can only give a smaller rate. Rewrite the dot product as \|
abla f(\mathbf p)\|\cos	heta, where 	heta is the angle between \mathbf u and the gradient. Which value of 	heta makes \cos	heta as large as it can be?

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Why does the gradient cut straight across a contour? Under the smoothness and nonzero-gradient assumptions just stated, walking along a level curve keeps the value of f constant, so the rate of change along the curve is 0. Explain why this single fact forces the gradient to be perpendicular to the level curve, rather than tilted at some other angle to it. If \mathbf t is a unit tangent to the level curve, then \nabla f\cdot\mathbf t=0. What does a zero dot product say about the angle between two nonzero vectors?

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Two slopes, not enough? Suppose you stand at a point and you know both partial derivatives f_x and f_y exist there. Why does that still not guarantee the function is differentiable? Think about which displacements those two numbers actually report on, and which ones they say nothing about. A partial derivative only watches the function along a single coordinate line. A small step like (\Delta x,\Delta y) with both parts nonzero travels along none of those lines.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: What does the limit buy you? The total derivative needs more than the partial derivatives merely existing. In the definition, what is the extra demand placed on the error R(\Delta x,\Delta y), and why is it stronger than just asking that R\to 0? Look at what R is divided by before the limit is taken. The error must shrink faster than the step length \sqrt{(\Delta x)^2+(\Delta y)^2}, and it must do so for every direction of approach at once.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Why a whole plane? The two partial derivatives already give you a slope going east and a slope going north. Why does differentiability promise something more, namely a single genuine tangent plane rather than just two tangent lines crossing at the point? Two tangent lines fix the plane's tilt, but a plane also has to approximate the surface along every direction in between. Differentiability is exactly the condition that makes one plane do that job for all small displacements at once.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: A number or a function? We could have defined df_{\mathbf p} as the single number 34 we got from the bakery, the predicted cost change for one particular move. Instead we kept it as the whole linear function df_{\mathbf p}(\Delta u,\Delta v)=4\Delta u+6\Delta v. Why is the function the better object? What would we lose if we collapsed df_{\mathbf p} down to a tiny number? A single number answers one question; a function answers infinitely many at once. Ask yourself what changes (and what stays the same) if the bakery picks a different step (\Delta u,\Delta v).

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: When does \Delta f\approx df hold up? In the line f(\mathbf p+\Delta\mathbf x)-f(\mathbf p)=df_{\mathbf p}(\Delta\mathbf x)+R(\Delta\mathbf x), the remainder satisfies |R|/\|\Delta\mathbf x\|\to0. Explain in your own words why this makes df a good estimate for a small step. Then describe a situation where you should not trust \Delta f\approx df, even though the formula is still technically true. The condition only says R shrinks faster than \|\Delta\mathbf x\| as the step goes to zero, it promises nothing for a large step. Think about the leftover 0.12 and 0.000194 terms in the worked examples, and what happens to them when the step is no longer small.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: What does df eat, and what does it return? People often call a 1-form like df a machine: feed it a direction (a small displacement) at a point and it hands back a single number. Using df_{(2,1)}=2\,dx-2\,dy as your example, say in plain words what you must supply to the machine and what it gives you back. In what sense is df therefore a different kind of object than the function f itself? The function f eats a point and returns a value; df at a point eats a direction and returns a rate of change. Notice that dx and dy are themselves such machines, they just read off one component of the displacement you feed in.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Why a whole matrix? A map F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m sends inputs to outputs, yet its derivative turns out to be a whole m\times n matrix of partial derivatives rather than a single number. Where do the m rows and the n columns come from? What is each partial derivative \partial F_i/\partial x_j actually keeping track of? Think about what you must specify to predict an output change: there are m separate output components to track, and each one can respond to a nudge in any of the n input directions.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: What does the Jacobian see? The local linearization says F(\mathbf p+\mathbf h)\approx F(\mathbf p)+J_F(\mathbf p)\mathbf h. In plain words, what is the Jacobian matrix J_F(\mathbf p) telling you about how the map behaves in a tiny neighborhood of \mathbf p? What kind of map does F look like up close, and why does the curving part of F not appear in this picture? Imagine zooming in on \mathbf p until the bending of F is too small to notice. What is left of the map is captured entirely by J_F(\mathbf p) acting on the displacement \mathbf h.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: What does the determinant measure? When F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n is differentiable at \mathbf p, the number \det J_F(\mathbf p) appears. What does this single number tell you about how the map treats a tiny region near \mathbf p? And what extra information is carried by its sign that its size alone does not? A tiny square or cube near \mathbf p gets pushed to a tiny parallelogram or parallelepiped. Think about how its area or volume changes, and about whether the map flips the region over or keeps its orientation.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Sufficient or necessary? The continuous-partials test is a sufficient condition for differentiability, not a necessary one. In your own words, what is the difference between a sufficient condition and a necessary condition, and why does that distinction matter when you fail the test? If a function's partial derivatives turn out not to be continuous at a point, what may you conclude about differentiability there? A sufficient condition is enough to guarantee the conclusion; a necessary condition is one the conclusion cannot do without. Try filling in the implication arrow: \text{continuous partials} \Rightarrow \text{differentiable}. Does the arrow run the other way too? Think about what the x^2\sin(1/x) example just showed you.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Both partials exist, yet no derivative? For this G, both partial derivatives exist at the origin, yet the function is not differentiable there. How can that happen? What does each partial derivative actually measure, and what does it miss? Explain why knowing the behavior along the two coordinate axes is not enough to pin down the behavior in every direction at once. A partial derivative only watches the function along one coordinate slice, where the other variable is held fixed. Differentiability is a stronger demand: a single linear map must approximate the change for every small displacement. Look at what the diagonal path y=x did that the axes could not see.

chapter.title: Partial Derivatives, Differentials, and the Jacobian Matrix

text: Why might the plane not be tangent? The plane z=0 is built from the partial derivatives G_x(0,0)=0 and G_y(0,0)=0, and it hugs the graph perfectly along both coordinate axes. Yet it is not a genuine tangent plane. Why can a plane assembled from the partials fail to be tangent to the surface? What would a true tangent plane have to do that this one does not? The partials only certify the fit along two special directions. A true tangent plane must match the surface to first order in all directions. Ask yourself how the graph behaves along the diagonal y=x: does the plane z=0 still cling to the surface there, or does the surface peel away with a nonzero slope?

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Why a sum? The chain rule for f(x(t),y(t)) adds two pieces: f_x\,x'(t) and f_y\,y'(t). Why should we add the contribution from the changing x and the contribution from the changing y, rather than, say, multiply them or keep only the larger one? Picture a single small time step dt. It nudges both coordinates at once, and each nudge moves the value of f a little. Think about how the differential dz=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy accumulates those independent nudges into one total change.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: One dot product, two slopes? The two-variable chain rule has two separate terms, f_x\,x'(t)+f_y\,y'(t), yet the gradient form collapses them into the single dot product \nabla f\cdot\mathbf r'(t). What feature of the dot product lets it carry exactly the same information as that sum of products? Write out \nabla f=(f_x,f_y) and \mathbf r'(t)=(x'(t),y'(t)) and recall how a dot product is defined component by component. The collapse is really just a name for a pattern you already know.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Shape, or motion? A moving observer's measured rate \nabla f(\mathbf r(t))\cdot\mathbf r'(t) depends on both the field's gradient and the observer's velocity. Could the observer report a rate of zero even while standing in a region where the field genuinely varies from point to point? What about the reverse? The dot product vanishes when the two vectors are perpendicular. Think about what direction the observer would have to travel relative to the gradient, and connect that to the level-curve idea just above.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Why does composing maps become matrix multiplication? The chain rule says linearize each map, then compose the linearizations. Each linearization is a linear map, recorded as a Jacobian matrix. Explain why composing the two linear maps shows up as the matrix product J_F\,J_G rather than a sum, and why the outer Jacobian J_F must sit on the left of the inner Jacobian J_G. Think about what happens to a displacement step by step: it passes through J_G first, and the result of that step is what J_F acts on next. Which matrix touches the displacement first, and where does the matrix that acts last have to be written so the sizes line up?

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: What does the dependency tree tell you to add? Look at the dependency diagram for w. Without computing anything, explain how you read off the formula for w_u directly from the picture: which features of the diagram become the individual products, and which feature tells you that you must add those products together rather than keep them separate. Trace every route that leads from u all the way to w. Each arrow you walk along carries one derivative. Ask yourself: what does a single complete path contribute, and why do several paths from the same input get summed?

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Why may you replace each map by its linear part? To track a small displacement through F\circ G, we replace G by its best linear approximation, replace F by its best linear approximation, and then compose those two linear pieces. Explain why this swap does not corrupt the answer: why are the leftover, nonlinear errors safe to ignore when we only care about the first-order behavior at the point? Recall what best linear approximation guarantees about the size of the error: it shrinks faster than \|\Delta\mathbf u\| itself. Track an error from the inner map as it is carried through the outer map, and ask whether it stays smaller than first order in the original displacement.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Why so mechanical? When you change variables, the differential of a function substitutes almost without thinking: replace each old differential by its formula in the new variables, and you are done. Why does this work so cleanly? What property of linear maps is doing the quiet labor that makes substitution feel mechanical rather than miraculous? The symbol d keeps only the linear part of a change. Ask yourself what happens when you compose two linear maps, and whether their coordinate descriptions combine in the same way the symbols dx and dy seem to.

optional_markers.title: Pullback preview: moving formulas to parameter space

text: Pullback preview: moving formulas to parameter space A 1-form in the plane has the shape \omega=P(x,y)\,dx+Q(x,y)\,dy. A parametrization or coordinate change G(u,v)=(x(u,v),y(u,v)) moves this form to the (u,v)-plane by substituting: \boxed{ G^*\omega = P(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,d(x(u,v)) + Q(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,d(y(u,v)). } This new 1-form G^*\omega is called the pullback of \omega by G. The name sounds abstract, but the action is concrete: replace x,y,dx,dy by their expressions in the new variables. Which way does it travel? The map G sends points from the (u,v)-plane forward into the (x,y)-plane. Yet the operation G^* takes a form living in the (x,y)-plane and produces one in the (u,v)-plane — it travels the opposite way. What does it really mean to pull back a differential through G, and why does a form move against the direction of the map while points move along it? A 1-form is something you feed a displacement to and get a number. If you want to measure a displacement in (u,v), first push it forward with G into (x,y), then let the original form read it. Trace which space each arrow starts and ends in. Pulling the swirl form into polar coordinates Consider the swirling 1-form \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy. Use the polar coordinate map G(r,\theta)=(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta). Then x=r\cos\theta, \qquad y=r\sin\theta. Also, dx=\cos\theta\,dr-r\sin\theta\,d\theta, and dy=\sin\theta\,dr+r\cos\theta\,d\theta. Substitute into \omega: G^*\omega \amp= -r\sin\theta(\cos\theta\,dr-r\sin\theta\,d\theta) + r\cos\theta(\sin\theta\,dr+r\cos\theta\,d\theta) \amp= (-r\sin\theta\cos\theta+r\cos\theta\sin\theta)\,dr \amp\qquad + r^2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)\,d\theta \amp= r^2\,d\theta. So \boxed{ G^*(-y\,dx+x\,dy)=r^2\,d\theta. } The trigonometry disappeared. In polar coordinates, the swirl form simply measures angular motion, weighted by r^2. This is the first real glimpse of why differential forms fit coordinate changes so well. They are built to be substituted into.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Power in hiding? The statement d(f\circ G)=G^*(df) never mentions x, y, u, or v. It might seem that naming the coordinates would only make things clearer. Why is differential notation actually more powerful because it hides the coordinate names, rather than in spite of it? Think about what stays the same when you switch from one coordinate grid to another — Cartesian, polar, or some slanted grid. A statement that never commits to particular names is a statement that survives every such change unaltered. What does that buy you when you later integrate over curves and surfaces?

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Why isn't the polar gradient just (F_r,F_\theta)? When you compute a gradient in rectangular coordinates, you simply stack the partials: \nabla f = (f_x,f_y). So why can't you do the same in polar coordinates and write \nabla f = (F_r,F_\theta)? What goes wrong if you treat the angular partial F_\theta on equal footing with the radial partial F_r? Ask yourself what each partial measures: a change per unit of which quantity? A step dr and a step d\theta do not cover the same physical length on the ground.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Why does the Jacobian scale area? The determinant of the derivative matrix is r, the factor that gives the first-order area prediction for a small polar rectangle. Why should a determinant of partial derivatives have anything to do with how much area or volume gets stretched? What is it about a determinant that makes it the right measure of local size change? Think about what a determinant does for a plain linear map: it reports how it scales the area of a unit square. Near a point, the coordinate change looks like such a linear map.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Why do the coordinates break at the origin and poles? The functions x=r\cos\theta and y=r\sin\theta are perfectly smooth everywhere, so nothing in the formulas looks broken. Why, then, do polar coordinates fail at the origin, and spherical coordinates fail along the z-axis where \sin\phi=0? What is it about those special points that makes an angle stop carrying information? Try to recover a point from its coordinates. At r=0, how many different values of \theta name the same spot? A working coordinate system should label each point just once.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Why an inverse matrix, not a reciprocal? In one variable, the inverse rule turns f'(a) into the reciprocal 1/f'(a). In several variables, the derivative of G=F^{-1} is the inverse matrix \bigl(DF(\mathbf p)\bigr)^{-1}, not some matrix of reciprocals. Why must it be the matrix inverse? Differentiate G(F(\mathbf x))=\mathbf x and read off what the chain rule says DG times DF has to equal. Which matrix undoes another matrix?

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Local guarantee, global gap? A nonzero Jacobian determinant at \mathbf p promises a local inverse near \mathbf p, yet it says nothing about a single inverse on the whole domain. Why does the same hypothesis give you reversibility up close but not everywhere? The determinant lives at one point and controls only a small neighborhood. Picture the log-polar map: locally tidy, yet F(u,v+2\pi)=F(u,v) reuses outputs far apart. What can a purely local condition never see?

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: What collapses at a zero? Where \det J_F=0, the best linear approximation is not invertible. Geometrically, what is the linear part doing to a tiny patch around that point, and why does that make recovering the inputs from the outputs hopeless to first order? A singular matrix sends some nonzero direction to \mathbf 0, so a little patch gets squashed onto something lower-dimensional. If two directions land on top of each other, can the output still remember which input it came from?

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Slope without solving? We never solved F(x,y)=0 for y as a formula, yet we obtained dy/dx=-F_x/F_y. What fact about the curve lets us differentiate F(x,g(x))=0 and read off the slope, even though we have no explicit expression for g(x)? You do not need the formula for g, only the promise that some differentiable g exists nearby. Think about what the chain rule does to the identity F(x,g(x))=0 when you treat g(x) as an unknown but differentiable quantity.

Why does F_y
e0 matter? Under its continuity hypotheses, the theorem guarantees a solution of F(x,y)=0 for y near a point whenever \partial F/\partial y
e0 there. Geometrically, what does F_y
e0 say about how the curve sits relative to the vertical direction, and why is that the condition that guarantees one nearby y-value above each x? text: What breaks at a bad point? Failure of a hypothesis removes the guarantee. At (3,0) on the oval, or at the crossing of y^2=x^2, describe what you would see if you tried to read off y as a single function of x near that point. Why can no graph y=g(x) capture the curve there? Hover just to one side of the bad point and count how many y-values sit above a single x. A function is allowed only one output per input. A vertical tangent and a crossing each violate that count in their own way.

text:
Worked review example: a moving thermometer Let S(x,y,z)=12+xz-y^2 be a salinity field in a tank. A probe moves along \mathbf r(t)=(1+t,\;2-t^2,\;3e^t). Find the rate of change of salinity seen by the probe at t=0. The probe starts at \mathbf r(0)=(1,2,3). Its velocity is \mathbf r'(t)=(1,-2t,3e^t), so \mathbf r'(0)=(1,0,3). The gradient of S is 
abla S(x,y,z)=(z,-2y,x). At the starting point, 
abla S(1,2,3)=(3,-4,1). Therefore  rac{d}{dt}S(\mathbf r(t)) igg|_{t=0} \amp= 
abla S(1,2,3)\cdot\mathbf r'(0) \amp= (3,-4,1)\cdot(1,0,3) \amp= 6. The probe sees salinity increasing at rate 6 salinity units per second. The calculation can also be read as dS_{\mathbf r(0)} igl(\mathbf r'(0) igr)=6. The differential dS eats the velocity vector and returns the observed rate.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Worked review example: a matrix chain rule calculation Let G(u,v)=(u^2+v,\;e^u-v), and let F(x,y)=(xy,\;x+y^2). Set H=F\circ G. Find J_H(0,1) without expanding H. First compute the intermediate point: G(0,1)=(1,0). The Jacobian matrix of G is J_G(u,v)=\begin{pmatrix} 2u \amp 1\\ e^u \amp -1 \end{pmatrix}, so J_G(0,1)=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \amp 1\\ 1 \amp -1 \end{pmatrix}. The Jacobian matrix of F is J_F(x,y)=\begin{pmatrix} y \amp x\\ 1 \amp 2y \end{pmatrix}. At (x,y)=(1,0), J_F(1,0)=\begin{pmatrix} 0 \amp 1\\ 1 \amp 0 \end{pmatrix}. Therefore J_H(0,1) \amp= J_F(G(0,1))J_G(0,1) \amp= \begin{pmatrix} 0 \amp 1\\ 1 \amp 0 \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} 0 \amp 1\\ 1 \amp -1 \end{pmatrix} \amp= \begin{pmatrix} 1 \amp -1\\ 0 \amp 1 \end{pmatrix}. The order matters. A small (u,v)-change first passes through G, and only then through F. That is why the matrix for G stands on the right.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Worked review example: area scaling from differentials Let a coordinate change be given by x=s^2-t,\qquad y=s+t^2. Find the local signed area factor. Differentiate: dx=2s\,ds-dt, and dy=ds+2t\,dt. Then dx\wedge dy \amp= (2s\,ds-dt)\wedge(ds+2t\,dt) \amp= 4st\,ds\wedge dt-dt\wedge ds \amp= 4st\,ds\wedge dt+ds\wedge dt \amp= (4st+1)\,ds\wedge dt. Thus \boxed{\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(s,t)}=4st+1.} At points where 4st+1\ne0, the coordinate change does not collapse tiny areas. The inverse function theorem says that the map has a local inverse there. At points where 4st+1=0, tiny signed area is collapsed to first order. The theorem no longer promises a local inverse. The same number comes from the determinant: \det\begin{pmatrix} x_s \amp x_t\\ y_s \amp y_t \end{pmatrix}=\det\begin{pmatrix} 2s \amp -1\\ 1 \amp 2t \end{pmatrix}=4st+1.

chapter.title: The Chain Rule, Coordinate Changes, and Implicit Functions

text: Worked review example: an implicit surface Consider the surface F(x,y,z)=x^2+yz+z^2-3=0. The point (1,1,1) lies on the surface because 1+1+1-3=0. Can the surface be solved near this point as z=g(x,y)? If so, find g_x(1,1), g_y(1,1), and the tangent plane. Compute F_x=2x,\qquad F_y=z,\qquad F_z=y+2z. At (1,1,1), F_z(1,1,1)=3\ne0. So the implicit function theorem says that the surface can be solved locally as z=g(x,y). The partial derivatives are g_x=-\frac{F_x}{F_z},\qquad g_y=-\frac{F_y}{F_z}. Therefore g_x(1,1)=-\frac23,\qquad g_y(1,1)=-\frac13. The tangent plane is F_x(1,1,1)(x-1)+F_y(1,1,1)(y-1)+F_z(1,1,1)(z-1)=0. So \boxed{2(x-1)+(y-1)+3(z-1)=0.} The same answer comes from dF=0. At the point, dF=2\,dx+dy+3\,dz. A first-order motion tangent to the surface must satisfy 2\,dx+dy+3\,dz=0.

text:
Why perpendicular? A curve that stays on the level set f(x,y)=c never lets f change as you travel along it. Use that single fact to explain, in your own words, why 
abla f(\mathbf p) must be perpendicular to the level curve at a point \mathbf p (where 
abla f(\mathbf p)
e\mathbf 0). Walking along the curve means the directional derivative in the tangent direction is zero. What does 
abla f(\mathbf p)\cdot \mathbf r'(t)=0 say about the angle between those two vectors?

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: From normal to plane? Many different curves can pass through a point \mathbf p on the level surface F(x,y,z)=c, yet \nabla F(\mathbf p) is perpendicular to every one of their tangent directions at once. Why does that force \nabla F(\mathbf p) to be a normal vector to the whole surface, and how does knowing one normal vector hand you the tangent plane? All those tangent directions sweep out a single plane through \mathbf p. A plane is pinned down by one point and one normal vector. Picture the gradient as the spoke that sticks straight out of that plane.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text:
Right-angle crossings? A path of steepest ascent moves along 
abla f, and steepest descent moves along -
abla f. Explain why both kinds of path cross the contour lines at right angles, and why that makes intuitive sense for the path of fastest possible climb or descent. Each contour's tangent direction is perpendicular to 
abla f. If your velocity is parallel to 
abla f (or -
abla f), how can it sit relative to that tangent direction? Sliding any bit along a contour would waste effort on motion that does not change height.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why isn't a zero gradient enough? We just saw a point where \nabla f=\mathbf 0 that is neither a maximum nor a minimum. In your own words, why does \nabla f=\mathbf 0 fail to guarantee an extremum, and what feature of a saddle point makes it different from a peak or a valley? Walk away from the point in two different directions. At a saddle, what happens to the value of f along one direction compared with the other?

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why does the gradient vanish at an interior peak? Suppose f has a local maximum or local minimum at an interior point \mathbf p, and all its first partial derivatives exist there. Why must \nabla f(\mathbf p)=\mathbf 0? Try to explain it in terms of one-variable slices through \mathbf p. Freeze every variable but one. What kind of point does the resulting single-variable slice have at \mathbf p, and what did Fermat's theorem say about its derivative there?

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why examine the boundary on its own? The condition \nabla f=\mathbf 0 found no candidates here, yet the maximum is real and sits on the boundary. Why can a maximum or minimum live at a boundary point even when \nabla f is never zero, so that boundary points must be examined separately from interior critical points? Fermat's theorem needs the point to be interior, so that motion is allowed in every direction. At a boundary point, which directions are no longer available to you?

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why is the Hessian symmetric? The Hessian places f_{xy} in the top-right corner and f_{yx} in the bottom-left corner. Explain why the equality f_{xy}=f_{yx} is exactly the statement that the matrix equals its own reflection across the main diagonal — that is, why equal mixed partials force the Hessian to be symmetric. A matrix is symmetric when the entry in row i, column j matches the entry in row j, column i. Which two entries of the Hessian are the mixed partials, and where do they sit?

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: What does the Hessian see? At a critical point the gradient is zero, so the gradient alone cannot tell a peak from a valley from a saddle. What information about the shape of the surface does the Hessian carry that the gradient cannot? Describe, in your own words, the kind of geometric behavior the second partials are recording. The gradient measures slope — how fast f is rising. The second partials measure how that slope itself is changing. Think about bending or curvature rather than steepness.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why the Hessian is the quadratic term Compare the one-variable Taylor term \frac12 f''(a)h^2 with the two-variable quadratic correction \frac12\begin{pmatrix}u\amp v\end{pmatrix}H_f(a,b)\begin{pmatrix}u\\v\end{pmatrix}. Explain why the Hessian plays the role of f'' here — that is, why this matrix product is exactly the second-order piece of the local model of f. Multiply out the matrix product. Which second partials appear, and how do the factors of u and v match the powers u^2, uv, and v^2 you would expect in a quadratic?

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why the quadratic part decides Near a critical point the change f(\mathbf p+\mathbf u)-f(\mathbf p) is governed by the quadratic part \tfrac12\mathbf u^T H\mathbf u. Why should the sign behavior of this quadratic part settle whether the point is a maximum, a minimum, or a saddle? Think about what it would mean for the quadratic part to be positive in every nonzero direction, versus negative in every direction, versus positive in some directions and negative in others. A local minimum means the function goes up no matter which way you step away from \mathbf p; a saddle means you can find a direction that goes up and another that goes down. Match those phrases to the signs the quadratic part can take.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Reading \Delta together with f_{xx} Suppose you already know that \Delta = AC - B^2 \gt 0 at a critical point. What more does the sign of A = f_{xx} tell you, and why is one number not enough on its own? Try to say in words what \Delta\gt 0 rules out, and then what the sign of f_{xx} picks between. Look back at the completed square A\left(u+\tfrac{B}{A}v\right)^2+\tfrac{\Delta}{A}v^2. With \Delta\gt 0 both terms share the sign of A. So \Delta\gt 0 tells you the form is definite, and A tells you which way it is definite.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why \Delta=0 leaves the question open The two examples x^4+y^4 and x^4-y^4 share the very same zero Hessian, yet one gives a minimum and the other a saddle. Use this to explain why the test must fall silent exactly when \Delta = 0. What information has the quadratic part lost in that case, and where does the deciding behavior now hide? When \Delta=0 the quadratic part is flat in at least one direction, so it no longer reports a definite sign. The behavior is then decided by the first higher-order terms that the Hessian never sees.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why parallel, not just perpendicular? At a constrained maximum or minimum on a smooth curve, why must \nabla f be parallel to \nabla g? Try to say it in terms of the tangent direction the constraint allows, rather than by quoting the formula. Both gradients are perpendicular to the same allowed tangent direction. In the plane that tangent line is one-dimensional, so how much freedom is left for a vector forced to be perpendicular to it?

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why a compact set guarantees a winner A continuous function on a closed and bounded constraint set is guaranteed to attain its maximum and minimum. Why does that guarantee let us simply compare the values of f at our finite list of candidate points and trust the largest and smallest we find? If an extreme value is certain to occur somewhere on the set, and every place it could occur is already on your candidate list, what could possibly be hiding between the candidates?

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: What is \lambda really telling you? Beyond being a number that makes \nabla f=\lambda\nabla g work, what does the Lagrange multiplier \lambda actually measure about the constrained problem? Think of the constraint level c as a dial you could turn. How does \lambda relate to the rate at which the best value of f responds when you nudge that dial?

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Why does \nabla f=\mathbf 0 not settle the question? At a critical point we have \nabla f=\mathbf 0, yet the point may be neither a maximum nor a minimum. In your own words, why can a vanishing gradient fail to tell a peak from a valley from a saddle? A zero gradient only reports that f is flat to first order. Think about what the two axes do in f(x,y)=x^2-y^2: along one direction the value rises, along another it falls.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Find the maximum and minimum of f(x,y)=x on the line segment -1\le x\le1,\qquad y=0. The smooth constraint is g(x,y)=y=0. Then \nabla f=(1,0),\qquad \nabla g=(0,1). The multiplier equation would be (1,0)=\lambda(0,1), which has no solution.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Where can Lagrange multipliers look the other way? The Lagrange-multiplier method can miss extrema that occur at endpoints or corners of a constraint. What assumption about the constraint does the method quietly rely on, and why does that assumption break down exactly at an endpoint or a corner? The multiplier equation \nabla f=\lambda\nabla g compares directions, so it needs a well-defined tangent direction along the constraint. Ask yourself whether such a direction exists where the allowed set simply stops.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: What has failed when f_{xy}\ne f_{yx}? Suppose at some point a function satisfies f_{xy}\ne f_{yx}. Which hypothesis of the mixed-partials theorem must have failed there, and what does its failure say about how trustworthy the order of differentiation is at that point? The theorem does not just ask that both mixed partials exist. Look at the regularity condition it requires near the point, and ask what guarantees the two orders of differentiation agree.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Worked review example: free critical points Let f(x,y)=x^3-3x+y^2-4y. Find and classify the critical points. First compute the gradient: f_x=3x^2-3, \qquad f_y=2y-4. Set both equal to zero: 3x^2-3=0, \qquad 2y-4=0. Thus x=\pm1, \qquad y=2. The critical points are (1,2) \qquad\text{and}\qquad (-1,2). Now compute the second partials: f_{xx}=6x, \qquad f_{xy}=0, \qquad f_{yy}=2. At (1,2), we have A=6,\qquad B=0,\qquad C=2. So \Delta=AC-B^2=12\gt 0, and A\gt 0. Therefore \boxed{(1,2)\text{ is a local minimum.}} At (-1,2), we have A=-6,\qquad B=0,\qquad C=2. So \Delta=(-6)(2)-0=-12\lt 0. Therefore \boxed{(-1,2)\text{ is a saddle point.}} The same function has both behaviors. The gradient found the silent points. The Hessian listened to the first nonzero shape near each one.

chapter.title: Gradients, Hessians, and Optimization

text: Worked review example: absolute extrema on a rectangle Let f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2-4x-4y on the rectangle 0\le x\le 3, \qquad 0\le y\le 2. Find the absolute maximum and minimum. The domain is closed and bounded, and f is continuous, so an absolute maximum and minimum exist. First check the interior. The gradient is \nabla f=(2x-4,\;4y-4). Set it equal to zero: 2x-4=0, \qquad 4y-4=0. Thus x=2, \qquad y=1. This point lies inside the rectangle. Its value is f(2,1)=4+2-8-4=-6. Now check the boundary. On the left edge, x=0,\qquad 0\le y\le2. Then f(0,y)=2y^2-4y=2(y-1)^2-2. The minimum on this edge is -2, and the maximum is 0, reached at y=0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad y=2. On the right edge, x=3,\qquad 0\le y\le2. Then f(3,y)=9+2y^2-12-4y=2(y-1)^2-5. The minimum on this edge is -5, and the maximum is -3. On the bottom edge, y=0,\qquad 0\le x\le3. Then f(x,0)=x^2-4x=(x-2)^2-4. The minimum on this edge is -4, and the maximum is 0, reached at x=0. On the top edge, y=2,\qquad 0\le x\le3. Then f(x,2)=x^2+8-4x-8=x^2-4x=(x-2)^2-4. The minimum on this edge is -4, and the maximum is 0, reached at x=0. Compare all candidates: \begin{array}{c|c} \text{candidate} \amp f(x,y) \\ \hline (2,1) \amp -6\\ (0,0) \amp 0\\ (0,2) \amp 0\\ \text{other boundary candidates} \amp -5,\,-4,\,-3,\,-2 \end{array} Therefore \boxed{\text{absolute minimum }-6\text{ at }(2,1),} and \boxed{\text{absolute maximum }0\text{ at }(0,0)\text{ and }(0,2).} The interior gradient found the minimum. The maximum lived on the boundary.

text:
Worked review example: one smooth constraint Find the maximum and minimum of p(x,y)=x+2y on the ellipse x^2+4y^2=16. Let g(x,y)=x^2+4y^2. The constraint is g=16. The gradients are 
abla p=(1,2), \qquad 
abla g=(2x,8y). The Lagrange multiplier equation is 
abla p=\lambda
abla g. So 1=2\lambda x, \qquad 2=8\lambda y. Thus x= rac{1}{2\lambda}, \qquad y= rac{1}{4\lambda}. Substitute into the constraint: x^2+4y^2=16. This gives  rac{1}{4\lambda^2} + 4\cdot rac{1}{16\lambda^2} = 16, so  rac{1}{2\lambda^2}=16. Therefore \lambda^2= rac{1}{32}, and \lambda=\pm  rac{1}{4\sqrt2}. When \lambda= rac{1}{4\sqrt2}, we get x=2\sqrt2, \qquad y=\sqrt2. When \lambda=- rac{1}{4\sqrt2}, we get x=-2\sqrt2, \qquad y=-\sqrt2. The values are p(2\sqrt2,\sqrt2)=2\sqrt2+2\sqrt2=4\sqrt2, and p(-2\sqrt2,-\sqrt2)=-4\sqrt2. The ellipse is closed and bounded, so these are the absolute extrema:  oxed{	ext{maximum }4\sqrt2	ext{ at }(2\sqrt2,\sqrt2),}  oxed{	ext{minimum }-4\sqrt2	ext{ at }(-2\sqrt2,-\sqrt2).} Geometrically, the level lines x+2y=c slide across the ellipse. At the largest and smallest values, the line just touches the ellipse. At those touching points, the normal direction to the line is parallel to the normal direction to the ellipse.

text: Discovery project: least squares and the geometry of best fit A line rarely passes exactly through experimental data. Suppose a lab records four points: (0,1),\qquad (1,2),\qquad (2,2),\qquad (3,4). We want a line y=mx+b that fits them as well as possible. For each data point (x_i,y_i), the vertical error is mx_i+b-y_i. Instead of minimizing the sum of errors, which can cancel positive and negative mistakes, minimize the sum of squared errors: \boxed{E(m,b)=\sum_{i=1}^4(mx_i+b-y_i)^2.} For these data, \boxed{E(m,b) = (b-1)^2+(m+b-2)^2+(2m+b-2)^2+(3m+b-4)^2.} The best-fit line is found by minimizing E. This is an optimization problem in the two variables m \qquad\text{and}\qquad b. Part 1. The normal equations Differentiate: E_m=2\sum_{i=1}^4 x_i(mx_i+b-y_i), and E_b=2\sum_{i=1}^4 (mx_i+b-y_i). At the minimum, E_m=0, \qquad E_b=0. These are called the normal equations. For the four data points, compute \sum x_i=6, \qquad \sum x_i^2=14, \qquad \sum y_i=9, \qquad \sum x_iy_i=18. Show that the equations become \boxed{14m+6b=18,} and \boxed{6m+4b=9.} Solve them to get \boxed{m=\frac{9}{10}, \qquad b=\frac{9}{10}.} So the least-squares line is \boxed{y=\frac{9}{10}x+\frac{9}{10}.} Part 2. Why this critical point is a minimum The Hessian of E is H_E = 2 \begin{pmatrix} \sum x_i^2 \amp \sum x_i\\ \sum x_i \amp 4 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 28 \amp 12\\ 12 \amp 8 \end{pmatrix}. Compute \Delta=28\cdot8-12^2=224-144=80\gt 0. Since A=28\gt 0, the Hessian is positive definite. Therefore the critical point is a local minimum. Because E(m,b) is a quadratic function whose leading quadratic part is positive definite, this local minimum is the absolute minimum. Part 3. The geometry of the residual Let \mathbf y=(1,2,2,4) be the vector of measured y-values. Let \mathbf 1=(1,1,1,1), \qquad \mathbf x=(0,1,2,3). The predicted values from the line y=mx+b form the vector \widehat{\mathbf y}=m\mathbf x+b\mathbf 1. The residual vector is \mathbf r=\widehat{\mathbf y}-\mathbf y. At the best-fit line, m=b=\frac9{10}. So \widehat{\mathbf y} = \left(\frac9{10},\frac{18}{10},\frac{27}{10},\frac{36}{10}\right), and \mathbf r = \left(-\frac1{10},-\frac2{10},\frac7{10},-\frac4{10}\right). Check that \boxed{\mathbf r\cdot \mathbf 1=0} and \boxed{\mathbf r\cdot \mathbf x=0.} The residual is perpendicular to every change caused by adjusting b or adjusting m. This is the geometric meaning of the normal equations: the error left over is orthogonal to the space of possible predictions. What to hand in Write a short report with the following pieces. A plot of the four data points and the best-fit line. The error function E(m,b). The two normal equations E_m=0,\qquad E_b=0. The solution m=b=\frac9{10}. The Hessian calculation showing that this point gives a minimum. The residual vector and the two dot products \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf 1=0, \qquad \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf x=0. A paragraph explaining why best fit means a perpendicular residual.

text:
Discovery project: designing a container under constraints A rectangular open-top container has base side lengths x,\qquad y and height z. It must have volume 32 cubic units: xyz=32. The amount of material needed is A(x,y,z)=xy+2xz+2yz. The term xy is the base. The terms 2xz and 2yz are the four side walls. There is no top. Find the dimensions that use the least material. Part 1. Set up the Lagrange equations Let g(x,y,z)=xyz. The constraint is g=32. The gradients are 
abla A=(y+2z,\ x+2z,\ 2x+2y), and 
abla g=(yz,\ xz,\ xy). The Lagrange multiplier equation is 
abla A=\lambda

Multiply the second equation by y: xy+2yz=\lambda xyz. Subtract: 2xz-2yz=0. Since z\gt 0, we get  oxed{x=y.} Set x=y=a. The third Lagrange equation becomes 4a=\lambda a^2, so \lambda= rac4a. The first equation becomes a+2z=\lambda az. Substitute \lambda= rac4a: a+2z=4z. Therefore  oxed{a=2z.} So z= rac a2. Use the volume constraint: a^2z=32. The inequality (\sqrt{x}-\sqrt{y})^2\ge0 gives x+y\ge2a. chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why does a finer grid help? We claim that shrinking the squares makes the estimate N\Delta A close in on the true area. The interior squares are not the problem; the trouble lives in the boundary squares, which are partly in and partly out. Why does refining the grid shrink that error toward zero? Think about where the error lives. The boundary squares form a thin band hugging the curved edge. As the squares shrink, how does the total area of that band compare with the area of the whole region?

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: From thin columns to exact volume? Each flat-topped column only approximates the curved surface above its little rectangle, so every single term f(x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta A_{ij} is a bit wrong. Yet we claim the limit of these sums is the surface's exact volume. How can adding up many approximate pieces and taking a limit land on the true answer? Notice that on a tiny rectangle the surface barely changes height, so the gap between the flat top and the real surface is small compared to that piece. Picture all those gaps shrinking faster than the pieces themselves as \Delta A_{ij}\to 0.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: More than volume? A double integral can give area, volume, mass, or total charge, all from the same symbol \iint_R f\,dA. If f need not be a height, what role does it actually play in each tiny piece, and why does that single idea cover so many different physical quantities? Look at the units of f\,dA in each row of the table. In every case f is some quantity per unit area; multiplying by dA turns it into a small amount of the thing you care about. What is being accumulated then?

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Choose a sample point (x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*)\in R_{ij} for each subrectangle. The corresponding Riemann sum is \boxed{ S= \sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n} f(x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*)\,\Delta x_i\,\Delta y_j. }

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why do the sample points stop mattering? For a continuous function f, two friends compute Riemann sums over the same rectangle, but they pick different sample points (x_{ij}^*,y_{ij}^*) inside each subrectangle, so their sums disagree. As the grid is refined and every subrectangle shrinks, why should this disagreement shrink to 0, no matter how stubbornly each friend keeps choosing different points? Think about how much f can change across a single tiny subrectangle. Two sample points in the same cell can differ in value by at most the spread of f on that cell, and that contribution is weighted by \Delta A_{ij}.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: What kind of bad behavior breaks integrability? We just asked that the sample points stop mattering as the grid refines. Imagine a bounded function for which that never happens: no matter how fine the grid, you can still pick sample points that push the sum high and others that push it low. What would such a function have to be doing on every tiny subrectangle to keep the upper and lower estimates from closing in on each other? Integrability fails when f keeps oscillating wildly at every scale, so that even the smallest subrectangle still contains points with large values and points with small values. Picture a function whose graph never settles down, no matter how far you zoom in.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why does dividing by area give the average? Suppose f were a constant, say f(x,y)=7, on a rectangle R. What is \iint_R f\,dA in that case, and what do you get when you divide it by \operatorname{Area}(R)? Use that simplest case to explain why dividing a general integral by the area deserves to be called the average value of f. The average value should be the single constant height that, spread evenly over R, accumulates the same total \iint_R f\,dA. Setting (\text{height})\times\operatorname{Area}(R)=\iint_R f\,dA and solving for the height gives the formula.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Same roof, same volume? We sliced the roof first into vertical strips (freezing x) and then into horizontal strips (freezing y), and both routes gave 120. Without doing any new arithmetic, explain why slicing the very same solid in two different directions must produce the same total volume. Picture chopping the solid into many tiny columns of volume h(x,y)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y. Vertical and horizontal slicing are just two ways of grouping the very same little columns before you add them.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: What does each inner integral measure? Fubini's theorem lets us compute \iint_R f\,dA in either order, dy\,dx or dx\,dy. For a fixed x, what does the inner integral \int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy represent geometrically, and why should adding those quantities over all x give the same answer as adding the inner integrals \int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx over all y? Think of each inner integral as the area of one cross-sectional slice of the surface above a single line. The outer integral stacks those slices. Both orders are stacking slices of the very same solid.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: When can the order matter? For this f the two orders of integration gave \tfrac{\pi}{4} and -\tfrac{\pi}{4}. What feature of this function caused swapping the order to change the answer, and which hypothesis of Fubini's theorem would you check first before trusting that two orders must agree? Look at what happens near (0,0). Fubini's theorem asks for a continuous (in particular bounded) integrand on the rectangle. Ask whether this f meets that requirement everywhere on the square.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why can the inner limits move? In a Type I setup, the outer limits a and b are plain constants, but the inner limits \phi_1(x) and \phi_2(x) are functions of x. Why must it be this way? What would go wrong if you tried to use constant y-limits for a region whose top and bottom edges are slanted? Picture two different vertical slices, one at a small x and one at a large x. Do they start and end at the same height? Think about what the inner limits are describing versus what the outer limits are describing.

text: Write the outer limits from the shadow of the region on the outer axis.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Write the inner limits from the slice.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why redraw, not just swap? When you reverse the order of integration, it is tempting to simply exchange the inner and outer limits. Why doesn't that shortcut work? What information about the region would you miss if you never redrew the picture? The limits encode the shape of D, not just two numbers. Ask yourself: for a fixed x, where does a vertical slice begin and end? Is that the same as where a horizontal slice begins and ends for a fixed y?

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why split at all? Some regions force you to break the integral into two or more pieces. What feature of a region tells you that a single pair of limits cannot describe it honestly? Why would one set of limits accidentally include points that aren't in the region? Run a single slice across the region and watch where it enters and leaves. If it leaves the region and then re-enters it, what does that say about the empty space in between?

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Where does the extra r come from? In rectangular coordinates a tiny cell has area dx\,dy, but in polar coordinates the area element is dA=r\,dr\,d\theta instead of just dr\,d\theta. Without computing anything, explain why a polar cell must pick up that extra factor of r. What is it about the shape of a polar grid that forces this? Two opposite sides of a polar cell are little arcs, not straight segments. Think about the arc-length rule (\text{length})=(\text{radius})(\text{angle}), and ask how the length of that arc depends on how far out you are.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Same bounds, different size? Picture two polar rectangles with the same spans \Delta r and \Delta\theta: one hugging the origin, the other far out near the edge of a disk. Even though they share identical (r,\theta) dimensions, the far one encloses much more physical area. Why does a polar rectangle of fixed (r,\theta) size grow as it moves outward? The two slanted sides are rays through the origin, so they spread apart as r increases. How wide is the cell at radius r? Compare the arc r\,\Delta\theta near the origin with the same arc far away.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why does symmetry simplify so much? When the integrand depends only on the distance from the origin, the polar double integral collapses to a single integral with a clean factor of 2\pi out front. Why does radial symmetry let one of the two integrations happen almost for free? What role does the choice of polar coordinates play in making this possible? If f=F(r), the integrand does not change as \theta sweeps around. Ask what the inner \theta-integral of a quantity that is constant in \theta must equal, and where the 2\pi comes from.

text: Check that the polar description covers the region once.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why a weighted average? The center of mass is built from \iint_D x\,\sigma\,dA divided by the total mass m, rather than just averaging the coordinates of the region. Why should the position of each tiny piece be weighted by its mass \sigma\,dA before we average? What would go wrong physically if we weighted every point equally instead? Picture a seesaw: a heavy child close to the pivot can balance a light child far away. Think about which pieces of the lamina "pull harder" on the balance point.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why squared distance? For moment of inertia each piece of mass is weighted by r^2, its squared distance from the axis, not just by r. Suppose you move a small bead from distance r to distance 2r from the axle. How many times harder does that bead now make the object to spin up? Why does putting mass far from the axis matter so much more for rotation than for ordinary mass? A point at distance r traveling at angular speed \omega moves with speed r\omega, and its kinetic energy involves the square of its speed. See what that squaring does to the bead at 2r.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: One symbol, many stories? The single expression \iint_D f(x,y)\,dA can compute mass, total charge, a probability, or the quantity used for an average, with nothing changing except what f means. How can one calculation answer such different questions? What is the common idea, shared by all these settings, that the double integral is actually carrying out? Look at the building block f\,\Delta A by itself: it is "how much of the quantity sits on a tiny patch." Ask what the integral does with all those tiny patches, regardless of whether f is density, charge, or probability.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: What does convergence even mean here? When we say an integral over an infinite region converges, we are not adding up infinitely many things all at once. In your own words, what limiting process are we actually watching, and what would it mean for that process to fail to settle on a finite number? Look back at how M(A) was built: we measured the mass on a disk of radius A first, and only then asked what happens as A\to\infty. Picture the running total as the disk grows.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why does comparing settle the question? We never computed the integral of c(x,y) itself, yet we still concluded it is finite. Why is it enough to know that c stays below a simpler function whose integral we can evaluate? What feature of nonnegative functions makes this trapping argument trustworthy? For a nonnegative function, the accumulated integral can only grow as the region expands. If it is forever held below a finite ceiling, where is the only place it can end up?

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Why does polar make it work? On the line, \int e^{-x^2}\,dx has no elementary antiderivative and resists every direct attack. After squaring it into a double integral and switching to polar coordinates, the computation suddenly goes through. What new factor appears in dA=r\,dr\,d\theta, and why is the extra r exactly the gift that makes \int e^{-r^2}r\,dr easy? Compare the missing antiderivative of e^{-x^2} with how cleanly the substitution u=r^2 handles e^{-r^2}r. Where did that helpful r come from?

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Worked review example: drawing the region before integrating Let R be the region bounded by y=x^2\qquad\text{and}\qquad y=2x. Compute \iint_R y\,dA. First find the intersection points: x^2=2x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x(x-2)=0. So x=0\qquad\text{or}\qquad x=2. On 0\le x\le2, the line y=2x lies above the parabola y=x^2. Therefore R=\{(x,y):0\le x\le2,\ x^2\le y\le 2x\}. Set up the integral: \iint_R y\,dA \amp= \int_0^2\int_{x^2}^{2x} y\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\left[\frac12y^2\right]_{x^2}^{2x}\,dx \amp= \frac12\int_0^2(4x^2-x^4)\,dx \amp= \frac12\left[\frac43x^3-\frac15x^5\right]_0^2 \amp= \frac12\left(\frac{32}{3}-\frac{32}{5}\right) \amp= \boxed{\frac{32}{15}}. The same region can be described the other way. Since y=2x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\frac y2, and y=x^2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x=\sqrt y on the right-hand branch, the reversed description is R=\left\{(x,y):0\le y\le4,\ \frac y2\le x\le \sqrt y\right\}. So the same integral is \boxed{\iint_R y\,dA=\int_0^4\int_{y/2}^{\sqrt y}y\,dx\,dy.} This is the same quantity with a different slicing direction.

chapter.title: Double Integrals

text: Worked review example: a circular sprinkler pattern A sprinkler waters a circular garden of radius 2 meters. The water density at a point depends only on distance from the center: w(r)=10-r,\qquad 0\le r\le2. Find the total water and the average water density over the garden. The region is a disk, and the density is radial, so use polar coordinates: 0\le r\le2,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. The total water is W \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2 (10-r)r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\int_0^2(10r-r^2)\,dr \amp= 2\pi\left[5r^2-\frac13r^3\right]_0^2 \amp= 2\pi\left(20-\frac83\right) \amp= \boxed{\frac{104\pi}{3}}. The garden area is \pi(2)^2=4\pi. Therefore the average water density is \boxed{w_{\mathrm{avg}}=\frac{W}{4\pi}=\frac{26}{3}.} The value \frac{26}{3} is less than 10, because most of the garden is not near the center. In polar coordinates, the factor r reminds us that larger rings contain more area.

text: Project: estimating rainfall from gridded data A storm passes over a rectangular watershed. The watershed is 0\le x\le8,\qquad 0\le y\le6, where x and y are measured in kilometers. The region is divided into rectangles of size 2\text{ km}\times 2\text{ km}. Rainfall is measured at the center of each rectangle, in centimeters. \begin{array}{c|cccc} \amp x=1 \amp x=3 \amp x=5 \amp x=7 \\ \hline y=5 \amp 3.2 \amp 4.1 \amp 4.6 \amp 3.8\\ y=3 \amp 2.4 \amp 3.5 \amp 5.0 \amp 4.2\\ y=1 \amp 1.1 \amp 2.0 \amp 3.1 \amp 2.7 \end{array} Each grid cell has area 4\text{ km}^2. Part 1. Estimate the total rainfall integral Use a midpoint sum: \iint_R r(x,y)\,dA\approx 4\sum r(x_i^*,y_j^*). For the data above, \sum r(x_i^*,y_j^*) \amp= 3.2+4.1+4.6+3.8 \amp\qquad +2.4+3.5+5.0+4.2 \amp\qquad +1.1+2.0+3.1+2.7 \amp= 39.7. So \boxed{\iint_R r(x,y)\,dA\approx 4(39.7)=158.8\text{ cm}\cdot\text{km}^2.} Part 2. Convert to water volume One centimeter of rain over one square kilometer equals 10{,}000\text{ m}^3 of water. Therefore the estimated water volume is \boxed{158.8(10{,}000)=1{,}588{,}000\text{ m}^3.} Part 3. Estimate average rainfall The watershed area is 8\cdot6=48\text{ km}^2. The average rainfall is \boxed{r_{\mathrm{avg}}\approx \frac{158.8}{48}\approx 3.31\text{ cm}.} Part 4. What to hand in Write a short report with the following pieces. A sketch of the watershed grid. The midpoint-sum estimate for \iint_R r(x,y)\,dA. The conversion from \text{cm}\cdot\text{km}^2 to cubic meters. The estimated average rainfall. A contour-style sketch showing where the rainfall appears largest. A paragraph explaining one possible source of error in the estimate. For example, what if the heaviest rain fell between two sensors?

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Why does adding 1 give volume? We wrote \operatorname{Volume}(E)=\iiint_E 1\,dV. Why does adding the constant 1 throughout E measure volume, and what changes in the story when the constant 1 is replaced by a density f(x,y,z) so that the integral becomes \iiint_E f\,dV? Each tiny piece contributes (\text{value})\times \Delta V. Ask yourself what one small piece adds when the value is 1, and what it adds when the value is the local density.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Why three integrals, one at a time? A triple integral asks us to add over a whole solid at once, yet we compute it by doing three ordinary single integrals in sequence. Why is it legitimate to peel the sum apart this way, holding two variables fixed while we integrate the third? Think about grouping the tiny contributions before adding them: first total a thin line in one direction, then collect those lines, then collect again. Holding two variables constant is just deciding which pieces to add first.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Why six orders, one answer? There are exactly six orders in which we can integrate x, y, and z. Why are there six, and why should all six produce the very same number for a well-behaved integrand on a box? Count the ways to arrange three variables in a line. Then remember that each order only regroups the same little volume pieces f\,\Delta V before adding—the pieces themselves never change.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: From inequalities to limits? We described the tetrahedron with the nested chain 0\le x\le6, then 0\le y\le 6-x, then 0\le z\le 6-x-y, and then simply copied those bounds into the integral \int_0^6\int_0^{6-x}\int_0^{6-x-y}\,dz\,dy\,dx. Why is the chain of nested inequalities already the integration limits, with no translation step in between? Think about what each inequality fixes. When you write 0\le z\le 6-x-y, the bounds on z are allowed to mention x and y because those are already chosen. Which variable is allowed to appear in which set of limits, and how does that ordering match the inside-to-outside order of the integral?

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Why a slice drops a dimension? For a z-simple solid we computed \iiint_E f\,dV by first integrating along each vertical slice, \int_{g_1(x,y)}^{g_2(x,y)} f\,dz, and then doing a double integral over the shadow D. Why does integrating along the vertical line segments parallel to the z-axis leave a double integral over D, instead of leaving you with three integrals to do all at once? After the inner dz-integral is done, the result no longer depends on z; it is just a number attached to each point (x,y) of the shadow. How many free variables are left, and what kind of region do they range over?

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Why not just shuffle the limits? When we switched from \int_0^6\int_0^{6-x}\int_0^{6-x-y}\,dz\,dy\,dx to an order with x innermost, the new limits 0\le z\le6-y and 0\le x\le6-y-z were not the old limits rearranged. Why does changing the order force us to re-describe the solid from scratch, rather than simply permuting the limits we already had? Each set of limits answers the question “given the variables chosen so far, where can the next one go?” Changing the order changes which variables are chosen first, so it changes which surface bounds the slice and which coordinate plane the shadow lives on. Try sketching the shadow in the yz-plane versus the xy-plane and compare.
