text: Tubes and turning profiles A solid of revolution is made by spinning a flat profile around the z-axis. If you slice the result into thin cylindrical tubes, each tube has a radius r and a tiny thickness. Why does this picture of nested tubes match a solid of revolution so naturally, and where in the volume integral does the factor r for each tube appear? Imagine the surface of one thin tube at radius r. As you go once around in \theta, how far does that surface travel? That circumference is what the r in r\,dr\,d\theta is keeping track of.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Why \rho^2\sin\phi? Without computing any integral, explain why the spherical volume element carries the factor \rho^2\sin\phi, so that dV=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta. Where does each piece of that factor come from geometrically? Picture the three edges of a tiny spherical box. One edge has length d\rho, but the other two are arcs whose radii are not 1. How long is the arc that sweeps through an angle d\phi, and how long is the arc that goes around the z-axis through d\theta? Notice that the second arc lives on a circle of radius \rho\sin\phi, not \rho.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Why are balls and shells so easy? In spherical coordinates, why are a solid ball and a spherical shell almost trivial to set up, while the same regions felt awkward in cylindrical coordinates? Think about what happens to the bounds on \rho, \phi, and \theta. A region is easiest when every bound is a constant rather than a function of the other variables. What do the surfaces \rho=2 and \rho=5 look like, and do the angular limits \phi and \theta depend on \rho at all here?

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Why does the angular part split off? When the density depends only on \rho, the mass integral collapses to a single radial integral times the constant 4\pi. Explain why a density of the form \delta=\delta(\rho) lets the \phi and \theta integrals factor out, and why that would fail for a density like \delta=\delta(\rho,\phi). A product integrates as a product of integrals only when each variable appears in its own separate factor. Group the integrand \delta(\rho)\,\rho^2\sin\phi: which pieces involve \theta, which involve \phi, and which involve \rho? Does any factor mix two of the variables together?

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Distance to what? In a moment of inertia I=\iiint_E s^2\delta\,dV, the symbol s is the distance from a point to the rotation axis, not the distance to the origin. Why should the axis, rather than the origin, be the thing we measure distance to? Picture a point sitting directly on the spin axis but far below the origin: how fast is it actually moving as the solid turns, and what does that say about its share of the resistance to rotation? Ask what each little piece is physically doing while the solid spins. A piece right on the axis traces a circle of radius zero, so it barely moves no matter how far it is from the origin.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: One integral, many meanings? Mass is \iiint_E \delta\,dV, total charge is \iiint_E q\,dV, and total energy is \iiint_E u\,dV — the same triple integral each time, with only the integrand renamed. What is the integral really doing in all three cases, and why does swapping the meaning of the density (mass per volume, charge per volume, energy per volume) automatically change what the total represents, without changing a single step of the computation? Look at the building block (\text{density})\times(\text{tiny volume}). The integral only knows how to add up those little pieces; the units you attach to the density decide whether each piece is a bit of mass, a bit of charge, or a bit of energy.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Why exactly 1? A probability density must satisfy \iiint_E p\,dV=1 over all of space. Why must the total come out to exactly 1, and not 2 or \tfrac12? Think about what event the integral over all of space is describing: if you pick a random point, how sure are you that it lands somewhere, and what number should that certainty correspond to? The integral over the whole region is the probability that the point lands somewhere in it — an event that is guaranteed to happen. A probability of 1 is the language we use for “certain.”

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: What carries over, what bends? Moving from \mathbb R^3 to \mathbb R^n for large n, the integral is still built by chopping the region into tiny boxes and adding up f(\mathbf x_i^*)\,\Delta V_{n,i}. Which parts of this story stay exactly the same, and which parts (the pictures, the geometry, the sizes of things) stop matching your three-dimensional intuition? Separate the bookkeeping of the integral (Riemann sums, Fubini, the adding rule) from the geometry it describes. One of these is dimension-blind; the other is not.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Where did the middle go? Take the cube [-1,1]^n and shrink it toward its center by halving each side, giving the smaller cube [-1/2,1/2]^n. As n grows, why does almost all of the big cube's volume end up near its surface, far from the center, leaving the inner cube with a vanishing share? Compare the two volumes as a ratio. The inner cube keeps only a factor of \left(\tfrac12\right)^n of the volume, and that fraction goes to 0. Ask what is left over, and where it must sit.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: The ball that fades away The volumes 2R, \pi R^2, \tfrac43\pi R^3, \tfrac{\pi^2}{2}R^4, \tfrac{8\pi^2}{15}R^5 seem to keep growing. Yet for a fixed radius such as R=1, the volume of the unit ball eventually decreases toward 0 as the dimension n grows. How can adding more dimensions make the unit ball smaller? A new dimension adds a slicing variable that ranges only over |x|\le 1, and each slice is itself a ball of radius \sqrt{1-x^2}\le 1 in one fewer dimension. Picture stacking many slices that are each smaller than the one you started with. Does the stack have to grow?

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Worked review example: a wedge with density A storage wedge has rectangular floor 0\le x\le2,\qquad 0\le y\le1, and slanted roof z=4-x-y. The floor is z=0. Its density is \delta(x,y,z)=1+z. Find the mass. The solid is E=\{(x,y,z):0\le x\le2,\ 0\le y\le1,\ 0\le z\le4-x-y\}. So M \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1\int_0^{4-x-y} (1+z)\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 \left[ z+\frac12z^2 \right]_0^{4-x-y} \,dy\,dx \amp= \int_0^2\int_0^1 \left( (4-x-y)+\frac12(4-x-y)^2 \right)dy\,dx. Expand the integrand: (4-x-y)+\frac12(4-x-y)^2 = 12-5x-5y+\frac12x^2+xy+\frac12y^2. Now integrate in y: \int_0^1 \left( 12-5x-5y+\frac12x^2+xy+\frac12y^2 \right)dy \amp= \frac{29}{3}-\frac92x+\frac12x^2. Then M \amp= \int_0^2 \left( \frac{29}{3}-\frac92x+\frac12x^2 \right)dx \amp= \frac{58}{3}-9+\frac43 \amp= \frac{35}{3}. Thus \boxed{ M=\frac{35}{3}. } The bounds came from the geometry. The integrand came from the density. The calculation only came after both were clear.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Worked review example: a round tank in cylindrical coordinates A round tank has radius 2. Its floor is z=0, and its roof height depends on distance from the central axis: z=3+\frac r2. The density is \delta(r,z)=1+r. Find the mass. The solid is rotationally symmetric, so cylindrical coordinates fit: 0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le r\le2, \qquad 0\le z\le 3+\frac r2. Remember the volume factor: dV=r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta. So M \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_0^{3+r/2} (1+r)r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\int_0^2 (1+r)r\left(3+\frac r2\right)dr. Expand: (1+r)r\left(3+\frac r2\right) = 3r+\frac72r^2+\frac12r^3. Thus M \amp= 2\pi\int_0^2 \left( 3r+\frac72r^2+\frac12r^3 \right)dr \amp= 2\pi \left[ \frac32r^2+\frac76r^3+\frac18r^4 \right]_0^2 \amp= 2\pi \left( 6+\frac{28}{3}+2 \right) \amp= \frac{104\pi}{3}. So \boxed{ M=\frac{104\pi}{3}. } The factor r is doing real work. Rings near r=2 contain more volume than rings near the central axis.

chapter.title: Triple and Higher-Dimensional Integrals

text: Worked review example: probability in a spherical cone A random point is chosen in the solid inside the sphere \rho\le2 and inside the cone 0\le\phi\le\frac{\pi}{3}. The probability density is proportional to distance from the origin: p(\rho,\phi,\theta)=C\rho. Find C. Then find the probability that \rho\le1. The region is 0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le\phi\le\frac{\pi}{3}, \qquad 0\le\rho\le2. The density must integrate to 1: 1 \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_0^2 C\rho\cdot \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \amp= C \left(\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta\right) \left(\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin\phi\,d\phi\right) \left(\int_0^2\rho^3\,d\rho\right) \amp= C(2\pi)\left(1-\frac12\right)(4) \amp= 4\pi C. Therefore \boxed{ C=\frac{1}{4\pi}. } Now restrict to 0\le\rho\le1. Then \operatorname{Prob}(\rho\le1) \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/3}\int_0^1 \frac{1}{4\pi}\rho^3\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \amp= \frac{1}{4\pi}(2\pi)\left(\frac12\right)\left(\frac14\right) \amp= \frac{1}{16}. So \boxed{ \operatorname{Prob}(\rho\le1)=\frac{1}{16}. } The ball of half the radius has much less than half the probability. Part of the reason is geometry: volume grows like \rho^2. Another part is density: this density also grows like \rho.

text: Project: comparing volume formulas numerically A unit ball has volume \frac{4\pi}{3}. That formula is familiar, but this chapter gives several ways to approach the same number. The goal of this project is to compare three numerical estimates of the unit ball volume. The unit ball is B=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2+z^2\le1\}. Method 1. Counting small cubes Divide the cube -1\le x\le1,\qquad -1\le y\le1,\qquad -1\le z\le1 into N^3 equal small cubes. Each small cube has side length \Delta x=\frac{2}{N} and volume \Delta V=\left(\frac{2}{N}\right)^3. Use the center of each small cube as a test point. Count how many centers satisfy x^2+y^2+z^2\le1. If that number is K_N, then \boxed{ V_N^{\mathrm{box}} = K_N\left(\frac{2}{N}\right)^3. } Method 2. Cylindrical slices In cylindrical coordinates, the ball is 0\le r\le1, \qquad -\sqrt{1-r^2}\le z\le \sqrt{1-r^2}, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. Its volume is V= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1\int_{-\sqrt{1-r^2}}^{\sqrt{1-r^2}} r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta. After integrating in z and \theta, this becomes V=4\pi\int_0^1 r\sqrt{1-r^2}\,dr. Use a midpoint sum with r_i^*=\left(i-\frac12\right)\Delta r, \qquad \Delta r=\frac1N. Then \boxed{ V_N^{\mathrm{cyl}} = 4\pi\sum_{i=1}^N r_i^*\sqrt{1-(r_i^*)^2}\,\Delta r. } Method 3. Spherical shells In spherical coordinates, the unit ball is simply 0\le\rho\le1,\qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi,\qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. The volume is V= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^1 \rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta = 4\pi\int_0^1\rho^2\,d\rho. Use a midpoint sum with \rho_i^*=\left(i-\frac12\right)\Delta\rho, \qquad \Delta\rho=\frac1N. Then \boxed{ V_N^{\mathrm{sph}} = 4\pi\sum_{i=1}^N (\rho_i^*)^2\,\Delta\rho. } Sample results The exact value is \frac{4\pi}{3}\approx 4.18879. Here are typical midpoint estimates. \begin{array}{c|c|c|c} N \amp V_N^{\mathrm{box}} \amp V_N^{\mathrm{cyl}} \amp V_N^{\mathrm{sph}} \\ \hline 4 \amp 4.00000 \amp 4.34530 \amp 4.12334\\ 8 \amp 4.37500 \amp 4.24276 \amp 4.17243\\ 16 \amp 4.25000 \amp 4.20738 \amp 4.18470\\ 32 \amp 4.21289 \amp 4.19522 \amp 4.18777 \end{array} The spherical estimate improves quickly because the spherical bounds match the ball. The cube-counting estimate also improves, but its boundary is rough: small cubes do not fit a sphere very naturally. What to hand in Write a short report with the following pieces. A picture or description of the three methods. A table of your estimates for at least four values of N. The absolute error for each method: \left|V_N-\frac{4\pi}{3}\right|. A paragraph explaining which method converges fastest in your computation. A paragraph explaining why the coordinate system matters even though all three methods are estimating the same volume. The last paragraph is the point of the project. A coordinate system is not just notation. It shapes the pieces being added.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why a stretch factor at all? We could imagine simply renaming x as u and copying the integral across unchanged. Why does honest accounting force the factor dx/du to appear, rather than letting the integrand alone carry the whole story? Picture two equal steps in u near u=1/10 and near u=2. Do they cover equal amounts of x?

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why insist on tiny tiles? For a nonlinear map, a large rectangle's image can have bent sides, and its local area scale can vary across the tile. Yet near a point we use a single Jacobian determinant. In what sense does shrinking the tile rescue the parallelogram picture, and what would go wrong if we trusted that picture for a big tile? Think about how the curvature of the image edges compares to the side lengths as \Delta u,\Delta v shrink toward zero.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why a determinant, not a product? The two coordinate velocity vectors T_u and T_v each have a length, so a tempting guess for the area factor would be the product of those lengths. Why is the determinant the right measure of how area is rescaled, while that product is not? Imagine the two vectors nearly parallel: their lengths stay positive, but how much area does the parallelogram they span enclose?

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why columns? We read the area scale factor straight off the matrix A, yet A is just a box of numbers. What is it about the columns of A that lets them carry the geometry of the unit square, no matter which square we start with? Ask what A does to the two coordinate directions \mathbf e_u=(1,0) and \mathbf e_v=(0,1), and where those images show up inside A.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: What does collapse mean? The formula \operatorname{Area}(R)=|\det A|\,\operatorname{Area}(S) still gives an answer when \det A=0 -- it just says the image has area 0. So why is \det A=0 forbidden for a change of variables, rather than simply being an interesting special case? A change of variables has to be reversible: every point of R should come from exactly one point of S. What happens to that requirement when a whole region is crushed onto a line?

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why keep the sign? For computing ordinary area we throw the sign away and use |\det A|. So what information is the sign of \det A actually recording about the map, and why might we want to hold on to it rather than discard it? Picture the ordered pair of arrows \mathbf e_u,\mathbf e_v before and after the map. The sign is not about how big the image is -- it is about which way it turns.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why does the scale factor wander? For a linear change of variables the area scale factor |\det A| was a single number, but here |J_T(u,v)|=u changes from point to point. What is it about a map that makes its scale factor depend on where you are? Is such variation inevitable for every nonlinear map, or only possible? Check the shear (u,v)\mapsto(u,v+u^2). Think about the derivative vectors T_u and T_v. For a linear map they are the same everywhere; for a nonlinear map, how do they behave as you move from one point to another?

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Local truth, global error? The Jacobian determinant correctly measured how each tiny tile was stretched, yet the integral came out as 2 instead of the true area 1. How can a quantity be right about every small piece and still give the wrong total? The Jacobian only knows about one tile at a time. It cannot tell whether two different tiles land on the same spot in the image. What does the one-to-one condition guarantee that the determinant alone cannot?

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Compute: x_r=\cos\theta, \qquad x_\theta=-r\sin\theta, and y_r=\sin\theta, \qquad y_\theta=r\cos\theta. Therefore \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(r,\theta)} \amp= \det \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta \amp -r\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta \amp r\cos\theta \end{pmatrix} \amp= r\cos^2\theta+r\sin^2\theta \amp= r. So \boxed{ dA=r\,dr\,d\theta. } This is the old polar area element, now explained by the same determinant rule used for every coordinate change.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why exactly r? The factor r in dA=r\,dr\,d\theta once came from the length of a small circular arc, and now it falls out of the Jacobian determinant. Why should these two very different-looking arguments produce the very same r? Both are measuring the area of one tiny tile of the polar grid. Picture the little patch between radii r and r+\Delta r and angles \theta and \theta+\Delta\theta — how do its two side lengths depend on r?

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Compute the volume directly: \operatorname{Vol}(E) \amp= \int_1^2\int_1^3\int_0^{xy}1\,dz\,dy\,dx \amp= \int_1^2\int_1^3 xy\,dy\,dx \amp= \left[\int_1^2 x\,dx\right]\left[\int_1^3 y\,dy\right] \amp= \frac32\cdot4 \amp= 6.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why a determinant? A tiny coordinate box gets carried to a tiny parallelepiped. Why is the absolute value of the determinant exactly the right number to measure how much that box's volume is stretched or squeezed, rather than, say, the sum or product of the edge lengths of T_u\,\Delta u, T_v\,\Delta v, and T_w\,\Delta w? Think back to what a 3\times3 determinant computes for three vectors. The edge lengths alone cannot see how the edges are tilted relative to one another.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: What happens at the axis? The spherical factor \rho^2\sin\phi drops to 0 when \rho=0 or when \phi=0 or \phi=\pi. Geometrically, what is happening to a small coordinate box at those places that makes its volume shrink to nothing? Picture the three coordinate edges and their lengths 1, \rho, and \rho\sin\phi. Where do points with different \theta pile up on top of one another?

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why read the region? In the ellipsoid example, the substitution came from the boundary of the region, not from the function being integrated. Why is the shape of the region so often a better guide to a good change of variables than the integrand is? A change of variables earns its keep mostly by turning awkward limits of integration into simple ones. Ask what makes a triple integral hard to set up in the first place.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why two correct answers? The same map gave area 2 but signed area -2. In words, what extra piece of information does the form dx\wedge dy record that the plain area does not, and why might you want to keep it? Think about what changes if you list the coordinate directions in the opposite order. Does ordinary area notice? Does the sign?

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Where did the other terms go? When the three differentials are wedged together, six terms can survive; together they give one multiple of du\wedge dv\wedge dw. What is it about \wedge that makes every term with a repeated differential disappear, and why does that leave exactly the determinant behind rather than some other combination? Recall how du\wedge du behaves, and how swapping two factors changes the sign. The pattern of surviving signs is the same pattern that defines a determinant.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why the absolute value? Ordinary integration uses |J|, while oriented integration with dx\wedge dy uses J itself. Conceptually, why does measuring plain size force us to throw away the sign, and what question are we no longer able to answer once we do? A length or an area can never come out negative. So if the determinant is negative, something has to give. Ask which of the two readings still remembers the flip.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Where did the extra area come from? The Jacobian J=r was correct at every single point, yet the integral over 0\le\theta\le4\pi reported twice the area of the disk. Which hypothesis of the change-of-variables theorem was quietly violated here, and why can a perfectly correct local measurement still add up to the wrong total? The determinant only ever looks at one tiny tile near one point. Ask yourself whether two different parameter points were allowed to land on the same place in the disk.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: What is the vanishing Jacobian trying to tell us? At the origin the determinant collapses to J_T(0,0)=0. We saw that for polar coordinates a vanishing Jacobian at a single point did no harm. Here it does signal real trouble. What is the geometric difference between the two situations, and what does a zero Jacobian say about whether T can serve as a coordinate system near that point? A genuine coordinate chart needs a smooth inverse nearby. Think about what happens to two directions leaving the origin once the map doubles every angle.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Why must we keep the minus sign? This map is one-to-one and its Jacobian never vanishes, so it breaks none of the hypotheses that caused the earlier failures. Yet ordinary area uses |J_T|=1 while the oriented form keeps J_T=-1. What information would be thrown away if oriented integrals also took the absolute value, and why does the boundary's reversed direction make that information worth keeping? Notice that the counterclockwise uv-loop became a clockwise xy-loop. If both loops gave the same answer, how would an integral ever tell the two directions apart?

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Worked review example: a slanted window A thin glass window occupies the parallelogram-like region R=\{(x,y):1\le x+y\le3,\ 0\le x-y\le2\}. The density of tint on the glass is q(x,y)=x+y. Find the total amount of tint: \iint_R (x+y)\,dA. The boundary equations suggest u=x+y, \qquad v=x-y. Then R becomes the rectangle 1\le u\le3, \qquad 0\le v\le2. Solve for x and y: x=\frac{u+v}{2}, \qquad y=\frac{u-v}{2}. The Jacobian determinant is \frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)} \amp= \det\begin{pmatrix} 1/2\amp 1/2\\ 1/2\amp -1/2\end{pmatrix} \amp= -\frac14-\frac14 \amp= -\frac12. So the ordinary area factor is \left|\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}\right|=\frac12. The integrand becomes x+y=u. Therefore \iint_R (x+y)\,dA \amp= \int_1^3\int_0^2 u\cdot\frac12\,dv\,du \amp= \int_1^3 u\,du \amp= \left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_1^3 \amp= 4. Thus \boxed{\iint_R (x+y)\,dA=4.} The signed Jacobian was negative. That means the ordered variables (u,v) reverse the usual orientation of the xy-plane. The glass does not have negative area, so the ordinary integral uses the absolute value.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Worked review example: a curved plate between hyperbolas A thin metal plate lies in the first quadrant. Its edges are xy=1,\qquad xy=4, and \frac{y}{x}=1,\qquad \frac{y}{x}=3. Its density is \delta(x,y)=xy. Find its mass. The boundary equations almost name the new variables: u=xy, \qquad v=\frac{y}{x}. Then the plate becomes the rectangle 1\le u\le4, \qquad 1\le v\le3. Because we are in the first quadrant, x\gt0 and y\gt0. From u=xy, \qquad v=\frac{y}{x}, we get y=vx. Then u=x(vx)=vx^2, so x=\sqrt{\frac{u}{v}}. Also, y=vx=\sqrt{uv}. Thus x=\sqrt{\frac{u}{v}}, \qquad y=\sqrt{uv}. Compute the Jacobian. A quick way is to compute the determinant of the forward map (x,y)\longmapsto (u,v). Since u=xy, \qquad v=\frac{y}{x}, we have \frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}=\det\begin{pmatrix} y\amp x\\ -y/x^2\amp 1/x\end{pmatrix}. Therefore \frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} \amp= y\cdot\frac1x - x\left(-\frac{y}{x^2}\right) \amp= \frac{y}{x}+\frac{y}{x} \amp= 2\frac{y}{x} \amp= 2v. So \boxed{\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\frac{1}{2v}.} The density becomes \delta(x,y)=xy=u. Thus M \amp= \iint_R xy\,dA \amp= \int_1^4\int_1^3 u\cdot\frac{1}{2v}\,dv\,du \amp= \frac12 \left(\int_1^4 u\,du\right)\left(\int_1^3 \frac{1}{v}\,dv\right) \amp= \frac12 \left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_1^4 \left[\ln v\right]_1^3 \amp= \frac12\cdot\frac{15}{2}\cdot\ln 3 \amp= \frac{15}{4}\ln 3. So \boxed{M=\frac{15}{4}\ln 3.} The region looked awkward in x,y. It was a rectangle in the variables its own edges were already using.

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Compute the Jacobian. A quick way is to compute the determinant of the forward map (x,y)\longmapsto (u,v). Since u=xy, \qquad v=\frac{y}{x}, we have \frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)}=\det\begin{pmatrix} y\amp x\\ -y/x^2\amp 1/x\end{pmatrix}. Therefore \frac{\partial(u,v)}{\partial(x,y)} \amp= y\cdot\frac1x - x\left(-\frac{y}{x^2}\right) \amp= \frac{y}{x}+\frac{y}{x} \amp= 2\frac{y}{x} \amp= 2v. So \boxed{\frac{\partial(x,y)}{\partial(u,v)}=\frac{1}{2v}.} The density becomes \delta(x,y)=xy=u. Thus M \amp= \iint_R xy\,dA \amp= \int_1^4\int_1^3 u\cdot\frac{1}{2v}\,dv\,du \amp= \frac12 \left(\int_1^4 u\,du\right)\left(\int_1^3 \frac{1}{v}\,dv\right) \amp= \frac12 \left[\frac{u^2}{2}\right]_1^4 \left[\ln v\right]_1^3 \amp= \frac12\cdot\frac{15}{2}\cdot\ln 3 \amp= \frac{15}{4}\ln 3. So \boxed{M=\frac{15}{4}\ln 3.}

chapter.title: Change of Variables in Multiple Integrals

text: Worked review example: a stretched ball Let E be the ellipsoid \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2\le1. Its density is \delta(x,y,z)=1+\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2. Find the mass. The ellipsoid is a stretched unit ball. Use x=2u, \qquad y=3v, \qquad z=w. Then \frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2=u^2+v^2+w^2. So the solid E becomes the unit ball B=\{(u,v,w):u^2+v^2+w^2\le1\}. The Jacobian determinant is \det\begin{pmatrix} 2\amp0\amp0\\ 0\amp3\amp0\\ 0\amp0\amp1\end{pmatrix}=6. The density becomes \delta=1+u^2+v^2+w^2. Therefore M \amp= \iiint_E \left(1+\frac{x^2}{4}+\frac{y^2}{9}+z^2\right)dV \amp= \iiint_B 6(1+u^2+v^2+w^2)\,du\,dv\,dw. Now use spherical coordinates in the uvw-space: u^2+v^2+w^2=\rho^2, \qquad dV_{uvw}=\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta. The unit ball is 0\le\rho\le1, \qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi, \qquad 0\le\theta\le2\pi. Thus M \amp= 6\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^1 (1+\rho^2)\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta \amp= 6 \left(\int_0^{2\pi}d\theta\right)\left(\int_0^\pi \sin\phi\,d\phi\right)\left(\int_0^1(\rho^2+\rho^4)\,d\rho\right) \amp= 6(2\pi)(2)\left(\frac13+\frac15\right) \amp= 24\pi\cdot\frac{8}{15} \amp= \frac{64\pi}{5}. So \boxed{M=\frac{64\pi}{5}.} Two coordinate changes worked together. The first turned the ellipsoid into a ball. The second used spherical coordinates because the new ball had radial symmetry.

text: Project: Gaussian integrals and polar coordinates The integral \int e^{-x^2}\,dx has no elementary antiderivative. That is a single-variable problem. The surprising way through it is to square the integral and make it two-dimensional. Let I=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx. This integral is positive, so if we can find I^2, then we can find I. Part 1. Square the integral Write I^2=\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx\right)\left(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-y^2}\,dy\right). The bounded-square Fubini argument and disk comparison in justify the limiting step. The second variable is called y so the two copies can be combined as a double integral: \boxed{I^2=\iint_{\mathbb R^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dA.} The integrand is now radial: e^{-(x^2+y^2)}=e^{-r^2}. The region is the whole plane. Polar coordinates fit both the integrand and the region. Part 2. Change to polar coordinates In polar coordinates, dA=r\,dr\,d\theta. Therefore I^2=\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta. The inner integral uses the substitution s=r^2, \qquad ds=2r\,dr. So \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}r\,dr \amp= \frac12\int_0^\infty e^{-s}\,ds \amp= \frac12. Thus I^2 \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\frac12\,d\theta \amp= \pi. Since I\gt0, \boxed{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\pi}.} This is one of the most famous uses of polar coordinates. A one-variable antiderivative was unavailable, but a two-dimensional symmetry solved the definite integral. Part 3. A careful finite-radius version For a radius R\gt0, define G(R)=\iint_{x^2+y^2\le R^2} e^{-(x^2+y^2)}\,dA. Use polar coordinates: G(R) \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^R e^{-r^2}r\,dr\,d\theta \amp= 2\pi\left[-\frac12e^{-r^2}\right]_0^R \amp= \pi(1-e^{-R^2}). So \boxed{G(R)=\pi(1-e^{-R^2}).} As R\to\infty, G(R)\to\pi. That is the polar-coordinate shadow of I^2=\pi. Part 4. A scaled Gaussian Let a\gt0. Find I(a)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-ax^2}\,dx. Use the substitution u=\sqrt a\,x. Then dx=\frac{1}{\sqrt a}\,du, and I(a) \amp= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-u^2}\frac{1}{\sqrt a}\,du \amp= \frac{1}{\sqrt a}\sqrt\pi. Thus \boxed{\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-ax^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{a}}.} Part 5. Normalizing the normal density A probability density on the real line must integrate to 1. The bell-shaped density with mean 0 and spread parameter \sigma\gt0 has the form p(x)=C e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}. Find C. Using the scaled Gaussian formula with a=\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}, we get \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\,dx=\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}=\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}. Therefore 1=C\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}, so \boxed{C=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}.} Thus the normalized density is \boxed{p(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}.} What to hand in Write a short report with the following pieces. Explain why the single-variable antiderivative is not the point of this problem. Show how squaring the integral produces a double integral over \mathbb R^2. Evaluate the double integral using polar coordinates. Compute \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-ax^2}\,dx for a\gt0. Use the result to find the normalizing constant for C e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}. Write one paragraph explaining why polar coordinates were the right coordinates for the squared integral. The last paragraph is the heart of the project. The formula e^{-x^2} does not look circular. But after squaring the integral, the expression e^{-(x^2+y^2)} reveals a hidden disk symmetry.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: An instruction book, not a journey? We said the picture of \mathbf V is a whole instruction book rather than the path of one moving particle. What does it mean that the field assigns a vector to a point like (2,3) even if no leaf ever floats there? Why might it be misleading to read the arrows as if they trace out a single trajectory? Think about how many points the domain has, and ask what the arrow at (2,3) is promising: a velocity for whatever arrives there, not a record of where anything has been.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Why is a gradient field special? A force field or a wind field is just an arrow at every point. A gradient field \nabla f is also an arrow at every point, yet we say it is tied to the contour map of f. What extra information does a gradient field carry that a generic vector field need not, and why does that matter when you look at its arrows? Recall that \nabla f points across level curves at right angles and toward increasing f. Could you reconstruct something about the underlying surface from its gradient arrows alone? Could you do that for an arbitrary field of arrows?

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: What does the flow-line equation really say? The definition asks that \mathbf r'(t)=\mathbf F(\mathbf r(t)) at every instant. In plain words, why does this single equation force the curve to obey the field? And why does it matter that the right-hand side is evaluated at the curve's current position \mathbf r(t) rather than at some fixed point? Imagine reading the field like a set of directions handed to you wherever you happen to stand. If you stepped off the path even slightly, the instruction you receive would change. Along a proposed flow line, compare its instantaneous velocity with the arrow assigned by the field at that same point.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Why multiply by speed? The factor \|\mathbf r'(t)\| turns dt into a piece of arc length ds. In plain words, what does this factor measure about how the curve is being traced, and why would leaving it out give the wrong total? Think about the difference between clock time dt and distance on the wire. If the parametrization speeds up, one second of t covers more length.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Is t the same as distance? The text warns that the parameter t is not necessarily arc length. What would have to be true about a parametrization for t itself to measure distance along the curve, so that the speed factor became simply 1? Ask what value \|\mathbf r'(t)\| would need to have at every instant. A curve traced at unit speed has a special name.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Why doesn't direction matter? A scalar line integral such as mass gives the same value whether the curve is traced one way or the other, yet later in the chapter work will change sign when you reverse direction. What is it about adding up f\,ds that makes orientation simply not register? Notice that ds is always a positive length, never a signed displacement. Reversing the trace reorders the pieces but does not turn any of them negative.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: No work? Suppose at every instant the force \mathbf F happens to point exactly perpendicular to the direction the cart is moving. Without computing anything, what should the total work be, and why does the dot product give you that answer automatically? Think about \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r at a single instant when the two vectors are at right angles. What does the dot product of perpendicular vectors equal, and what does adding up many copies of that give you?

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Why no absolute value? A scalar line integral uses ds=\|\mathbf r'(t)\|\,dt, but a work integral uses d\mathbf r=\mathbf r'(t)\,dt with no norm. In words, why does keeping the velocity vector itself (instead of just its length) make the integral able to tell forward travel from backward travel? A norm can never be negative, so it forgets which way the arrow points. Ask yourself what happens to \mathbf r'(t) when you walk the same road the other way.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: What does circulation feel? The swirling field (-y,x) has nonzero circulation around a circle, while the radial field (x,y) has zero. Geometrically, what is it about how each field sits relative to the direction of travel around the circle that explains the difference? Picture the arrows of each field at a point on the circle and compare them with the tangent direction of motion. Only the part of the field along the path does any work.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: What does the form actually eat? We keep saying that a 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy is a machine that eats a tiny displacement vector and returns a number. Why is it important that the input is a vector (a direction and size of a step) rather than just a point? What information would be missing if you only handed \omega a location and no step? Look at the rule \omega_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v)=P(\mathbf p)v_1+Q(\mathbf p)v_2. The point \mathbf p fixes the coefficients, but what role do the components v_1,v_2 still have to play before a number comes out?

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Why no ds? An arc-length integral carries a length element ds, but the integral of a 1-form does not. In your own words, why does a 1-form not need to know how long the path was? What is it measuring along the curve instead of length, and how does that explain why reversing the curve flips the sign? A 1-form reads tiny steps (dx,dy,dz), and a step has a direction. Distance ds is always positive no matter which way you walk, but a directed step is not. Which of these two notions changes sign when you turn around?

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Arrow or measuring rule? In Cartesian coordinates a vector field and its work 1-form look almost identical, yet in polar coordinates the angular part of the form picks up a factor of r while the vector field does not. What does this mismatch reveal about the difference between an arrow (a vector field) and a measuring rule (a 1-form)? Why should we trust the form, not the dot product, as the thing being integrated along a curve? The dot product that turns \mathbf F into \omega_{\mathbf F} secretly uses the geometry of the plane (how long the basis vectors are). The line integral \int_C P\,dx+Q\,dy never asks about that geometry. Think about which object is defined without reference to lengths and angles.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Why a domain? The text insists that a potential is a formula on a domain, not just a formula. For the angle form \alpha=(-y\,dx+x\,dy)/(x^2+y^2), the integral \oint_C \alpha=2\pi around the counterclockwise unit circle is nonzero even though \alpha looks locally like d\theta. This differs from the earlier form \eta=-y\,dx+x\,dy. What goes wrong if we pretend \theta is a single potential defined on the whole punctured plane? Imagine walking once around the origin and asking what value \theta hands back to you when you return to your starting point. Does it agree with where you began?

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: What does the converse buy us? One direction is easy: an exact form is automatically path independent. The converse says path independence alone produces a potential \phi(X)=\int_A^X\omega. Why is the converse the more surprising and useful half? What does it let you conclude when you have not been handed a formula for \phi? Think about what you can check directly about a field versus what you would love to know. Which one is easier to observe, and which one does the converse promise to deliver from it?

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Why must the loop give zero? For a conservative field, \oint_C \omega=0 around every closed loop, no matter how large or twisted. Explain in your own words why this has to be true, using the idea of a potential rather than any computation. If a field gave nonzero work around some closed loop, what would that say about whether a potential can exist? A closed loop ends where it began, so A=B. Look at what the fundamental theorem reports for \phi(B)-\phi(A) in that case, and ask whether a single-valued \phi could ever produce a nonzero answer.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Which way does the arrow point? We just argued that every exact form satisfies P_y=Q_x. Suppose a friend computes P_y=Q_x for some form and announces, “Great, so it’s exact!” What is the logical gap in that announcement, and why does the implication we proved only run in one direction? Reread the theorem as “exact \Rightarrow closed.” Passing the test is a necessary condition. Ask yourself whether necessary and sufficient are the same thing here—and recall that the upcoming rectangle theorem needs an extra hypothesis before it can turn the arrow around.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: What does the hole actually break? The curl test P_y=Q_x only looks inside tiny neighborhoods, yet the conclusion we want—“\omega is exact on all of D”—is a statement about the whole region. In your own words, why should the presence of a hole be able to spoil a global conclusion even when the local test passes at every single point? Think about a closed curve that wraps around the hole. Simple connectivity is exactly the permission to shrink such a curve to a point. If you cannot shrink it, what guarantee about line integrals over closed loops are you no longer entitled to?

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Why won’t the patches glue? On every small patch, \alpha equals d\theta for an honest potential, so the curl test passes everywhere and local potentials genuinely exist. What goes wrong when you try to stitch all these local angle functions into one continuous potential on the whole punctured plane, and how does this story show that zero curl alone does not guarantee a global potential on every domain? Follow \theta once around the origin and watch its value when you return to the start. A single-valued function must come back to where it began—does the angle? The missing point is what prevents the loop from shrinking, and that is precisely the failure of simple connectivity.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Write \alpha=P\,dx+Q\,dy, where P(x,y)=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad Q(x,y)=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. Compute: P_y \amp= \frac{-(x^2+y^2)+2y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} \amp= \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, and Q_x \amp= \frac{(x^2+y^2)-2x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} \amp= \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. Thus P_y=Q_x everywhere on D.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: What did the test not check? The condition P_y=Q_x only looks at derivatives at each individual point. Why is it possible for this point-by-point test to pass everywhere on D and still leave room for a loop integral like \oint_C\alpha=2\pi to be nonzero? What feature of D is the local test simply unable to notice? A derivative only knows what happens in a tiny neighborhood of a point. Ask yourself whether any such neighborhood can ever “feel” the missing origin, and what a whole loop can sense that a single point cannot.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Why won't shrinking help? We found \oint_{C_R}\alpha=2\pi for every radius R\gt 0, no matter how tiny. If we could only contract the loop down to a single point, the integral would have to vanish. Conceptually, why can't we ever finish shrinking the loop here, and what does that stubborn 2\pi reveal about the hole at the origin? Imagine pulling the loop tighter and tighter toward the center. Is the point you are trying to reach actually part of the domain? A loop that cannot be shrunk to a point inside D is exactly what detects something the formula alone hides.

chapter.title: Vector Fields, Work, and 1-Forms

text: Same formula, different fate? On the right half-plane D_+ the form \alpha is exact, with potential \theta=\arctan(y/x), yet on the punctured plane D the identical formula is closed but not exact. The local rule never changed. Conceptually, what is it about D_+ that lets a single-valued potential exist, and what does the hole in D do to that same potential? Think about whether you can loop all the way around the origin while staying inside D_+. Then picture following \theta continuously once around the origin in D and ask whether you arrive back at the same value you started with.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Why compare opposite sides? The constant parts of the field canceled, and only the differences between opposite sides survived. What is it about a constant push that makes it unable to drive any net circulation around the loop, no matter how strong it is? Picture walking the rectangle once around. A truly uniform push helps you on one side and hinders you equally on the side you traverse in the opposite direction.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Why one number in the plane? In space the curl will need three numbers, but in the plane a single signed number Q_x-P_y is enough. What feature of motion confined to a flat plane makes one number capture the entire rotational behavior at a point? Ask yourself where the axis of any in-plane spinning has to point, and how many independent directions remain for it once the motion is trapped in the page.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: What does interior cancellation mean? When all the interior edges cancel and only the outer boundary survives, the messy inside of the region seems to vanish from the bookkeeping. What is this telling us about the relationship between the total circulation of the field and the field's behavior strictly along the outer edge? Notice that the inside still matters through the accumulated curl. The cancellation says two very different-looking sums are secretly measuring the same thing.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Why call them the same? The boxed identity says a boundary integral \oint_{\partial R}\omega equals a double integral \iint_R(Q_x-P_y)\,dA over the whole inside. One number comes from walking the edge; the other adds up something at every interior point. What does it mean that these two very different-looking quantities are always equal? Think about the cancellation picture: each tiny piece of interior curl is really a tiny loop, and neighboring loops share edges. Where do those shared edges go?

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Compute the boundary integral directly. On the bottom and top edges, dy=0. On the right edge, Q=1 and y goes from 0 to 1, giving \int_0^1 dy=1. On the left edge, Q=0. Therefore \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\omega=1. }

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Where did the circulation go? For \alpha=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} the scalar curl Q_x-P_y is zero at every point where \alpha is defined, yet the boundary integral around the circle is 2\pi, not 0. If the curl vanishes everywhere we can see, what is the boundary integral actually detecting? Green's theorem needs the form to be smooth on all of the inside, including the origin. Ask what the region of the disk includes that the region where \alpha lives does not.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Why must the hole count? For the annulus the two boundary circles are traversed in opposite directions, and their circulations 2\pi and -2\pi cancel to give 0. Why does Green's theorem insist on including the inner circle at all, instead of just the outer one we might naturally draw? The double integral only sees the material that is actually part of the region. Picture standing inside the region with the wall always on your left: which way does that force you to walk around the hole?

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: What does zero divergence really say? Suppose a field has \operatorname{div}\mathbf F=0 at a point. Does that mean nothing is happening there, or could the field still be doing something interesting near that point? Explain in your own words what the zero is actually measuring. Remember that \operatorname{div}\mathbf F records net outflow per unit area. Think about a tiny box: what must be true about what enters versus what leaves, and is that the same as the field being still?

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: One theorem wearing two hats? The flux form and the circulation form of Green's theorem look like two different results, yet the text obtains one from the other just by changing the 1-form being integrated. Why is it reasonable that a single theorem can describe both circulation and flux? Look at what both boundary integrals have in common. Each turns a measurement along \partial R into an integral of a derivative density over R. What is the object that is really being integrated around the boundary?

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Where could a hidden source hide? The hypotheses ask \mathbf F to have continuous partial derivatives on an open region containing R. If we quietly ignored a singularity or a jump inside R, why might the interior integral of \operatorname{div}\mathbf F come out too small compared to the true boundary flux? A place where the field is not smooth can act like an extra, unseen boundary. Ask yourself where flux could be entering or leaving that the integral over the smooth part of R never gets to count.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Why two forms? The vector field (M,N) never changes, yet swapping M\,dx+N\,dy for M\,dy-N\,dx turns a circulation measurement into a flux measurement. In your own words, what is the 1-form actually deciding when you choose one over the other? Think about what each form reads at a single tiny step along the curve: a step's motion along the boundary versus its motion through the boundary.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: How can d\alpha=0 yet the loop integral not vanish? For the punctured-plane form we have d\alpha=0 everywhere it is defined, but \oint_C\alpha=2\pi around the unit circle. If Green's theorem says the boundary integral equals \int_R d\omega, why does this not force the loop integral to be zero? The equation \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega only speaks about a region R on which the form is defined and smooth. Ask whether the disk bounded by the circle is such a region.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: What stays the same as the dimension climbs? The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus and Green's theorem both fit the single shape \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega, just one dimension apart. What is the common idea that this one sentence is expressing, the part that does not change as we move from an interval to a region to a surface? Focus on the relationship between a boundary and the derivative d\omega living inside it, rather than on the particular formulas. What role does the boundary play in every version?

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Why does the shared edge vanish? The two rectangles compute the same integrand Q(1,y) along the same edge E, yet the contributions add to zero. Without doing any new computation, explain what feature of the boundary, other than the integrand, is responsible for the cancellation. Ask what is different about how R_1 and R_2 each walk along E, and recall how a line integral responds to that difference.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: What plays the role of the endpoints? In the one-dimensional sum, the intermediate values f(x_1),\ldots,f(x_{n-1}) cancel and only f(x_n)-f(x_0) survives. In the tiled region, what is the two-dimensional analogue of those vanishing intermediate values, and what survives in their place? Each interior edge belongs to exactly two rectangles, while each piece of the outer boundary belongs to only one. Let that asymmetry guide you.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Where could the cancellation hide trouble? The cancellation of interior edges seems automatic, so why must we still insist that the boundary include every component of the region? Describe, conceptually, what could go wrong with the argument if a hole in the region were left without a boundary curve. A hole's edge is also an interior edge of the surrounding tiles. Think about whether that edge finds a partner to cancel with, or whether it should have remained as part of \partial S.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Where does the disk argument break? We found d\alpha=0 at every point where \alpha is defined, yet \oint_C\alpha=2\pi rather than 0. Which exact hypothesis of Green's theorem fails for the disk bounded by C, and why is it not enough that d\alpha=0 at every point except the origin? Read the theorem's domain requirement literally: it asks for the form to be defined and smooth on all of the region, not just on most of it. Where does \alpha live, and what single point sits inside the disk?

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Why isn't the area enough? Suppose you only adjusted for the missing area of the hole but kept integrating over the outer circle alone. Why would Green's theorem still disagree with you? In terms of the cancellation idea from the proof, what does the inner curve do that no other piece of the boundary can undo? Picture slicing the annulus into rectangles. Interior edges pair up and cancel, but the edge hugging the hole has no neighbor on the other side. What happens to a boundary piece that never finds a partner?

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: What does the jump act like? The coefficient Q has Q_x=0 everywhere it is differentiable, so the naive interior integral is 0, yet the boundary integral is 1. Which hypothesis of Green's theorem does the jump violate, and why does the section describe the line x=0 as a hidden edge rather than an ordinary interior point? The theorem assumes P and Q are C^1 on the whole region. Ask yourself what the missing contribution would look like if you redrew the region's boundary to run along the jump line.

chapter.title: Green's Theorem and the Beginning of Stokes' Idea

text: Compute the boundary integral. On the bottom and top edges, dy=0. On the left edge, Q=0. On the right edge, Q=1, and y goes from 0 to 1. Thus \boxed{\oint_{\partial R}\omega=1.}

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why two parameters? A surface lives in three-dimensional space, yet we describe it using only two parameters (u,v). Why two and not three? What does this say about how a surface sits inside space? Think about how many directions you can actually walk while staying on the rubber sheet, before it is bent or after.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: What does the order encode? Swapping \mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v for \mathbf r_v\times \mathbf r_u flips the normal to the other side of the surface. Geometrically, the surface itself has not changed at all. So what extra piece of information are we choosing when we pick an order for the cross product? The surface is the same either way, but you select which normal direction counts as positive. An arbitrary patch need not have an inside or an outside.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: What do the two tangents build? Holding v fixed and varying u gives one grid curve; holding u fixed and varying v gives another. Why does this produce two tangent vectors \mathbf r_u and \mathbf r_v at a point, and at a regular point, what geometric object does their cross product \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v describe? Each parameter direction traces its own curve through the point, and each curve has its own tangent. Recall that a cross product is perpendicular to both factors. If \mathbf r_u and \mathbf r_v both lie in its tangent plane, where must \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v point?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: A coordinate defect or a sharp tip? Both the cone coordinates and the spherical coordinates have a zero cross product at a collapsed edge. Why does this fact alone not decide whether the image has a tangent plane? What additional argument distinguishes the cone? Use the regular graph patch for the sphere and the three independent generator directions for the cone.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why a length, not a vector? The cross product \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v is a vector with a direction, yet the area element dS keeps only its length \|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|. What goes wrong if you tried to call the whole vector the area? What is the length alone telling you about the little patch of surface? Think about what a number like area should and should not depend on. Where does the direction of \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v point, and is that the same kind of information as how big is the parallelogram?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why multiply before adding? To find the mass of a thin shell we compute \iint_S \sigma\,dS rather than just multiplying a single density value by the total area. Why does a varying density \sigma(x,y,z) force us to multiply inside the integral, patch by patch, instead of multiplying once at the end? Imagine the shell is heavy near the top and light near the bottom. Would one single number for density honestly describe every patch? Picture what each tiny \sigma\,\Delta S contributes before the sum.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Compute: \mathbf r_\phi=(a\cos\phi\cos\theta,\,a\cos\phi\sin\theta,\,-a\sin\phi), and \mathbf r_\theta=(-a\sin\phi\sin\theta,\,a\sin\phi\cos\theta,\,0). A direct cross product gives \|\mathbf r_\phi\times\mathbf r_\theta\|=a^2\sin\phi. Therefore \boxed{dS=a^2\sin\phi\,d\phi\,d\theta.}

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Whose fault is the extra area? Letting \theta run from 0 to 4\pi gave 40\pi for a cylinder whose true area is 20\pi. The physical cylinder never changed. So what did the integral actually measure, and what does this tell you about the difference between a surface and a way of sweeping it out? The formula faithfully adds up area for every (u,v) in the parameter region. Ask not is the answer wrong? but how many times did my map pass over each point of the cylinder?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Choosing a side? Choosing an orientation of a surface means making a consistent choice of normal direction, or equivalently a consistent choice of side. What goes wrong on a Möbius strip that prevents such a consistent choice from existing? Picture sliding a normal vector all the way around the strip and asking where it ends up. Imagine carrying a small normal arrow once around the Möbius strip without ever flipping it. When it returns to the starting point, which way is it pointing compared to how it began? What does that say about having a single well-defined side?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Tangent flow, zero flux? Suppose the fluid is racing along quickly but everywhere stays tangent to the surface, so \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=0. The flux is zero even though nothing is standing still. What does a flux of zero actually tell you about how the surface experiences this flow? Think of the screen as a turnstile: flux counts what passes through it, not what glides past it. Which of those is happening here?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why does signed flux require an orientation? A Möbius strip has only one side, so it cannot be oriented. In your own words, why does the signed flux integral defined above fail to have a global meaning once we lose a continuous choice of positive side? Imagine sliding the unit normal \widehat{\mathbf n} once around the strip and asking which side counts as out. What happens to your answer when it returns to the start?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Practice: the cylinder normal For \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), compute \mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z. Does it point inward or outward?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: For \mathbf r(\theta,z)=(2\cos\theta,2\sin\theta,z), compute \mathbf r_\theta\times\mathbf r_z. Does it point inward or outward?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: What does zero net flux mean? A closed surface reports a total outward flux of zero. Does that force the field to be tangent to the surface everywhere, or could fluid still be streaming in and out? Explain what the single number zero is and is not promising you about the region inside. Zero is a balance, not an absence. Picture water entering the bottom of a box and leaving the top at the same rate.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why three shadows? The plane only needed a single oriented-area form, dx\wedge dy, but flux in space uses three: dy\wedge dz, dz\wedge dx, and dx\wedge dy. What is it about a surface sitting in \mathbb R^3 that makes one shadow insufficient, and why exactly three rather than two or four? A tiny tilted parallelogram in space casts a shadow on each of the three coordinate planes. Think about how many independent ways its orientation can lean.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: What does the sign remember? When you flip a surface's orientation, the integral of \Phi_{\mathbf F} changes sign even though the surface occupies the very same points in space. What physical or geometric information is the sign keeping track of, and why should a measurement of flux care which way the surface faces? Imagine the field as flowing fluid. Crossing a window from inside to outside is not the same event as crossing from outside to inside.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: What does the form reveal? The cross product computes flux faster, yet the text insists the 2-form \Phi_{\mathbf F}=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy is more revealing. What does writing flux as a sum of wedge terms make visible that the single symbol \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS hides from you? Notice that the cross product is a trick special to three dimensions. Ask what each wedge term is separately telling you about how the field pierces a particular kind of oriented area.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why three numbers? A paddle wheel in the plane reported a single circulation number, but in space the curl needs three components. What does each component actually measure, and why can't a single number capture spinning in space the way it did in the plane? Think about which way the paddle wheel faces. A wheel lying flat in the xy-plane feels a different swirl than one standing up in the yz-plane.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why doesn't the surface matter? The flat disk and the curved cap share the same boundary circle, and they returned the same curl flux \pi. In your own words, why should two such different surfaces be forced to agree? What does Stokes' theorem reveal about what the answer really depends on? The line integral on the right of Stokes' theorem only sees the boundary curve. If that curve is fixed, what freedom does the surface in the middle really have?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: One story, many shapes? The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Green's theorem, and Stokes' theorem all share the pattern \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega. What is the single idea common to all three, and what role does taking a derivative d play in lifting the integral up by one dimension? In each case, information on the inside is recovered by looking only at the edge. Ask yourself how the degree of the integrand changes when applying d; the geometric region itself is not being differentiated.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Can fluid move where divergence is zero? A friend says, If \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=0 at a point, then the fluid must be sitting still there. Is that right? Explain what \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=0 actually tells you about the flow near that point, and what it does not tell you. Divergence measures net outward flow from a tiny box, not speed. Think about the swirling field (-y,x,0): things are clearly moving, yet nothing piles up or drains out.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why does only the boundary survive? When we add up the outward flux over all the little boxes, the contributions from interior faces cancel and only the outer boundary is left over. Why does that cancellation have to happen? What feature of two neighboring boxes guarantees their shared face contributes equal and opposite amounts? Picture the single face shared by two boxes. Each box wants its own outward normal there. How do those two outward normals compare on that one shared wall?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Reading the inside from the boundary The divergence theorem lets you compute the total source strength inside a region by measuring only the flux across its boundary. Why is it remarkable that you can learn what is happening throughout a solid without ever looking inside it? What does this say about how local sources and sinks relate to the boundary as a whole? Whatever a source creates deep inside has to get out somewhere, and the only exit is the boundary. Think about how a hidden source eventually announces itself on \partial E.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Compute its curl: \nabla\times(\nabla T) \amp= \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y+3) - \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(x^2+z), \right. \amp\qquad \frac{\partial}{\partial z}(2xy) - \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(y+3), \amp\qquad\left. \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(x^2+z) - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2xy) \right) \amp= (1-1,\ 0-0,\ 2x-2x) \amp= \mathbf 0.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why is closed-loop circulation zero? Let f have continuous second partial derivatives on a neighborhood of a small disk. Use the fundamental theorem for work integrals from to explain why \oint_C\nabla f\cdot d\mathbf r=0 around its boundary C. How does this agree with the local paddle-wheel interpretation of curl? The integral is the final potential minus the initial potential. A closed path has the same starting and ending point.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Two ingredients, one zero? The computation of d(df) relied on two separate facts: the wedge product is antisymmetric (so dx\wedge dy=-\,dy\wedge dx), and the mixed partials are equal (f_{xy}=f_{yx}). What does each fact contribute, and why does the result fail to be zero if either one is missing? Picture the two surviving terms before cancellation. One ingredient lines them up as a difference; the other makes that difference vanish. Try removing each in turn and see which structure collapses.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Same derivative, different verdict? The field \mathbf A has zero curl everywhere it is defined, yet its loop integral around the circle is 2\pi rather than 0. Since the curl test is purely local, what is it about the shape of the domain—not the formula for \mathbf A—that lets a curl-free field still fail to have a global potential? A potential would make every closed-loop integral zero. Ask whether the loop could be shrunk to a point while staying inside the domain, and what the missing z-axis has to do with that.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Why does area survive but flux does not? On a Möbius strip the scalar surface integral \iint_S f\,dS is perfectly well defined, yet the flux integral \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS is not. What feature of flux, which area simply does not have, is the one that fails on a one-sided surface? Think about what each integral asks at a point. Does measuring a little patch of area require you to know which way the patch faces?

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: Which hypothesis did the origin break? Someone argues: since \nabla\cdot\mathbf G=0 everywhere we computed it, the divergence theorem forces the flux to be 0, so the value 4\pi must be an arithmetic slip. Which exact hypothesis of the divergence theorem does this argument quietly assume, and where in E does that hypothesis fail? The theorem asks for something to be true throughout the solid, not just on the boundary. Look at the single point the sphere encloses.

chapter.title: Surfaces, Flux, Curl, and Divergence in Space

text: No contradiction, but why not? Here the surface integral gave \pi while the boundary integral gave -\pi, and yet we insist Stokes' theorem is unharmed. What unstated compatibility condition between the surface's normal and the boundary's direction had to hold for the two numbers to be required to agree? Ask which boundary direction the upward normal actually pairs with. The clockwise loop is the boundary of which orientation?

text: A worked review problem: choose the easier surface Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(-y,x,z). Let C be the circle x^2+y^2=4,\qquad z=3, oriented counterclockwise as seen from above. Compute \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r. The curve bounds many surfaces. The easiest is the flat disk D:\quad x^2+y^2\le4,\qquad z=3, oriented upward. Compute the curl: \nabla\times\mathbf F \amp= (R_y-Q_z,\ P_z-R_x,\ Q_x-P_y) \amp= (0-0,\ 0-0,\ 1-(-1)) \amp= (0,0,2). On the upward disk, \widehat{\mathbf n}=(0,0,1). So \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r \amp= \iint_D(\nabla\times\mathbf F)\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp= \iint_D 2\,dS \amp= 2\cdot \operatorname{Area}(D) \amp= 2\cdot4\pi \amp= 8\pi. Thus \boxed{\oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r=8\pi.} The z-component of the original field did not affect the answer. Curl, not the field itself, is what Stokes' theorem sends through the spanning surface.

text: A worked review problem: close the surface Let S be the upper hemisphere x^2+y^2+z^2=9,\qquad z\ge0, oriented upward and outward. Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,2z). Find the flux through S. The surface S is not closed. Close it with the disk D:\quad x^2+y^2\le9,\qquad z=0, oriented downward, so that S\cup D is the outward boundary of the upper half-ball. The divergence is \nabla\cdot\mathbf F=1+1+2=4. The volume of the upper half-ball of radius 3 is \frac12\cdot\frac43\pi(3)^3=18\pi. So the total outward flux through S\cup D is 4\cdot18\pi=72\pi. On the disk D, we have z=0, so \mathbf F=(x,y,0). The downward normal is (0,0,-1). Thus \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}=0. The disk contributes no flux. Therefore the flux through the hemisphere is \boxed{72\pi.} The open surface was handled by adding the missing piece and then subtracting its contribution.
