chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Why orient a point?A 0-form just records a number at each point, so why do we bother attaching a sign to the point we integrate over? What would we lose if every point were treated as positive?Picture the two endpoints of an interval in \int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a). Which endpoint contributes with which sign, and what would happen to that formula if both came in positively?

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: What does the wedge remember?Ordinary area does not care about order, yet the wedge insists that dy\wedge dx=-dx\wedge dy. What information is the form trying to hold onto by refusing to let these two be equal?Think about which way you sweep around a little patch of the plane. A 2-form measures oriented area, so swapping the two directions is like flipping the patch over.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Why no 4-form in space?In three-dimensional space the volume form dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is the top of the ladder. Conceptually, why can there be no genuine 4-form here, in terms of the kind of tiny object a form is supposed to measure?A k-form is built to measure k-dimensional oriented pieces. Ask yourself what a 4-dimensional tiny object would even look like sitting inside ordinary space.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Why two kinds of object? A vector and a covector in \mathbb R^3 are each described by three numbers, so it is tempting to call them the same thing. What is the genuine difference in their jobs, and why does that difference deserve two separate names? Ask what each one does. One of them is something you can travel along; the other is a machine you feed a displacement to in order to get a number out.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: What does the subscript carry? A 1-form attaches a covector \omega_{\mathbf p} to every point \mathbf p. Conceptually, why must the measuring rule be allowed to change from point to point, rather than being a single fixed covector everywhere? Picture walking along a curve where the wind or terrain changes as you move. Should the rule that scores your tangent direction stay the same at every location?

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: What does the dot product add? The differential df_{\mathbf p} already turns a tangent vector into a number all by itself. So what extra ingredient does choosing a dot product supply, and why is the gradient vector unavailable until that choice is made? The differential measures; it never needs lengths or angles. The gradient is meant to be a vector that reproduces that measurement through a dot product, so something has to decide how vectors and measurements correspond.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: What is the minus sign really saying? We found dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx. Setting aside the algebra, what geometric fact about a parallelogram is this minus sign recording? Why should reversing the order of the two edge directions flip the sign of the area rather than its size? Picture walking around the parallelogram's boundary. What changes about the direction of that walk when you list the edges in the opposite order?

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Why must a covector wedged with itself vanish? We get dx\wedge dx=0, and more generally \alpha\wedge\alpha=0 for any covector \alpha. Without redoing the computation, explain why this has to happen. What does it mean to try to build an oriented area out of a single direction of measurement? Area needs two independent directions. If you only ever read the same component, how many genuinely different directions are you measuring?

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Why three basic 2-forms in space but only one in the plane? In the plane a 2-form has just one piece, dx\wedge dy, yet in space we need three: dy\wedge dz, dz\wedge dx, and dx\wedge dy. What is it about a surface patch sitting in three dimensions that forces three measurements, when a patch in the plane needs only one? Think about the shadows a tilted patch casts onto the coordinate planes. How many coordinate planes are there to cast a shadow on in the plane, and how many in space?

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Why can't we add a line and an area? We freely add two 1-forms, yet we refuse to add a 1-form and a 2-form into a single form. What is it about the meaning of a form's degree that makes the second sum a different kind of thing entirely? Ask what each form is built to measure. A 1-form reads a tangent vector; a 2-form reads an oriented patch of area. Adding numbers only makes sense when they answer the same question.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Why does space itself set a ceiling? In \mathbb R^3 every form of degree greater than 3 collapses to zero, and in \mathbb R^n the ceiling sits at degree n. Why should the dimension of the space we live in decide the highest degree a nonzero form can have? A degree-k wedge is built from k basic 1-forms, each pointing along a coordinate direction. If k exceeds the number of independent directions available, some direction must repeat. Recall what a repeated factor does to a wedge.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: What is the minus sign trying to tell us? The graded rule \beta\wedge\alpha=(-1)^{k\ell}\alpha\wedge\beta can feel like bookkeeping. But when swapping two factors flips the sign, what real feature of the geometry is that minus sign keeping track of, and why does a repeated factor then have to give zero? Think of the wedge as recording oriented volume. Swapping two directions reverses the orientation, the way exchanging two rows flips a determinant. Then ask what orientation an oriented region could possibly have if two of its directions coincide.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Why does the form move backward? The map T sends points forward, from the (u,v)-world to the (x,y)-world, yet T^* carries the form \omega the other way, from (x,y) back to (u,v). Why is it natural for a form to travel opposite to the points, rather than alongside them? Think about what a form does for a living: it waits to be fed a coordinate direction and report a number. If you only know how to build directions in the (u,v)-world, which world must the form end up living in so it can read them?

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Where did the cross product come from? Nothing in the setup of \mathbf r^*\Phi mentioned a cross product, yet the three coefficients turned out to be exactly the components of \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v. What is it about pulling back a 2-form through the wedge product that forces this cross product to appear on its own? Each basic 2-form like dy\wedge dz pulls back to a 2\times 2 determinant in the parameter derivatives. Recall how a cross product is assembled out of 2\times 2 determinants of the same columns.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: What does the Jacobian's sign mean? When T^*(dx\wedge dy) produces a negative Jacobian coefficient, the ordinary change-of-variables formula would simply take its absolute value. What information is the bare wedge product holding onto that the absolute value throws away, and why might we sometimes want to keep it? Ask what a sign could possibly be recording about the map T itself. Picture a small loop traced counterclockwise in the (u,v)-square and what happens to its turning direction after T sends it into the (x,y)-plane.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Why a 1-form for a curve? A curve is one-dimensional, and the object we integrate over it is a 1-form. Looking at the definition above, what is it about the pullback \mathbf r^*\omega=g(t)\,dt that makes a 1-form exactly the right kind of thing to integrate over a curve, rather than a 2-form or a plain function? The parameter domain [a,b] is one-dimensional. Count how many dt factors you need before \int_a^b has something to act on.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: What is the integral really about? We say the integral depends on the oriented geometric object, not on the clock or grid used to describe it. In your own words, why should we expect a quantity like circulation or flux to be independent of the chosen parametrization, and what role does the substitution rule play in turning that expectation into a fact? Think about what the parametrization is and is not part of: it names the points, but it does not change which oriented curve or surface you are standing on. The Jacobian factor from the substitution rule is exactly what cancels the change of clock.

chapter.title: Differential Forms and the Wedge Product

text: Where does the minus sign come from? Reversing the orientation of a curve, surface, or solid flips the sign of the integral, for example \int_{-C}\omega=-\int_C\omega. What does it mean to say a form is an oriented integrand, and why does this sign behavior feel natural once you remember that dx\wedge dy=-\,dy\wedge dx? Reversing orientation swaps the order of the basis pieces inside the wedge. Ask yourself what happens to a signed area or signed volume when you trace its boundary the other way around.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: A rule, not a reading? We found dT_P=3\,dx-\frac13\,dy, and feeding it the velocity \mathbf v=(2,-3) returned the single number 7. So why do we call dT_P a 1-form rather than just saying the temperature is changing at 7^\circ per second at P? The number 7 belonged to one particular direction. Ask what dT_P would report for a different velocity, and what kind of object can answer that for every direction at once.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Why does the gradient need a dot product? The differential df happily measures tangent vectors without any mention of a dot product, yet to even speak of the gradient \nabla f we had to choose one. What does the dot product supply that turns the covector df into the vector \nabla f? A 1-form takes a vector and returns a number. To go the other way, from a measuring rule back to an arrow, you need a way to match directions with lengths and angles. Which structure carries that information?

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: What if you double your speed? Suppose you pass through \mathbf p along the same heading but twice as fast, so your velocity is 2\mathbf v instead of \mathbf v. Without recomputing anything, what does this say about df_{\mathbf p}(2\mathbf v) compared to df_{\mathbf p}(\mathbf v), and why is that exactly what a rate of change should do? Remember that df_{\mathbf p} is a linear measuring rule. Think about how the field looks the same along your path, but the clock is now running differently.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Why a 2-form? We started with a 1-form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy and its exterior derivative came out as a multiple of dx\wedge dy, a 2-form. Thinking about what \omega integrates over and what d\omega should measure, why is it natural that the derivative of a 1-form is a 2-form rather than another 1-form? A 1-form is integrated along a curve; d\omega is meant to report what happens inside the loop. What is the dimension of the region a 2-form is built to be integrated over?

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Is curl really a new idea? We just saw that d\omega_{\mathbf F}=\Phi_{\nabla\times\mathbf F}, so the curl is the exterior derivative of a work 1-form read through the flux-form dictionary. In your own words, what does this say about why curl shows up at all in vector calculus, and why it produces three components in space but only one scalar in the plane? Count the independent basic 2-forms in the plane versus in space (how many ways are there to write dx\wedge dy-type pieces?). The number of curl components is just the number of slots d\omega has to fill.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

optional_markers.title: Green's and Stokes' theorem previewed again

text: Green's and Stokes' theorem previewed again In the plane, the formula d(P\,dx+Q\,dy)=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy turns Green's theorem into the short statement \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega.} The left side is circulation around the boundary. The right side is circulation density added over the inside. What is \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega saying? The compact statement \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega equates a boundary integral with an integral over the inside. Conceptually, why should circulation measured only along the edge equal circulation density summed throughout the interior? What would go wrong with this balance if the density d\omega were not the local version of the boundary circulation? Imagine tiling R with many tiny loops. Adjacent edges are traversed in opposite directions and cancel; only the outer boundary survives. What is left adding up the tiny loop circulations is exactly the interior sum of d\omega. For example, with \omega=(3-y)\,dx+2x\,dy, we found d\omega=3\,dx\wedge dy. So Green's theorem says \boxed{\int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R 3\,dx\wedge dy=3\,\operatorname{Area}(R)} for every positively oriented plane region R to which the theorem applies. In space, the same statement becomes Stokes' theorem: \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega.} Now S is an oriented surface, and \partial S is its oriented boundary curve. The exterior derivative d\omega is the curl 2-form. The same boundary with a curved surface Let \omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy+z\,dz, so d\omega=2\,dx\wedge dy. Let S be the upper hemisphere x^2+y^2+z^2=1,\qquad z\ge0, oriented upward. Its boundary is the unit circle in the xy-plane, oriented counterclockwise as seen from above. Stokes' theorem predicts \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S 2\,dx\wedge dy. The form dx\wedge dy measures the signed xy-shadow of the surface. The upward-oriented upper hemisphere casts the unit disk as its positive shadow. Therefore \int_S 2\,dx\wedge dy=2\pi. Check the boundary integral directly. Parametrize the boundary by \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t,0),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dx=-\sin t\,dt,\qquad dy=\cos t\,dt,\qquad dz=0. So \mathbf r^*\omega \amp= -\sin t(-\sin t\,dt)+\cos t(\cos t\,dt)+0 \amp= dt. Hence \boxed{\int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}dt=2\pi.} The curved surface and the flat disk have the same boundary, and the same d\omega accounts for the boundary circulation. The hypotheses behind Green's and Stokes' theorem matter. The form must be defined and smooth on a region containing the surface or plane region we integrate over. A missing point can break the conclusion. A hidden singularity breaks the theorem Consider the 1-form \omega_0=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}\,dx+\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}\,dy. It is defined on \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, not at the origin. Away from the origin, P=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2},\qquad Q=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. A direct calculation gives Q_x-P_y=0, so d\omega_0=0 wherever the form is defined. Now integrate around the unit circle C:\quad \mathbf r(t)=(\cos t,\sin t),\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. On this circle, x^2+y^2=1, so \omega_0=-y\,dx+x\,dy. As before, \mathbf r^*\omega_0=dt. Therefore \boxed{\int_C\omega_0=2\pi.} If we pretended Green's theorem applied to the whole disk, we would get \int_C\omega_0=\int_{\text{disk}}d\omega_0=0, which is false. The problem is the missing origin. The form is not defined on the disk bounded by C. So the condition defined and smooth on the whole region is not a technical detail. It prevents a singularity from hiding inside the boundary. The exterior derivative has now turned functions into 1-forms and 1-forms into 2-forms: f\longmapsto df,\qquad \omega\longmapsto d\omega. The next step is forced by the divergence theorem. A flux 2-form measures flow through a surface. Its derivative should measure source density inside a volume. That will be a 3-form, and the old vector name for its coefficient is divergence.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

optional_markers.title: Green's and Stokes' theorem previewed again

text: What is \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega saying? The compact statement \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega equates a boundary integral with an integral over the inside. Conceptually, why should circulation measured only along the edge equal circulation density summed throughout the interior? What would go wrong with this balance if the density d\omega were not the local version of the boundary circulation? Imagine tiling R with many tiny loops. Adjacent edges are traversed in opposite directions and cancel; only the outer boundary survives. What is left adding up the tiny loop circulations is exactly the interior sum of d\omega.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Why one operation, three names? Gradient, curl, and divergence all turn out to be the single operation d applied in degrees 0, 1, and 2. What does it tell you about these three classical operators that they are really the same degree-raising step, just read on different kinds of forms? Think about what d always does: it raises a k-form to a (k+1)-form and measures how the form changes from the boundary of a small region to its interior. The classical name you read off depends only on the degree you started in.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: What does the balance really claim? The relation \int_{\partial B}\Phi = \int_B d\Phi sets a boundary integral equal to an interior integral. In plain words, why should the flux leaking out through the skin of a box be the same as the source density piled up inside it? What would it mean physically if these two numbers disagreed? Imagine nothing is created or destroyed inside the box. Then anything that flows out of the boundary had to come from somewhere within. The interior integral of d\Phi is just the bookkeeping that adds up every tiny source.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text:
The divergence theorem previewed again The divergence theorem is the 2-form version of the same boundary principle. Divergence theorem, form version Let E be a solid region whose boundary is made from finitely many smooth surface pieces. Give \partial E the outward orientation. Let \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy have C^1 coefficient functions on a region containing E. Then  oxed{ \int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_E d\Phi. } If \Phi=\Phi_{\mathbf F}, this is the classical formula  oxed{ \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E 
abla\cdot\mathbf F\,dV. } The theorem has three sign-and-domain traps. A disk is not a closed boundary Let D be the unit disk in the plane z=0, oriented upward, and let \mathbf F=(0,0,1). Its flux form is \Phi=dx\wedge dy. The flux through the disk is \int_D dx\wedge dy=\pi. But d\Phi=0. This does not contradict the divergence theorem. The disk alone is not the boundary of a solid. It has a rim. The theorem needs a closed boundary surface. Outward orientation matters Let E=[0,1]	imes[0,1]	imes[0,1] and \mathbf F=(x,0,0). Then 
abla\cdot\mathbf F=1. So \int_E d\Phi_{\mathbf F}=1. With outward orientation, the only nonzero flux is through the face x=1, and it is 1. With inward orientation, the same surface integral becomes -1. The theorem uses the outward orientation. A hidden singularity can carry source strength Consider the inverse-square radial field \mathbf G(x,y,z) =  rac{(x,y,z)}{(x^2+y^2+z^2)^{3/2}}, defined on \mathbb R^3\setminus\{(0,0,0)\}. Away from the origin, 
abla\cdot\mathbf G=0, so d\Phi_{\mathbf G}=0 where the form is defined. Now integrate through the sphere S_a of radius a, oriented outward. On the sphere, \widehat{\mathbf n}= rac{(x,y,z)}{a} and \mathbf G= rac{(x,y,z)}{a^3}. Thus \mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} =  rac{1}{a^2}. Therefore \int_{S_a}\Phi_{\mathbf G} = \iint_{S_a}\mathbf G\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS =  rac{1}{a^2}\cdot 4\pi a^2 = 4\pi. It would be wrong to say d\Phi_{\mathbf G}=0, \qquad 	ext{so the sphere flux is }0. The field is not defined at the origin, and the origin lies inside the sphere. The missing point is carrying the source. How can d\Phi=0 yet the flux be 4\pi? For the inverse-square field, d\Phi_{\mathbf G}=0 everywhere the form is defined, and yet the outward flux through a sphere around the origin is 4\pi, not 0. What is it about the hole at the origin that lets a source hide there, even though the source density vanishes at every point you can actually evaluate? The divergence theorem trades a boundary integral for an interior integral only when the form is defined on the whole solid. Here the origin is missing, so the interior integral is not allowed to swallow that point. Ask where the theorem's hypothesis quietly fails. The exterior derivative has now moved through every degree available in ordinary space: 0\longrightarrow 1\longrightarrow 2\longrightarrow 3. There is no new ordinary spatial integrand after 3-forms. But we can still ask a different question: what happens if we apply d twice? The answer is always zero for smooth forms. That one fact explains both 
abla	imes(
abla f)=\mathbf 0 and 
abla\cdot(
abla	imes\mathbf F)=0. It also has a geometric reason: a boundary has no boundary.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: How can d\Phi=0 yet the flux be 4\pi? For the inverse-square field, d\Phi_{\mathbf G}=0 everywhere the form is defined, and yet the outward flux through a sphere around the origin is 4\pi, not 0. What is it about the hole at the origin that lets a source hide there, even though the source density vanishes at every point you can actually evaluate? The divergence theorem trades a boundary integral for an interior integral only when the form is defined on the whole solid. Here the origin is missing, so the interior integral is not allowed to swallow that point. Ask where the theorem's hypothesis quietly fails.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Who does the cancelling? In the computation above, the cancellation in d(df)=0 came from two features of the wedge product: dx\wedge dx=0 and dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx. If the wedge were instead a symmetric product, with dx\wedge dy=+dy\wedge dx, would you still expect the second derivative to vanish? What does this tell you about where the rule d^2=0 really comes from? Trace which terms in the final sum relied on the minus sign to cancel. Ask what would survive without it, and notice it has nothing to do with the function f you chose.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Why can't a hill make you spin? We just read \nabla\times(\nabla f)=\mathbf 0 as saying a gradient field has no local rotation. In plain terms, why should the steepest-ascent directions of a surface refuse to swirl? Try to say what would be strange about a landscape whose uphill arrows curled around in little circles. Imagine walking a tiny closed loop on the hillside. A gradient measures change in height, and you return to the height you started at. Connect that round-trip with the absence of curl, no formula required.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Algebra and geometry, same sentence? This section paired two statements: the algebraic rule d^2=0 and the geometric rule \partial^2=0, the boundary of a boundary is zero. In your own words, what does it mean that these are the same idea seen from two sides? Why is it satisfying, rather than a coincidence, that they appear together in \int_{\partial M}\alpha=\int_M d\alpha? Look at the chain that applies the Stokes pattern twice. Which rule kills the left end, and which kills the right end? Ask why a single equation can only stay true if both rules hold at once.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Why is exactness the strong condition? We just saw that exact always forces closed, but not the other way around. In your own words, why should “\alpha=d\beta” be a stronger demand than “d\alpha=0”? What does an antiderivative \beta give you that merely knowing d\alpha=0 does not? Closedness is a condition you can check by a local computation at each point. Exactness asks for a single object \beta that works everywhere at once. Which of those is easier to satisfy?

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: What does the missing point actually break? The angle form satisfies d\alpha=0 at every single point of the punctured plane, yet it fails to be exact there. If the closedness test passes everywhere the form lives, what is it about the missing origin that can still spoil exactness? Picture building a potential \theta by integrating \alpha as you walk around a loop that encircles the hole. Do you arrive back at the same value you started with? An honest function cannot disagree with itself at one point.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Local clue, global verdict? The derivative d\alpha only inspects tiny rectangles, so it never sees a hole sitting far away. Why does that explain how a form can be closed (a purely local fact) and yet not exact (a global one)? What is the integral around a loop measuring that the local derivative cannot? Think of d\alpha=0 as a clue gathered point by point, and exactness as a verdict about the whole domain at once. The shape of the domain — whether a loop can be shrunk to a point — is the missing ingredient.

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Why does the loop notice the hole? The derivative d\alpha=0 everywhere on D, yet the integral around the unit circle is not zero. Explain, in words, what the loop is detecting that the local condition d\alpha=0 simply cannot see. Ask yourself whether the loop could be shrunk down to a single point while staying inside D. What stands in the way?

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Where does the flux come from? We found d\Phi=0 at every point where \Phi is defined, and yet the flux through the sphere is 4\pi. If the local source density vanishes everywhere, where is the flux coming from, and why does removing a tiny ball make the divergence theorem behave again? Think about the one point that the form refuses to talk about. Is it inside the sphere? Is it inside the shell?

chapter.title: Exterior Derivatives: Gradient, Curl, and Divergence Revisited

text: Two kinds of closed, one role for the hole? A form being closed (d\omega=0) and a curve or surface being closed (\partial C=0) are different statements. Yet in both the plane and space examples, it is a closed object wrapped around a missing point that exposes the failure of exactness. Why is it precisely the hole that lets these two notions of closed meet and produce a nonzero answer? Imagine filling in the missing point. Could the closed loop or sphere then be the boundary of something living entirely inside the domain? What would that force the integral to be?

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why does the hole turn the other way? The outer edge of the annulus is walked counterclockwise, but the inner edge around the hole is walked clockwise. Without computing anything, explain why these two opposite-looking directions are really the same rule. What single phrase ties them together? Stand on the boundary and ask: on which side does the gray material sit as you walk? Trace the inner circle clockwise in your mind and watch where the region lies.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: What does forced mean here? We say that picking a side of the surface (a normal \mathbf n) forces the direction you walk the boundary. What would go wrong if you tried to flip the boundary direction while keeping the same normal \mathbf n? Why can't the two choices be made independently? Point your right thumb along \mathbf n and let your fingers curl. There is only one way they curl. Think about what Stokes' theorem \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega would say if the two sides disagreed by a sign.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: What is the boundary of a boundary? The boundary \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\} is a pair of signed points, and a point has no boundary at all, so \partial\partial[a,b] is empty. Looking at the outward-first picture, why should it be no accident that taking the boundary twice always leaves nothing behind? What does that say about the edges where two faces of the box meet? Each shared edge of the box belongs to two faces, and those two faces walk it in opposite directions. You don't need a formula here, just imagine the contributions of neighboring faces meeting along an edge.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: One degree less?Each row of the table pairs \omega with an M whose dimension is exactly one more than the degree of \omega. Why must \omega always carry one fewer degree than the dimension of M for the statement \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega to even make sense? What would go wrong if the degrees did not line up this way?Ask where each object gets integrated: \omega over \partial M and d\omega over M. Compare the dimension of each domain with the degree of the form sitting on it.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why raise the degree?The diagram shows \omega living on \partial M and d\omega living on M. In your own words, why does it make conceptual sense that the operation d raises the degree of a form by one, rather than lowering it or leaving it unchanged?Think about what d\omega has to be ready for: it gets integrated over M, which is one dimension larger than \partial M. The form must match the size of the region it fills.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Where did the inside go?When the small pieces are added up, every interior edge is walked twice and the two contributions cancel, leaving only the outer boundary. What does this cancellation tell you about why the equality \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega reaches across an entire region while only mentioning its boundary?Picture the information as flowing outward: anything happening between two adjacent cells is shared and cancels. Ask what is left that no neighbor can cancel.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Where does the minus sign come from? The boundary of [a,b] is written \{b\}-\{a\}, with a minus in front of the left endpoint. In what sense is one endpoint positive and the other negative, given that both are just points on a line? What information is the minus sign actually recording? Think about which way the interval is being traveled. The sign is not a property of the point alone, but of how the oriented interval meets that point.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why do interior points cancel? When the small boundary contributions are added up, every interior point x_j appears twice and cancels, while only a and b survive. Why does each interior point pick up opposite signs, and what would break if neighboring pieces did not share their boundary signs this way? An interior point x_j is the right endpoint of one small interval and the left endpoint of the next. Ask what sign it gets in each role.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why call it a boundary theorem? Calling the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus a boundary theorem reframes f(b)-f(a) as a value living on the boundary of the interval. What does this shift in viewpoint let you anticipate about a plane region, before you have seen Green's theorem at all? The boundary of an interval is two points; the boundary of a plane region is a curve. Picture what signed value on the boundary should become when the boundary is no longer just endpoints.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: What does the coefficient measure? The number Q_x-P_y appears as the lone coefficient in d\omega. Without computing anything, what is this coefficient telling you about the flow described by \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy at a single point, and why is it sensible that the rest of d\omega is just the area form dx\wedge dy? Think of d\omega as a local rate. The area form supplies the per unit area part; the coefficient supplies the how much circulation part. What spinning motion would make this coefficient large and positive?

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why does the hole turn the other way? The outer rim is traveled counterclockwise, yet the rim of the hole is traveled clockwise. What goes wrong with the identity \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega if you instead orient both boundary circles the same way, and what is the shared rule about the region that both orientations are obeying? Picture walking along each boundary curve. The positive convention asks you to keep the region R on one fixed side the whole time. Stand inside the annulus and ask which way is region on your left for the inner circle.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: One theorem wearing two costumes? The circulation form and the flux form look like two separate results, but here they collapse into the single statement \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega. In your own words, what is the one structural fact that both forms share, and what is the only thing you actually changed to pass from one to the other? Both statements integrate something on \partial R on the left and its exterior derivative d\omega on R on the right. Look only at which 1-form you fed in: P\,dx+Q\,dy versus A\,dy-B\,dx.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Compute d\omega: d\omega \amp= dP\wedge dx+dQ\wedge dy+dR\wedge dz\\ \amp= (R_y-Q_z)\,dy\wedge dz\\ \amp\quad+ (P_z-R_x)\,dz\wedge dx\\ \amp\quad+ (Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why does curl show up at all? The right-hand side of Stokes' theorem could have been any combination of derivatives of P,Q,R. Why is it exactly the curl that appears, rather than, say, the divergence or some other mixture? What feature of d\omega forces this particular answer? Look back at the coefficients that came out of computing d\omega for a work 1-form. Nobody chose them by hand — ask what produced them.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Compute the boundary integral. Parametrize C by x=a\cos t,\qquad y=a\sin t,\qquad z=0, \qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dx=-a\sin t\,dt, \qquad dy=a\cos t\,dt. So \omega \amp= -\frac{a\sin t}{2}(-a\sin t\,dt) + \frac{a\cos t}{2}(a\cos t\,dt)\\ \amp= \frac{a^2}{2}(\sin^2 t+\cos^2 t)\,dt\\ \amp= \frac{a^2}{2}\,dt. Thus \boxed{ \int_C\omega=\pi a^2. }

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: What does “only sees the boundary” mean? We bent the surface from a flat disk into a dome, yet the value of \int_S d\omega did not budge. What is the theorem really telling us about which features of a surface affect the answer and which are irrelevant? Could you replace the hemisphere with a wildly crumpled sheet and still get \pi a^2? Both sides of \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega share one curve. Think about what would have to change for the answer to change.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: How can one point matter? The form \alpha satisfies d\alpha=0 everywhere it is defined, so its exterior derivative seems to contribute nothing. Yet the loop integral came out to 2\pi, not 0. How can a single excluded point at the origin be responsible for all of that circulation, when the surface integrand vanishes everywhere it exists? Stokes' theorem needs \alpha defined on the whole surface. Ask what the disk contains that the form refuses to live at.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Compute the boundary integral face by face.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why does the degree go up? The flux form \Phi_{\mathbf F} is a 2-form, but its exterior derivative d\Phi_{\mathbf F} is a 3-form. Why is it natural that differentiating a 2-form should produce something that measures volume rather than surface area, and how does that match the picture of flux leaving the boundary and accumulating inside? Think about what each degree counts: a 2-form responds to oriented surface pieces, a 3-form to oriented chunks of volume. Where does the boundary live, and where does its "source" live?

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: What is the boundary "remembering"? The theorem equates a quantity living only on the surface \partial E with a quantity spread throughout the solid E. In your own words, how can a measurement taken entirely on the outer skin "know" about all the sources hidden deep inside? What does it mean that the interior detail is invisible from outside except through its total? Imagine two solids with very different source patterns inside but the same total source strength. What would an observer measuring only the boundary flux be able to distinguish?

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why must a curl's flux cancel? If the 2-form is already d\omega for a globally defined 1-form \omega, its total flux through any closed surface \partial E is zero. Conceptually, why does writing the form as d\omega force the cancellation, when an arbitrary 2-form need not cancel at all? What role does "a boundary has no boundary" play here? Apply generalized Stokes one extra time, to the closed surface itself, and ask what \partial(\partial E) can possibly be. There is nothing left for \omega to be integrated over.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why does the inside disappear? Every interior edge is shared by two neighboring rectangles. Without computing anything, explain why those two contributions cancel rather than add. What feature of the shared edge is different for the two rectangles, and why does that difference flip the sign of a 1-form integral? Ask yourself which direction each rectangle walks along that shared edge as it traces its own counterclockwise boundary. They are neighbors looking at the same wall from opposite sides.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: From local to global? On a single rectangle the theorem is just the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Yet adding many such local statements produces a fact about the one outer boundary. Conceptually, what does the cancellation of interior boundaries accomplish that lets a pile of tiny local equalities become a single global one? Track what happens to the two sides of the equation separately. The right sides simply add up to the whole region. Something special must happen on the left so that the interior bookkeeping vanishes and only the rim is left to speak.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why are the twins twins? The algebraic fact d^2=0 and the geometric fact \partial(\partial M)=\emptyset look like they belong to different worlds, one about forms and one about shapes. Using only the idea that Stokes' theorem links d with \partial, explain why these two facts are forced to mirror each other rather than being a lucky coincidence. Imagine applying Stokes' theorem twice in a row to \omega. Each application can push a d across to a \partial. What must the two zeros on the two sides be saying about each other?

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why subtract at one end? The boundary \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\} attaches opposite signs to the two endpoints, even though both are just points. What is the minus sign actually keeping track of here, and why would the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus collapse if both endpoints came in with a plus? Think about orientation: the interval runs from a to b. The boundary should remember which end is the start and which is the finish.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Why a 2-form here? For a curve we integrated a 1-form, but for the boundary of a solid we suddenly need a 2-form. Without computing anything, what feature of the boundary \partial E forces the form to have degree 2 rather than degree 1? Ask what kind of object \partial E is. The degree of a form should match the dimension of the thing you are integrating it over.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: One theorem, four faces? FTC, Green, Stokes, and the divergence theorem each fill exactly one row of the table, yet all four collapse into the single line \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega. In your own words, why does choosing the dimension of M and the degree of \omega determine which classical theorem you are looking at? Once M, \partial M, and \omega are fixed, everything else is forced. Try reading one row of the table and naming what changed from the row above it.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Which line actually changed? When we walked the square clockwise we landed on the false statement -1=1. Yet neither \int_R d\omega nor the form \omega changed. So which of the two sides of \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega was secretly altered, and which hypothesis of the theorem is the one we quietly violated? Ask yourself what the symbol \partial M is actually told to mean by the theorem. Only one side of the equation depends on the direction we walk.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: If d\alpha=0, why isn't the loop integral zero? Everywhere it is defined, \alpha satisfies d\alpha=0, and yet \int_C\alpha=2\pi\neq 0. The careless argument tries to write \int_C\alpha=\int_D d\alpha=0 over the unit disk D. Exactly which requirement of the generalized Stokes theorem does the disk D fail to meet, and why does switching to the annulus rescue the computation? The theorem asks \omega to be defined on an open set containing all of M. Look hard at the single point sitting at the center of the disk.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

text: Where did the missing -2 come from? On each open half of the square H(y) is constant, so the careless reader sets d\omega=0 and predicts \int_{\partial R}\omega=0; the honest boundary calculation gives -2. Since the theorem balances \int_{\partial R}\omega against \int_R d\omega, which hypothesis broke along the line y=0, and what is the geometric object the jump is secretly standing in for? Constant on each piece is not the same as smooth across the seam. Think about what d\omega would have to record at y=0 for the two sides to balance.

text: If \nabla\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0, then every line integral of \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r around a closed curve is 0, even if the domain has holes.

chapter.title: The Generalized Stokes Theorem

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: Why a minus sign? Suppose every reading of \mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} on the boundary is positive. Without computing anything, is the stored amount inside E going up or down at that instant, and why does the balance law need a minus sign in front of the flux to record that? Picture the arrows: positive normal flux means stuff is heading out through the surface. Ask yourself what leaving does to the count of what is still inside.

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: Fast flow, no flux? A strong current runs parallel to one face of E, never pointing into or out of it. The flow is fast, yet it contributes nothing to the flux across that face. What feature of \mathbf J\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} explains how something so vigorous can still cross no boundary? The dot product only listens to the part of \mathbf J that lines up with \widehat{\mathbf n}. What is that component when the flow and the normal are at right angles?

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: Window or blob? The dye in a moving cloud can stay constant while the dye in our fixed window rises and then falls as the cloud drifts by. What is the balance law actually keeping track of here—the contents of a fixed place in space, or the contents of a chosen lump of material—and why does that choice change the story? The boundary \partial E never moves in our setup. Think about whose perspective you are taking: someone standing still watching one window, or someone riding along with the dye.

text: Compute the two local terms: \rho_t=-1, and \nabla\cdot\mathbf J = \frac{\partial x}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial 0}{\partial y} + \frac{\partial 0}{\partial z} = 1. So \boxed{\rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=0.}

text: Why every region? The argument concludes that the integrand vanishes only because \iiint_E(\rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J-s)\,dV=0 holds for every small region E, not just one. In your own words, why would knowing this for a single fixed region not be enough to pin down the integrand at a point? Picture the integrand being positive in one corner of E and negative in another. What can the regions you are allowed to choose do that a single fixed region cannot?

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: Still, yet not still? It is tempting to read \nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0 as nothing is moving. Yet a rotating or shearing flow can be vigorously in motion and still be divergence-free. What, precisely, is the quantity that incompressibility holds fixed, and why does that leave so much freedom for the flow to swirl and stir? Watch a tiny blob carried by the flow. Divergence reports one specific thing about that blob. Its shape and orientation are not on that list.

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: What is the Laplacian really telling us? The heat equation says u_t=\alpha\Delta u. In plain words, what does the sign of \Delta u at a point tell you about how that point compares to its immediate surroundings, and why does that comparison decide whether the point warms up or cools down? Think of \Delta u as comparing a point's temperature to the average of nearby points. Heat always moves from warmer to cooler. Which way must heat flow if a point sits below the local average?

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: Why does a wave travel but heat fade? The heat equation has a single time derivative, u_t, while the wave equation has a second, u_{tt}. Both share the same spatial operator \Delta u. Why should changing only the order of the time derivative turn a profile that smooths and fades into one that travels and oscillates? A first-order time law sets the rate of change directly, like friction settling toward rest. A second-order time law sets the acceleration, the way Newton's law does. What does a system that stores momentum tend to do when pushed back toward equilibrium?

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: Why the same operator for different physics? Heat conservation, Newton's law for a vibrating membrane, and the equilibrium condition are three completely different physical stories, yet each produces the same operator \Delta. What feature common to all three situations forces this shared mathematics, even though the underlying physics is not the same? Look at what \Delta u measures geometrically: a net second-order imbalance between a point and its neighbors. Ask what each story is ultimately responding to. Is it the point's value, or how that value compares with the surrounding ones?

text: Why should the surface not matter? The contradiction came from getting two different answers for \int_C\mathcal H depending on whether we spanned the loop C with S_1 or S_2. Why should a quantity attached to the boundary loop be blind to the choice of spanning surface? What does this expectation reveal about the kind of object \mathcal J+\mathcal D_t has to be? Think about Stokes' theorem: \int_{\partial S}\mathcal H=\int_S d\mathcal H. If the left side depends only on the loop, what must be true of the right side as we slide the surface around? Closing a small gap between S_1 and S_2 turns two surfaces into the boundary of a solid region.

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

optional_markers.title: Maxwell's equations as a forms gateway

text: Built in, not bolted on? We derived charge conservation after writing down Maxwell's equations, yet the text insists conservation was there all along. In what sense is conservation a consequence of the structure rather than an extra physical law we chose to add? What role does d^2=0 play in making it unavoidable? Notice that the only physics we used was Ampere--Maxwell and Gauss. The step d(d\mathcal H)=0 is pure geometry, true for any form. Ask yourself what would have to fail for charge not to be conserved.

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

optional_markers.title: Maxwell's equations as a forms gateway

text: What did d_4 buy us? Four separate vector equations collapsed into just d_4F=0 and d_4G=\mathscr J. Beyond looking tidier, what does this compression actually tell us? Why is it meaningful that the homogeneous pair becomes a single statement that F is closed, and what does that suggest about how \mathcal E and \mathcal B are related? A single equation d_4F=0 treats \mathcal E and \mathcal B as two faces of one space-time form. Ask what changing your point of view (mixing t with a space coordinate) would then do to that one object, and why a frame-independent statement is more honest than four frame-dependent ones.

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: What does harmonic really say? The saddle u=x^2-y^2 is harmonic, yet it is far from flat. In plain words, what is being balanced when we say \Delta u=0, and why does that allow a surface to bend a lot while still counting as harmonic? Look at u_{xx} and u_{yy} separately. The Laplacian adds them, so it is the sum of the bendings that must vanish, not each one on its own.

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: Why can the hot spot only live on the edge? Using the mean value property as your guide, explain intuitively why a harmonic temperature cannot reach its highest value at an interior point unless it is constant. What goes wrong at a would-be interior peak? At a peak, every nearby value is no larger than the center value. Now ask: how can the average over a surrounding circle still equal that center value?

chapter.title: Conservation Laws and the Language of Fields

text: Why fix the boundary before minimizing? The theorem says a harmonic u has the least Dirichlet energy among functions sharing its boundary values. Conceptually, why is that boundary restriction essential? What would minimize the energy mean if we were allowed to change the boundary too? Think about the flat function w=0. Its energy is as small as possible, but compare its edge values to those of u=x. Without a fixed frame, what stops the membrane from simply collapsing?

text: Project 1: conservation of mass in a pipe network A small water system has three tanks connected by pipes. Let M_1(t),\quad M_2(t),\quad M_3(t) be the mass of water in the tanks. Water flows from tank 1 to tank 2 at rate q_{12}=0.4M_1, from tank 2 to tank 3 at rate q_{23}=0.3M_2, and from tank 3 back to tank 1 at rate q_{31}=0.2M_3. An external pump adds water to tank 1 at rate 5, and water leaves tank 3 at rate 2. Write the balance law for each tank: \frac{d}{dt}(\text{mass in tank}) = \text{inflow}-\text{outflow}+\text{source}. Show that M_1+M_2+M_3 changes at rate 3. Explain why the internal pipe flows cancel in the total balance. Change the external pump rate from 5 to 2. Show that the total mass is then conserved. Interpret the cancellation of internal flows as a discrete version of the divergence theorem: what leaves one small region enters a neighboring one. This project is deliberately finite. It uses tanks instead of a continuum. The same logic becomes \rho_t+\nabla\cdot\mathbf J=s when the tanks shrink to tiny regions.

text: Project 2: heat diffusion on a plate A square metal plate occupies 0\le x\le1,\qquad 0\le y\le1. Its boundary is held at temperature 0. The initial temperature is u(x,y,0)=\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y). Verify that u(x,y,t)=e^{-2\alpha\pi^2t}\sin(\pi x)\sin(\pi y) solves u_t=\alpha(u_{xx}+u_{yy}) and satisfies the boundary condition. Explain why the factor e^{-2\alpha\pi^2t} shrinks in time. Compute the total heat, up to a constant heat capacity factor: H(t)=\int_0^1\int_0^1 u(x,y,t)\,dy\,dx. Now compare with the higher-frequency initial temperature u(x,y,0)=\sin(3\pi x)\sin(\pi y). Find the exponential decay rate. Which pattern fades faster? Give a physical explanation: why should a temperature pattern with sharper spatial oscillation smooth out faster? This project connects the Laplacian with smoothing. The second derivatives detect sharp bending, and sharp bending drives faster heat flow.

text: Project 3: incompressible vector fields and stream functions In the plane, let \psi(x,y) have continuous second partial derivatives, and define \boxed{ \mathbf v=(\psi_y,-\psi_x). } This construction produces a divergence-free vector field. Verify directly that \nabla\cdot\mathbf v=0. Take \psi(x,y)=\sin x\sin y. Compute \mathbf v=(\psi_y,-\psi_x). Show that the velocity field is tangent to the level curves of \psi. That is, show \mathbf v\cdot\nabla\psi=0. Explain why a particle following this flow stays on one level curve of \psi. Compute the scalar curl of \mathbf v: \operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{plane}}\mathbf v = Q_x-P_y, where \mathbf v=(P,Q). Show that \operatorname{curl}_{\mathrm{plane}}\mathbf v=-\Delta\psi. The function \psi is called a stream function. Its level curves are stream lines of the incompressible flow. This is another place where a scalar field secretly organizes a vector field.

Let \mathcal E=E_1\,dx+E_2\,dy+E_3\,dz and \mathcal B=B_1\,dy\wedge dz+B_2\,dz\wedge dx+B_3\,dx\wedge dy. Compute d\mathcal E. text: Project 4: compare parameter grids on a sphere, torus, and cone A parametrization is a coordinate system on a surface. It does more than draw the surface. It creates a grid, gives tangent directions, chooses an orientation, and supplies the area scale factor \|\mathbf r_u\times \mathbf r_v\|. Different parametrizations reveal different parts of the geometry. They also hide different parts. The three surfaces. Use the following parametrizations. 1. Sphere of radius a. \mathbf r_S(\theta,\phi) = (a\sin\phi\cos\theta,\, a\sin\phi\sin\theta,\, a\cos\phi), where 0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le\phi\le\pi. 2. Torus. Let R>r>0. The torus with major radius R and minor radius r is \mathbf r_T(\theta,\phi) = \bigl((R+r\cos\phi)\cos\theta,\, (R+r\cos\phi)\sin\theta,\, r\sin\phi\bigr), where 0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le\phi\le2\pi. 3. Upper cone. \mathbf r_C(\theta,s) = (s\cos\theta,\, s\sin\theta,\, s), where 0\le\theta\le2\pi, \qquad 0\le s\le a. The same two-parameter idea produces very different surface grids. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.) sphere // 3-D interactive (WebGL) surface. import graph3; size(6cm); currentprojection=orthographic(5,4,3); surface s=surface(new triple(pair t){real u=t.x, v=t.y; return (sin(v)*cos(u), sin(v)*sin(u), cos(v));},(0,0),(2pi,pi),32,16); draw(s, rgb(0.55,0.75,0.95)+opacity(0.9), meshpen=rgb(0.15,0.35,0.55)+linewidth(0.2pt)); torus // 3-D interactive (WebGL) surface. import graph3; size(6cm); currentprojection=orthographic(5,4,3); surface s=surface(new triple(pair t){real u=t.x, v=t.y; return ((2+0.7*cos(v))*cos(u), (2+0.7*cos(v))*sin(u), 0.7*sin(v));},(0,0),(2pi,2pi),40,20); draw(s, rgb(0.95,0.70,0.40)+opacity(0.9), meshpen=rgb(0.55,0.35,0.10)+linewidth(0.2pt)); cone z=r // 3-D interactive (WebGL) surface. import graph3; size(6cm); currentprojection=orthographic(5,4,3); surface s=surface(new triple(pair t){real u=t.x, s=t.y; return (s*cos(u), s*sin(u), s);},(0,0),(2pi,2.5),32,12); draw(s, rgb(0.70,0.55,0.90)+opacity(0.9), meshpen=rgb(0.35,0.20,0.55)+linewidth(0.2pt)); Your task. For each surface: Draw the parameter domain. Draw the two families of parameter curves: \theta=\text{constant}, \qquad \phi=\text{constant} or \theta=\text{constant}, \qquad s=\text{constant}. Compute the two tangent vectors. Compute the magnitude of the cross product: \|\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\|. Find where the parametrization repeats points. Find where the parametrization collapses or becomes nonregular: \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v=\mathbf 0. Describe how the parameter grid stretches or crowds on the surface. Useful checkpoints. For the sphere, \boxed{ \|\mathbf r_{S,\theta}\times\mathbf r_{S,\phi}\| = a^2\sin\phi. } The factor vanishes at the poles \phi=0,\qquad \phi=\pi. All longitude lines meet there. For the torus, \boxed{ \|\mathbf r_{T,\theta}\times\mathbf r_{T,\phi}\| = r(R+r\cos\phi). } Since R>r, this never vanishes. The grid is regular, but the outer side of the torus has larger area scale than the inner side. For the cone, \mathbf r_{C,\theta}=(-s\sin\theta,s\cos\theta,0), and \mathbf r_{C,s}=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta,1). Thus \boxed{ \mathbf r_{C,\theta}\times\mathbf r_{C,s} = (s\cos\theta,s\sin\theta,-s), } so \boxed{ \|\mathbf r_{C,\theta}\times\mathbf r_{C,s}\|=s\sqrt2. } The factor vanishes at s=0. That is the cone tip. What to hand in. Make one comparison table: \begin{array}{c|c|c|c} \text{Surface} & \text{Area scale} & \text{Repeats?} & \text{Collapses?} \\ \hline \text{sphere} & a^2\sin\phi & \theta=0,2\pi & \text{poles}\\[1mm] \text{torus} & r(R+r\cos\phi) & \theta,\phi \text{ periodic} & \text{no, if }R>r\\[1mm] \text{cone} & s\sqrt2 & \theta=0,2\pi & \text{tip} \end{array} Then write a short explanation of this sentence: \boxed{ \text{A parametrization is not just a drawing; it is a measurement system.} }

text: Project 1: constrained design problems A design problem becomes a calculus problem only after we name the variables. A tank has dimensions. A package has side lengths. A fence has segments. A shape has area, volume, cost, or strength. Optimization begins when those quantities become functions. A seed example: a closed cylindrical tank. A field station needs a closed cylindrical water tank with fixed volume V. Let r be the radius and h be the height. The volume constraint is \boxed{\pi r^2h=V.} The surface area is \boxed{A(r,h)=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh.} The first term is the top and bottom. The second term is the side. Use the constraint to eliminate h: h=\frac{V}{\pi r^2}. Then A(r) \amp = 2\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\frac{V}{\pi r^2}\right) \amp = 2\pi r^2+\frac{2V}{r}. Differentiate: A'(r)=4\pi r-\frac{2V}{r^2}. At a critical point, 4\pi r=\frac{2V}{r^2}, so 4\pi r^3=2V, and therefore \boxed{r^3=\frac{V}{2\pi}.} Now use the constraint: h=\frac{V}{\pi r^2}. Since V=2\pi r^3, we get \boxed{h=2r.} The height equals the diameter. This result is not a coincidence. If the tank is too tall and narrow, the side wall is expensive. If it is too flat and wide, the top and bottom are expensive. The optimum balances those costs. Your task. Choose one design problem from the list below, or create your own. Option A. Open-top box. An open-top rectangular box has side lengths x,\qquad y,\qquad z. Its volume must be xyz=32. The material area is A(x,y,z)=xy+2xz+2yz. Find the dimensions that minimize material. Option B. Closed cylindrical tank. A closed cylinder has volume V. Minimize A(r,h)=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh subject to \pi r^2h=V. Option C. Open cylindrical tank. An open cylindrical tank has no top. Its volume is V. Minimize A(r,h)=\pi r^2+2\pi rh subject to \pi r^2h=V. Compare your answer with the closed-tank answer. Option D. Rectangular package with square cross-section. A shipping tube has square cross-section x\times x and length L. Its volume is fixed: x^2L=V. The material cost is C(x,L)=2x^2+4xL. Find the least-cost dimensions. Required steps. For your chosen problem: Draw a diagram and label the variables. Write the quantity to be optimized. Write the constraint. Solve the problem in two ways if possible: \text{eliminate one variable} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \text{use Lagrange multipliers}. Check that your critical point is a minimum, not a maximum or a saddle. You may use a one-variable second derivative test after eliminating a variable. Interpret the answer in words. Why does the shape make physical or economic sense? What to hand in. Your report should include: \begin{array}{ll} 1. \amp \text{a labeled diagram,}\\ 2. \amp \text{the objective function,}\\ 3. \amp \text{the constraint,}\\ 4. \amp \text{the derivative or Lagrange multiplier equations,}\\ 5. \amp \text{the final dimensions,}\\ 6. \amp \text{a check that the point is a minimum,}\\ 7. \amp \text{a short interpretation.} \end{array} The interpretation is not optional. In a modeling problem, the formula and the story must agree.

text: Project 2: least-squares fitting and the Hessian A best-fit model usually does not pass through every data point. The errors remain. The least-squares idea chooses the model that makes the squared errors as small as possible. Chapter studied a best-fit line. This project moves one step higher: fitting a plane. A seed example: fitting a calibration plane. A sensor output z depends on two inputs x and y. A lab records the data \begin{array}{c|c|c} x \amp y \amp z \\ \hline 0 \amp 0 \amp 2\\ 1 \amp 0 \amp 3\\ 0 \amp 1 \amp 4\\ 1 \amp 1 \amp 6\\ 2 \amp 1 \amp 7 \end{array} Fit a plane \boxed{z=ax+by+c.} For the i-th data point, the residual is ax_i+by_i+c-z_i. The squared-error function is \boxed{E(a,b,c)=\sum_{i=1}^5(ax_i+by_i+c-z_i)^2.} For this data set, expanding gives E(a,b,c) \amp = 6a^2+6ab+8ac-46a \amp\qquad +3b^2+6bc-34b \amp\qquad +5c^2-44c+114. At a critical point, E_a=E_b=E_c=0. Compute: E_a=12a+6b+8c-46, E_b=6a+6b+6c-34, E_c=8a+6b+10c-44. So the normal equations are \boxed{ \begin{aligned} 12a+6b+8c\amp=46,\\ 6a+6b+6c\amp=34,\\ 8a+6b+10c\amp=44. \end{aligned} } Solving gives \boxed{a=\frac75,\qquad b=\frac{37}{15},\qquad c=\frac95.} So the best-fit plane is \boxed{z=\frac75x+\frac{37}{15}y+\frac95.} Now check that this critical point is a minimum. The Hessian is H_E= \begin{pmatrix} 12\amp6\amp8\\ 6\amp6\amp6\\ 8\amp6\amp10 \end{pmatrix}. Its leading principal minors are 12\gt0, \begin{vmatrix} 12\amp6\\ 6\amp6 \end{vmatrix} = 72-36=36\gt0, and \det H_E=120\gt0. We can verify positive definiteness directly from the sum of squares, without a further matrix criterion. For h=(h_a,h_b,h_c), h^T H_E h=2\sum_{i=1}^5(h_a x_i+h_b y_i+h_c)^2. The first three data points force h_c=h_a=h_b=0 if this sum is zero. Thus it is positive for every nonzero h. Since E is quadratic, its expansion at the critical point has zero linear term and this positive quadratic term. The critical point is the unique absolute minimum. Your task. Choose one of the following. Option A. Fit a line. Use data points (0,1),\qquad (1,2),\qquad (2,2),\qquad (3,4),\qquad (4,5). Fit y=mx+b by minimizing E(m,b)=\sum (mx_i+b-y_i)^2. Option B. Fit a plane. Use the calibration data from the seed example, or collect your own data with two inputs and one output. Fit z=ax+by+c. Option C. Fit a quadratic curve. Use data points (-2,5),\qquad (-1,2),\qquad (0,1),\qquad (1,2),\qquad (2,6). Fit y=Ax^2+Bx+C. Minimize E(A,B,C)=\sum (Ax_i^2+Bx_i+C-y_i)^2. Required steps. Write the model. Write the residuals. Write the squared-error function. Differentiate and set the partial derivatives equal to zero. Solve the resulting linear system. Compute the Hessian of the error function. Explain why the Hessian shows that the critical point is a minimum. Plot the data and the fitted model. The geometry of the residual. For a line fit, the predicted vector has the form \widehat{\mathbf y}=m\mathbf x+b\mathbf 1. At the best fit, the residual \mathbf r=\widehat{\mathbf y}-\mathbf y is perpendicular to the prediction directions: \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf x=0, \qquad \mathbf r\cdot\mathbf 1=0. For a plane fit, the same idea appears with three prediction directions: \mathbf x,\qquad \mathbf y,\qquad \mathbf 1. At the best-fit plane, the residual is perpendicular to all three. This is why the equations are called normal equations. The remaining error is normal to the space of predictions. What to hand in. Your report should include: the data table, the model, the error function, the normal equations, the fitted coefficients, the Hessian calculation, a plot, a paragraph explaining the perpendicular-residual interpretation. The best-fit model is not magic. It is the nearest point in a space of possible predictions.

text:
Project 3: entropy maximization as a Lagrange multiplier problem Optimization is not only about boxes and tanks. It also appears in probability. Suppose a system can fall into several states. A probability distribution is a list p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_n with p_i\ge0, \qquad p_1+\cdots+p_n=1. The entropy of this distribution is  oxed{S(p_1,\ldots,p_n)=-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\ln p_i.} Entropy measures spread. A distribution concentrated in one state has low entropy. A distribution spread evenly across many states has high entropy. For this project, use the convention 0\ln0=0. A seed example: no information except total probability. Suppose there are n possible states and no extra information. Maximize S=-\sum_{i=1}^n p_i\ln p_i subject to p_1+\cdots+p_n=1. Inside the region where all p_i\gt0, use a Lagrange multiplier: g(p_1,\ldots,p_n)=p_1+\cdots+p_n. The equation 
abla S=\lambda
abla g gives -\ln p_i-1=\lambda for every i. Therefore all the p_i's are equal: p_1=p_2=\cdots=p_n. Since they add to 1,  oxed{p_i= rac1n \qquad 	ext{for every }i.} The maximum-entropy distribution is uniform. The Hessian of S in the positive region is diagonal: H_S=  egin{pmatrix} -1/p_1\amp0\amp\cdots\amp0\ 0\amp-1/p_2\amp\cdots\amp0\ \vdots\amp\vdots\amp\ddots\amp\vdots\ 0\amp0\amp\cdots\amp-1/p_n \end{pmatrix}. For every nonzero vector h, h^TH_Sh=-\sum_i h_i^2/p_i\lt0. Along any line segment of positive probabilities starting at the uniform distribution, the first derivative is initially zero and the second derivative is negative. Entropy therefore decreases along that segment. Extending continuously to the boundary using 0\ln0=0 shows that no boundary distribution has larger entropy. This proves the claimed global maximum. Your task. Choose one of the following entropy problems. Option A. Four equally possible rooms. A robot is in one of four rooms, but you have no information about which room. Let p_1+p_2+p_3+p_4=1. Maximize S=-p_1\ln p_1-p_2\ln p_2-p_3\ln p_3-p_4\ln p_4. Show that  oxed{p_1=p_2=p_3=p_4= rac14.} Option B. A loaded three-state system. A system has three energy levels: E_1=0,\qquad E_2=1,\qquad E_3=2. The probabilities satisfy p_1+p_2+p_3=1. Suppose the average energy is fixed with 0\lt U\lt2: 0p_1+1p_2+2p_3=U. Maximize S=-p_1\ln p_1-p_2\ln p_2-p_3\ln p_3 subject to the two constraints. Use two Lagrange multipliers: 
abla S=\lambda
abla(p_1+p_2+p_3)+\mu
abla(p_2+2p_3). Show that the solution has the form  oxed{p_i=C e^{- eta E_i}} for constants C and  eta. This is the beginning of the Boltzmann distribution. Check that a positive solution exists for the prescribed U, and use the same strict-concavity argument to compare it with the boundary. At U=0 or U=2, only a distribution concentrated at the corresponding extreme energy is possible; it is not represented by finite  eta with all probabilities positive. Option C. Three states with average energy 1/2. Continue Option B with U= rac12. Write q=e^{- eta}. Then (p_1,p_2,p_3)=C(1,q,q^2). The constraints become C(1+q+q^2)=1, and C(q+2q^2)= rac12. Eliminate C to show that 3q^2+q-1=0. Thus  oxed{q= rac{-1+\sqrt{13}}{6}.} Then compute C= rac{1}{1+q+q^2} and find the three probabilities. Required steps. For your chosen option: Write the entropy function. Write every constraint. Set up the Lagrange multiplier equations. Solve the equations. Use the Hessian or a concavity argument to explain why the critical point gives a maximum. Interpret the result. Why does the distribution spread out as much as the constraints allow? What to hand in. Your report should include: the probability variables, the entropy function, the constraints, the Lagrange multiplier equations, the solution, a short explanation of why this is a maximum, a paragraph explaining what the answer means in ordinary language. This project shows a different face of Lagrange multipliers. The constraint is not a curve or a surface in physical space. It is a rule inside probability space.

text:
Project 4: numerical gradient descent The equation 
abla f=\mathbf 0 finds candidates for minima, but many functions are too large or too complicated to solve exactly. A computer often searches by taking small downhill steps. The simplest version is gradient descent:  oxed{\mathbf x_{n+1}=\mathbf x_n-\alpha
abla f(\mathbf x_n).} The number \alpha\gt0 is the step size. The gradient points uphill. The negative gradient points downhill. A seed example: a tilted quadratic bowl. Let f(x,y)= rac12(x-2)^2+2(y+1)^2. The minimum is visibly at (2,-1). The gradient is 
abla f(x,y)=(x-2,\ 4(y+1)). Start at \mathbf x_0=(6,4) and take step size \alpha=0.2. Then 
abla f(6,4)=(4,20), so \mathbf x_1 \amp = (6,4)-0.2(4,20) \amp = (5.2,0). Now 
abla f(5.2,0)=(3.2,4), so \mathbf x_2 \amp = (5.2,0)-0.2(3.2,4) \amp = (4.56,-0.8). The points are moving toward (2,-1). Gradient descent takes repeated steps in the negative-gradient direction.  egin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.78, >=stealth] \draw[->] (-0.5,0) -- (7,0) node[right] {\(x\)}; \draw[->] (0,-2.5) -- (0,5.5) node[above] {\(y\)};  oreach  in {0.7,1.2,1.8,2.5,3.3} { \draw[gray!45] (2,-1) ellipse ({0.9*} and {0.45*}); } \coordinate (A) at (6,4); \coordinate (B) at (5.2,0); \coordinate (C) at (4.56,-0.8); \coordinate (D) at (4.048,-0.96); \coordinate (M) at (2,-1); \draw[->, very thick, red!65!black] (A) -- (B); \draw[->, very thick, red!65!black] (B) -- (C); \draw[->, very thick, red!65!black] (C) -- (D);  ill (A) circle (2.2pt) node[above right] {\(\mathbf x_0\)};  ill (B) circle (2.2pt) node[above right] {\(\mathbf x_1\)};  ill (C) circle (2.2pt) node[below right] {\(\mathbf x_2\)};  ill (M) circle (2.5pt) node[below left] {minimum}; 
ode at (3.3,-3.0) {gradient descent follows downhill across contour curves}; \end{tikzpicture} Why step size matters. Even in one variable, the step size can break the method. Let f(x)=x^2. Then f'(x)=2x. Gradient descent gives x_{n+1}=x_n-\alpha(2x_n)=(1-2\alpha)x_n. If 0\lt\alpha\lt1, then |1-2\alpha|\lt1 as long as \alpha
e1, and the iterates move toward 0. If \alpha=1, then x_{n+1}=-x_n. The sequence bounces back and forth forever. If \alpha\gt1, then |1-2\alpha|\gt1, and the iterates grow in size. The method runs away from the minimum. The direction was right, but the step was too large. Your task. Choose one function from Group A and one from Group B. Group A: friendly quadratic bowls.  egin{array}{c} f_1(x,y)= rac12(x-2)^2+2(y+1)^2,\[2mm] f_2(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2-4x-2y,\[1mm] f_3(x,y)=3(x+1)^2+(y-2)^2. \end{array} Group B: functions with warnings.  egin{array}{c} g_1(x,y)=x^2-y^2,\[1mm] g_2(x,y)=x^4+y^4-4xy,\[1mm] g_3(x,y)=\sin x+\cos y. \end{array} For each function: Compute the gradient. Choose a starting point. Choose a step size \alpha. Compute at least five gradient descent steps by hand, spreadsheet, calculator, or code. Plot the contour map and draw the step path. Record the function values f(\mathbf x_0),\ f(\mathbf x_1),\ f(\mathbf x_2),\ldots or g(\mathbf x_0),\ g(\mathbf x_1),\ g(\mathbf x_2),\ldots Try a smaller step size and a larger step size. Compare what happens. Questions to answer. Did the function value decrease at every step? Did the points appear to approach a minimum? Did a large step size cause bouncing or divergence? What happened for a saddle-shaped function such as g_1(x,y)=x^2-y^2? How does the Hessian help explain the behavior near a critical point? What to hand in. Your report should include: the two functions you chose, the gradients, the starting points and step sizes, a table of iterates, a table of function values, contour plots with the descent path drawn, a paragraph explaining what worked and what failed. Gradient descent is simple enough to write in one line, but it is not magic. It listens only to local slope. If the landscape has a saddle, a flat valley, many wells, or a step size that is too large, the path can surprise us.

text: Project 1: estimate mass from measured density data A formula is not always available. Sometimes the density is known only from measurements. A lab technician may test a metal plate at several points. A geologist may sample soil density at grid locations. A medical scan may give density values one voxel at a time. The integral is still the right idea, but the integral has to be estimated from data. A seed example: a nonuniform plate. A thin rectangular plate occupies 0\le x\le6, \qquad 0\le y\le4, where x and y are measured in centimeters. The plate is divided into 3 columns and 2 rows. Each small rectangle has width 2 and height 2, so \Delta A=4\text{ cm}^2. The density, measured in grams per square centimeter, is sampled at the center of each small rectangle: \begin{array}{c|ccc} \amp x=1 \amp x=3 \amp x=5 \\ \hline y=3 \amp 2.4 \amp 2.8 \amp 3.1\\ y=1 \amp 2.0 \amp 2.3 \amp 2.6 \end{array} The mass is M=\iint_R \rho(x,y)\,dA. Using the midpoint rule, we estimate \begin{aligned} M \amp\approx \sum \rho(x_i^*,y_j^*)\,\Delta A\\ \amp= 4(2.0+2.3+2.6+2.4+2.8+3.1)\\ \amp= 4(15.2)\\ \amp= 60.8. \end{aligned} So the estimated mass is \boxed{ M\approx 60.8\text{ g}. } The area of the plate is 6\cdot4=24\text{ cm}^2. So the estimated average density is \boxed{ \overline{\rho} = \frac{M}{\operatorname{Area}(R)} \approx \frac{60.8}{24} \approx 2.53\text{ g/cm}^2. } Measured density data can be turned into a mass estimate by a Riemann sum. \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8, >=stealth] \draw[->] (-0.4,0) -- (6.8,0) node[right] {\(x\)}; \draw[->] (0,-0.4) -- (0,4.8) node[above] {\(y\)}; \draw[thick] (0,0) rectangle (6,4); \draw[gray!45] (2,0) -- (2,4); \draw[gray!45] (4,0) -- (4,4); \draw[gray!45] (0,2) -- (6,2); \foreach \x/\y/\d in { 1/1/2.0, 3/1/2.3, 5/1/2.6, 1/3/2.4, 3/3/2.8, 5/3/3.1 } { \fill (\x,\y) circle (2pt); \node[above] at (\x,\y) {\(\d\)}; } \node at (3,-0.85) {density samples at cell centers}; \end{tikzpicture} Your task. Choose one of the following. Option A. Plate from tabulated data. Use the density table from the seed example, or create your own 4\times4 or 5\times5 grid of density values. Estimate the mass of the plate. Option B. Temperature or pollution on a map. Use a rectangular map region. Let the data values represent temperature, pollution concentration, or rainfall. Estimate the total amount and the average value over the region. Option C. Three-dimensional density data. A box is divided into small rectangular boxes. At the center of each box, a density value is measured. Estimate M=\iiint_E \rho(x,y,z)\,dV. For a simple version, use a 2\times2\times2 grid. Required steps. Draw the region and the sampling grid. State the units of the density. State the area or volume of each small piece: \Delta A \qquad\text{or}\qquad \Delta V. Write the Riemann sum: \sum \rho(x_i^*,y_i^*)\,\Delta A or \sum \rho(x_i^*,y_i^*,z_i^*)\,\Delta V. Estimate the total mass or total amount. Estimate the average density: \overline{\rho} = \frac{\text{total amount}}{\text{area or volume}}. Discuss whether the estimate should improve with a finer grid. Questions to answer. Which parts of the region have the largest density? Does the data suggest a smooth density field or a sharp jump? If one measurement were wrong, which one would most affect the estimate? What changes if the data are sampled at corners instead of centers? How would your estimate change if the grid cells had unequal sizes? What to hand in. Your report should include: the data table, a grid drawing, the Riemann sum, the estimated total amount, the estimated average value, one paragraph explaining the main source of error. The main point is that an integral can survive without a formula. A formula is one way to know a field. Measurements are another.
