text: Project 4: Monte Carlo integration in two and three dimensions Some regions are too irregular for clean limits. Some functions are known only through simulation. Some dimensions are too high for ordinary grid methods to be practical. Monte Carlo integration uses random samples instead of a regular grid. The idea is simple: average many random values, then multiply by the size of the sampling box. A seed example: estimating water volume in a circular pond. A shallow circular pond has radius 2. Its depth is modeled by d(x,y)=5-x^2-y^2 inside the disk D=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le4\}. The volume of water is V=\iint_D (5-x^2-y^2)\,dA. We could use polar coordinates: \begin{aligned} V \amp= \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2(5-r^2)r\,dr\,d\theta\\ \amp= 2\pi \left[ \frac52r^2-\frac14r^4 \right]_0^2\\ \amp= 2\pi(10-4)\\ \amp= 12\pi. \end{aligned} So the exact volume is approximately 37.70. Now estimate the same integral by Monte Carlo sampling. Put the pond inside the square B=[-2,2]\times[-2,2]. The square has area 16. Define g(x,y)= \begin{cases} 5-x^2-y^2, \amp x^2+y^2\le4,\\ 0, \amp x^2+y^2>4. \end{cases} Then \iint_D(5-x^2-y^2)\,dA = \iint_B g(x,y)\,dA. Suppose five random points in B give the following values: \begin{array}{c|c|c} (x,y) \amp x^2+y^2 \amp g(x,y) \\ \hline (0.4,-1.1) \amp 1.37 \amp 3.63\\ (-1.8,0.6) \amp 3.60 \amp 1.40\\ (1.7,1.5) \amp 5.14 \amp 0\\ (-0.2,0.3) \amp 0.13 \amp 4.87\\ (1.1,-0.7) \amp 1.70 \amp 3.30 \end{array} The sample average is \frac{3.63+1.40+0+4.87+3.30}{5}=2.64. So the Monte Carlo estimate is \boxed{ V\approx 16(2.64)=42.24. } That is rough, because N=5 is tiny. With hundreds or thousands of samples, the estimate should settle closer to 12\pi. The general Monte Carlo formula. Let E be a region inside a box B. Define g(\mathbf x)= \begin{cases} f(\mathbf x), \amp \mathbf x\in E,\\ 0, \amp \mathbf x\notin E. \end{cases} If \mathbf X_1,\mathbf X_2,\ldots,\mathbf X_N are random points chosen independently and uniformly in B, then \boxed{ \int_E f \approx \operatorname{size}(B)\, \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^{N} g(\mathbf X_i). } Here \operatorname{size}(B) means area in two dimensions and volume in three dimensions. Your task. Choose one integral. Option A. Area of an irregular region. Estimate the area of a region E by taking f=1. Option B. Volume under a surface. Estimate \iint_E f(x,y)\,dA for a region E inside a rectangle. Option C. Mass inside a solid. Estimate \iiint_E \rho(x,y,z)\,dV for a solid E inside a box. Option D. Compare Monte Carlo with an exact answer. Choose an integral that can also be computed exactly, such as a disk, ball, cylinder, or box. Compare the Monte Carlo estimate with the exact value. Required steps. State the region E. Choose a sampling box B. Define the function g on the whole box. Generate random sample points. Compute the estimate for several values of N, such as N=100,\quad 500,\quad 1000,\quad 5000. Plot or tabulate the estimates as N grows. Compare with an exact or high-resolution numerical answer, if available. Questions to answer. Does the estimate appear to converge? How much does the answer change when you run the experiment again? What happens if the sampling box is much larger than the region E? Why are points outside E assigned value 0? What advantage does random sampling have in three dimensions? What to hand in. Your report should include: the integral being estimated, the sampling box, the Monte Carlo formula used, a table of estimates for increasing N, a plot of the estimates, if possible, a comparison with an exact or more accurate value, a paragraph about reliability and error.

text: Project 1: work around closed curves A closed curve returns to where it started. A conservative field does no net work around such a curve. A rotating field may do positive or negative work, depending on the direction of travel. The line integral detects the difference. A seed example: a field that measures area. Let \mathbf F(x,y)=\left(-\frac y2,\frac x2\right), and let \omega=-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy be its work 1-form. Walk counterclockwise around the rectangle R=[0,4]\times[0,3]. We compute the work around the four sides. Bottom side. Here y=0 and dy=0. So \omega=0. The bottom contributes 0. Right side. Here x=4, dx=0, and y goes from 0 to 3. Thus \int_{\text{right}}\omega \amp = \int_0^3 \frac{4}{2}\,dy \amp = 6. Top side. Here y=3, dy=0, and x goes from 4 back to 0. Thus \int_{\text{top}}\omega \amp = \int_4^0 -\frac32\,dx \amp = 6. Left side. Here x=0, dx=0, and y goes downward. Thus \omega=0. The left side contributes 0. So \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\omega=12. } The rectangle has area 4\cdot3=12. This is not a coincidence. Compute the exterior derivative: d\omega \amp = d\left(-\frac y2\,dx+\frac x2\,dy\right) \amp = \left(\frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac x2 - \frac{\partial}{\partial y}\left(-\frac y2\right) \right)dx\wedge dy \amp = \left(\frac12+\frac12\right)dx\wedge dy \amp = dx\wedge dy. Green's theorem gives \boxed{ \oint_{\partial R}\omega = \iint_R d\omega = \iint_R dx\wedge dy = \operatorname{Area}(R). } The work form is secretly an area-measuring instrument. A rotational field can do positive work around a closed curve. \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.8, >=stealth] \draw[->] (-0.5,0) -- (5.2,0) node[right] {\(x\)}; \draw[->] (0,-0.5) -- (0,4.2) node[above] {\(y\)}; \draw[fill=gray!10, thick] (0,0) rectangle (4,3); \draw[->, very thick, red!65!black] (0,0) -- (1.4,0); \draw[->, very thick, red!65!black] (4,0) -- (4,1.2); \draw[->, very thick, red!65!black] (4,3) -- (2.6,3); \draw[->, very thick, red!65!black] (0,3) -- (0,1.8); \foreach \x in {0.8,1.6,2.4,3.2} { \foreach \y in {0.7,1.5,2.3} { \draw[->, blue!65!black, thick] (\x,\y) -- ++({-0.14*\y},{0.14*\x}); } } \node at (2,-0.85) {counterclockwise work equals area for this field}; \end{tikzpicture} Your task. Choose one field and one closed curve. \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Field} \amp \text{Feature} \\ \hline \mathbf F=(-y,x) \amp \text{constant positive scalar curl }2\\[1mm] \mathbf F=\left(-\dfrac y2,\dfrac x2\right) \amp \text{work equals area}\\[4mm] \mathbf F=(2x,2y) \amp \text{gradient field}\\[1mm] \mathbf F=(y^2,x) \amp \text{nonconstant scalar curl}\\[1mm] \mathbf F=\left(\dfrac{-y}{x^2+y^2},\dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2}\right) \amp \text{punctured-plane warning} \end{array} For curves, use a circle, ellipse, rectangle, triangle, or a piecewise smooth curve of your own. Required steps. Draw the vector field and the closed curve. Choose an orientation for the curve. Write the work form \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. Compute the line integral directly, if possible. Compute d\omega=(Q_x-P_y)\,dx\wedge dy. Use Green's theorem if the field is defined on the region enclosed by the curve. Compare the direct calculation with the theorem calculation. text: Project 2: flux through complicated surfaces Flux measures how much a vector field crosses a surface. A flat disk is friendly. A curved dome is less friendly. A surface made of several pieces can look intimidating. The divergence theorem offers a shortcut, but only after the surface is closed. A seed example: flux through a paraboloid dome. Let S be the dome z=4-x^2-y^2, \qquad x^2+y^2\le4, oriented upward. Together with the disk D:\quad z=0,\qquad x^2+y^2\le4, the dome bounds a solid E. Let \mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,z). We want the flux through the dome S. The closed surface is \partial E=S\cup D, with outward orientation. On the dome, outward means upward and outward. On the bottom disk, outward means downward. The divergence is \nabla\cdot\mathbf F = 1+1+1 = 3. By the divergence theorem, \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS = \iiint_E 3\,dV = 3\operatorname{Volume}(E). Find the volume of E: \operatorname{Volume}(E) \amp = \int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2(4-r^2)r\,dr\,d\theta \amp = 2\pi\left[ 2r^2-\frac14r^4 \right]_0^2 \amp = 2\pi(8-4) \amp = 8\pi. So the total outward flux through the closed surface is 3(8\pi)=24\pi. Now check the bottom disk. On D, z=0, \qquad \widehat{\mathbf n}=(0,0,-1). Thus \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n} = (x,y,0)\cdot(0,0,-1) = 0. So the bottom disk contributes 0. Therefore the flux through the dome is \boxed{ \iint_S \mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS=24\pi. } In forms language, the flux form is \Phi_{\mathbf F} = x\,dy\wedge dz + y\,dz\wedge dx + z\,dx\wedge dy, and d\Phi_{\mathbf F} = 3\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. The same computation says \int_{\partial E}\Phi_{\mathbf F} = \int_E d\Phi_{\mathbf F}. Your task. Choose one surface. \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Surface} \amp \text{Suggested field} \\ \hline \text{paraboloid cap} \amp (x,y,z)\\[1mm] \text{hemisphere with disk base} \amp (0,0,z)\\[1mm] \text{cylinder side plus caps} \amp (x,y,1)\\[1mm] \text{box with one face removed} \amp (x^2,y,z)\\[1mm] \text{triangulated surface or mesh} \amp \text{constant or radial field} \end{array} Required steps. Draw the surface and state its orientation. Decide whether the surface is closed. If it is not closed, add simple pieces to close it. Compute the flux through the closed surface using the divergence theorem, if possible. Compute or subtract the flux through the added pieces. State the flux through the original surface. Translate the flux integral into a 2-form: \Phi_{\mathbf F} = F_1\,dy\wedge dz + F_2\,dz\wedge dx + F_3\,dx\wedge dy. Questions to answer. Is the surface open or closed? What does outward mean for each piece? Which pieces contribute zero flux by symmetry or by the direction of the field? Is the divergence theorem faster than a direct surface integral? What would change if the orientation were reversed? What to hand in. Your report should include: a drawing of the surface, the vector field, the orientation, the closed-surface construction, the divergence calculation, the flux through any added pieces, the final flux through the requested surface. A surface integral can be hard because the surface is curved. The divergence theorem moves the difficulty into the solid it bounds. Sometimes the inside is easier than the skin.

text: Project 1: translate a classical vector calculus problem into forms A classical vector calculus problem often begins with a vector field: \mathbf F=(P,Q) \qquad\text{or}\qquad \mathbf F=(P,Q,R). A forms solution begins by asking what kind of integral we are doing. For work or circulation, we use a 1-form: \boxed{\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy} in the plane, or \boxed{\omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz} in space. For flux through a surface, we use a 2-form: \boxed{\Phi_{\mathbf F} = P\,dy\wedge dz + Q\,dz\wedge dx + R\,dx\wedge dy.} The same vector field may produce different forms, depending on what we are measuring. A seed example: circulation around the unit circle. Let \mathbf F(x,y)=(-y,x). Classically, the work around a closed curve C is \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r. The corresponding 1-form is \boxed{\omega=-y\,dx+x\,dy.} Let C be the unit circle, oriented counterclockwise: x=\cos t,\qquad y=\sin t,\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dx=-\sin t\,dt, \qquad dy=\cos t\,dt. Pull back the form: \omega \amp = -\sin t(-\sin t\,dt)+\cos t(\cos t\,dt) \amp = (\sin^2t+\cos^2t)\,dt \amp = dt. Therefore \boxed{\oint_C\omega=\int_0^{2\pi}dt=2\pi.} Now use Green's theorem in forms language. Compute d\omega \amp = d(-y\,dx+x\,dy) \amp = 2\,dx\wedge dy. If D is the unit disk, then \int_D d\omega \amp = \int_D 2\,dx\wedge dy \amp = 2\operatorname{Area}(D) \amp = 2\pi. So \boxed{\int_{\partial D}\omega=\int_D d\omega.} The classical statement is \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r = \iint_D \left( \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y} \right) dA. The forms statement is \int_{\partial D}\omega=\int_D d\omega. They are the same calculation. The form notation simply keeps the integrand and the orientation together. The boundary integral measures circulation. The exterior derivative measures circulation per unit area. \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.9, >=stealth] \draw[->] (-2.4,0) -- (2.6,0) node[right] {\(x\)}; \draw[->] (0,-2.4) -- (0,2.6) node[above] {\(y\)}; \draw[fill=gray!10, thick] (0,0) circle (1.7); \draw[->, very thick, red!65!black] (1.7,0) arc[start angle=0,end angle=70,radius=1.7]; \foreach \x/\y in { 1.2/0,0.85/0.85,0/1.2,-0.85/0.85,-1.2/0, -0.85/-0.85,0/-1.2,0.85/-0.85 } { \draw[->, blue!65!black, thick] (\x,\y) -- ++({-0.35*\y},{0.35*\x}); } \node at (0,-2.95) {\(\displaystyle \int_{\partial D}(-y\,dx+x\,dy)=\int_D2\,dx\wedge dy\)}; \end{tikzpicture} Your task. Choose one classical vector calculus problem and translate it completely into forms. Use one of the following, or choose your own. \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Classical problem} \amp \text{Classical theorem} \amp \text{Forms version} \\ \hline \oint_C \mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r \amp \text{Green's theorem} \amp \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_R d\omega \\[1mm] \oint_{\partial S}\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf r \amp \text{Stokes' theorem} \amp \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_S d\omega \\[1mm] \iint_{\partial E}\mathbf F\cdot\widehat{\mathbf n}\,dS \amp \text{Divergence theorem} \amp \int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_E d\Phi \\[1mm] \int_C \nabla f\cdot d\mathbf r \amp \text{Fundamental theorem for line integrals} \amp \int_C df=\int_{\partial C}f \end{array} Suggested examples. \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Example} \amp \text{What to translate} \\ \hline \mathbf F=(-y/2,x/2) \text{ around an ellipse} \amp \text{area from circulation}\\[1mm] \mathbf F=(x,y,z) \text{ through a box} \amp \text{flux and divergence}\\[1mm] \mathbf F=(-y,x,0) \text{ around a disk in space} \amp \text{Stokes' theorem}\\[1mm] f(x,y,z)=x^2y+z \amp \text{gradient field and }df \end{array} Required steps. State the classical problem. Identify the correct form: \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz or \Phi=P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy. Compute the exterior derivative: d\omega \qquad\text{or}\qquad d\Phi. Compute the integral directly, if possible. Compute the integral using \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_Md\omega. Write a translation table showing each classical object and its forms version. Explain which notation made orientation easier to track. What to hand in. Your report should include: the original classical problem, the form version of the problem, the calculation of d\omega or d\Phi, both sides of the theorem, a short translation table, a paragraph explaining what the forms notation clarifies. The best reports do not merely replace dots and crosses by wedges. They explain why the form is the natural integrand for the geometric object.

text: Project 2: closed but not exact forms on punctured domains A 1-form \omega is called closed if d\omega=0. It is called exact if there is a function f such that \omega=df. Every exact form is closed, because d(df)=0. But the converse can fail when the domain has a hole. This project is about that failure. A seed example: the angular form. On the punctured plane \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}, define \boxed{\omega= \frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}.} This form measures change in angle around the origin. Let P=\frac{-y}{x^2+y^2}, \qquad Q=\frac{x}{x^2+y^2}. Then \omega=P\,dx+Q\,dy. Compute: Q_x \amp = \frac{(x^2+y^2)-2x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} = \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}, and P_y \amp = \frac{-(x^2+y^2)+2y^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2} = \frac{y^2-x^2}{(x^2+y^2)^2}. Thus Q_x-P_y=0. So \boxed{d\omega=0.} The form is closed. Now integrate around the unit circle: x=\cos t,\qquad y=\sin t,\qquad 0\le t\le2\pi. Then dx=-\sin t\,dt, \qquad dy=\cos t\,dt, and x^2+y^2=1. Therefore \omega \amp = -\sin t(-\sin t\,dt)+\cos t(\cos t\,dt) \amp = dt. So \boxed{\oint_C\omega=2\pi.} If \omega were exact on the punctured plane, say \omega=df, then every closed-curve integral would be zero: \oint_C df=f(\text{endpoint})-f(\text{starting point})=0. But we found \oint_C\omega=2\pi. So \omega is closed but not exact on \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}. The missing origin stores the obstruction. A closed form can fail to be exact when the domain has a hole. \begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.85, >=stealth] \draw[->] (-3,0) -- (3.2,0) node[right] {\(x\)}; \draw[->] (0,-3) -- (0,3.2) node[above] {\(y\)}; \fill[white] (0,0) circle (4pt); \draw[thick] (0,0) circle (4pt); \node[below right] at (0,0) {hole}; \draw[thick, red!65!black] (0,0) circle (2); \draw[->, very thick, red!65!black] (2,0) arc[start angle=0,end angle=60,radius=2]; \foreach \ang in {0,45,90,135,180,225,270,315} { \pgfmathsetmacro{\x}{2*cos(\ang)} \pgfmathsetmacro{\y}{2*sin(\ang)} \draw[->, blue!65!black, thick] (\x,\y) -- ++({-0.35*sin(\ang)},{0.35*cos(\ang)}); } \node at (0,-3.7) {\(\displaystyle \omega=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2}\) is closed, but loops detect the hole}; \end{tikzpicture} Your task. Study one closed form on a punctured domain. Use one of the following. \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Form} \amp \text{Domain} \\ \hline \displaystyle \omega_1=\frac{-y\,dx+x\,dy}{x^2+y^2} \amp \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\} \\[4mm] \displaystyle \omega_2=\frac{x\,dx+y\,dy}{x^2+y^2} \amp \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(0,0)\} \\[4mm] \displaystyle \omega_3= \frac{-(y-b)\,dx+(x-a)\,dy}{(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2} \amp \mathbb R^2\setminus\{(a,b)\} \end{array} The second form is different from the angular form. In fact, \omega_2=d\left(\ln\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\right). So \omega_2 is exact on the punctured plane. Comparing \omega_1 and \omega_2 is a good way to see that closed and exact are not the same idea. Required steps. State the domain carefully. Do not include points where the formula is undefined. Compute d\omega. Decide whether the form is closed. Integrate \omega around at least two closed curves: \text{one loop that surrounds the missing point} and \text{one loop that does not surround the missing point}. Decide whether the form is exact on the whole domain. If possible, find a potential function on a smaller domain, such as a plane with a ray removed. Explain what the hole changes. Questions to answer. Why does d\omega=0 not automatically imply \omega=df? What happens to the integral if a loop winds around the puncture twice? Why does a loop that does not surround the puncture give a different kind of answer? What is the role of the angle function \theta? Why can it be chosen locally but not globally around the puncture? What does this example teach about the hypotheses in conservative-field theorems? What to hand in. Your report should include: the form and its domain, the calculation of d\omega, at least two closed-curve integrals, a conclusion about closedness and exactness, a drawing of the domain and the loops, a paragraph explaining why the missing point matters. The important lesson is not the formula itself. The important lesson is that local information can miss global topology. A form may have no local curl and still remember a hole.

text: Project 3: the generalized Stokes theorem on a cube The generalized Stokes theorem says \boxed{\int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_M d\omega.} For a solid cube, the form \omega must be a 2-form, because the boundary of a solid is a surface. This project asks you to verify the theorem face by face. A seed example: a flux form on the unit cube. Let B=[0,1]\times[0,1]\times[0,1] with orientation dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Consider the 2-form \boxed{\Phi = x\,dy\wedge dz + y\,dz\wedge dx + z\,dx\wedge dy.} This is the flux form of the vector field \mathbf F=(x,y,z). First compute the exterior derivative: d\Phi \amp = d(x\,dy\wedge dz) + d(y\,dz\wedge dx) + d(z\,dx\wedge dy) \amp = dx\wedge dy\wedge dz + dy\wedge dz\wedge dx + dz\wedge dx\wedge dy. Both dy\wedge dz\wedge dx and dz\wedge dx\wedge dy are cyclic rearrangements of dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, so they have the same sign. Thus \boxed{d\Phi=3\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.} Therefore \boxed{\int_B d\Phi=3.} Now compute the boundary integral. The boundary has six faces. Using the outward orientation, the induced face orientations are: \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Face} \amp \text{Induced orientation} \\ \hline x=1 \amp dy\wedge dz\\ x=0 \amp -dy\wedge dz\\ y=1 \amp dz\wedge dx\\ y=0 \amp -dz\wedge dx\\ z=1 \amp dx\wedge dy\\ z=0 \amp -dx\wedge dy \end{array} On the face x=1, \Phi=1\,dy\wedge dz+\text{terms involving }dx. Terms involving dx vanish on this face because x is constant there. Hence \int_{x=1}\Phi=1. On the face x=0, the coefficient x is zero, so the contribution is 0. Similarly, \int_{y=1}\Phi=1, \qquad \int_{y=0}\Phi=0, and \int_{z=1}\Phi=1, \qquad \int_{z=0}\Phi=0. Thus \boxed{\int_{\partial B}\Phi=1+1+1=3.} So \boxed{\int_{\partial B}\Phi=\int_B d\Phi.} Your task. Verify the generalized Stokes theorem on a rectangular box or cube. Choose one of these. \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Region} \amp \text{Form} \\ \hline [0,1]^3 \amp x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy\\[1mm] [0,a]\times[0,b]\times[0,c] \amp x^2\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy\\[1mm] [0,1]^2 \amp (x^2+y)\,dx+xy\,dy\\[1mm] [0,a]\times[0,b] \amp -y\,dx+x\,dy \end{array} The three-dimensional choices verify the divergence theorem in forms language. The two-dimensional choices verify Green's theorem in forms language. Required steps. State the region and its orientation. State the form \omega. Compute d\omega. Compute the interior integral: \int_M d\omega. List all boundary pieces. State the induced orientation on each boundary piece. Compute each boundary contribution. Add the boundary contributions and compare with the interior integral. Questions to answer. Which boundary pieces contribute zero? Why? Where does orientation enter the calculation? What would change if the region were given the opposite orientation? In the three-dimensional case, what vector field has the chosen 2-form as its flux form? In the two-dimensional case, what vector field has the chosen 1-form as its work form? What to hand in. Your report should include: a drawing of the region, the form and its exterior derivative, the interior integral, a table of boundary pieces and orientations, the boundary integral, a sentence explaining how this example fits \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_Md\omega. A cube is simple enough that no geometry is hidden. Every sign must be earned. That is why it is such a good testing ground for Stokes' theorem.

text: Project 1: Hamilton, quaternions, and the birth of vector algebra Chapter began with a strange question: \text{Can we multiply vectors?} In the plane, complex numbers answered yes. Multiplication by a+bi rotates and stretches. But in three dimensions, the answer was harder. Hamilton's quaternions gave one answer, and modern vector algebra later split that answer into the dot product and cross product. This writing project asks you to explain that split. A seed calculation. A pure imaginary quaternion has the form A=a_1i+a_2j+a_3k. We identify it with the vector \mathbf a=(a_1,a_2,a_3). Similarly, B=b_1i+b_2j+b_3k corresponds to \mathbf b=(b_1,b_2,b_3). Using i^2=j^2=k^2=-1, and ij=k,\qquad jk=i,\qquad ki=j, with the reversed products changing sign, one finds \boxed{AB=-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b+\mathbf a\times\mathbf b.} More explicitly, AB \amp = -(a_1b_1+a_2b_2+a_3b_3) \amp \qquad + (a_2b_3-a_3b_2)i \amp \qquad + (a_3b_1-a_1b_3)j \amp \qquad + (a_1b_2-a_2b_1)k. The scalar part is -\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b. The vector part is \mathbf a\times\mathbf b. So the dot product and cross product were not born as two unrelated formulas. They are two pieces of one multiplication. Your task. Write an essay explaining how quaternions connect complex numbers, dot products, and cross products. Your essay should answer: Why does complex multiplication feel geometrically natural in the plane? What changes when we try to multiply triples? What are the rules for quaternion units i,j,k? Why is quaternion multiplication noncommutative? How do the dot product and cross product appear inside the product of two pure imaginary quaternions? Why did vector algebra eventually separate the scalar part and vector part? How does the wedge product give another way to think about oriented area? Required mathematical examples. Include at least two of the following: \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Example} \amp \text{Purpose} \\ \hline (1+i)(1-i)=2 \amp \text{Complex multiplication and length}\\[1mm] ij=k,\quad ji=-k \amp \text{Noncommutativity}\\[1mm] (i+j)(i-j) \amp \text{Scalar and vector parts}\\[1mm] (1,0,0)\times(0,1,0)=(0,0,1) \amp \text{Cross product orientation}\\[1mm] (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf a,\mathbf b) \amp \text{Oriented coordinate-area measurement} \end{array} What to hand in. Submit a 3- to 5-page essay with: a title, a clear thesis statement, at least two worked examples, one diagram, a short comparison between quaternions and the vector operations used in this book, a bibliography or source list if historical claims are included. A strong essay will not only say that quaternions came before vector algebra. It will show, through a calculation, why dot and cross products are two shadows of a larger multiplication.

chapter.title: Capstone Projects and Extended Explorations

text: Project 2: why the cross product is both useful and suspicious The cross product is one of the most useful tools in three-dimensional calculus: \mathbf u\times\mathbf v. It gives normal vectors, areas of parallelograms, torque, angular momentum, and the curl of a vector field. But it is also suspicious. Two vectors in the plane span an oriented parallelogram. Two vectors in space also span an oriented parallelogram. The cross product replaces that parallelogram by a perpendicular vector. This works beautifully in \mathbb R^3, because a plane has one perpendicular direction, up to sign. The ordered pair of vectors spans an oriented parallelogram. A coordinate 2-form, such as dx\wedge dy, measures its signed projected area. These forms are alternating bilinear measurements on pairs of vectors, as defined in . The cross product encodes the three coordinate area measurements as a vector by using the Euclidean geometry and orientation of space. A seed comparison. Let \mathbf u=(1,0,0),\qquad \mathbf v=(0,2,0). The parallelogram has area 2. The cross product is \mathbf u\times\mathbf v=(0,0,2). This vector has length 2 and points in the positive z-direction. Evaluating the wedge of coordinate covectors gives (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=1\cdot2-0\cdot0=2. It says that this parallelogram has signed xy-area 2. The form dx\wedge dy is the measuring rule; the vectors are its inputs. The number 2 is its output. Both descriptions contain the same area information in three dimensions. But they store it differently. Your task. Write an essay explaining the double personality of the cross product. Your essay should argue both sides: \begin{array}{c|l} \text{Useful} \amp \text{The cross product gives quick normal vectors and area vectors.}\\[1mm] \text{Suspicious} \amp \text{It turns an oriented area into a vector using special features of } \mathbb R^3. \end{array} Questions to answer. What geometric quantity is \norm{\mathbf u\times\mathbf v} measuring? Why does the direction of \mathbf u\times\mathbf v depend on orientation? Why does swapping the vectors change the sign? \mathbf v\times\mathbf u=-(\mathbf u\times\mathbf v). How do the coordinate area-measuring forms dx\wedge dy,\qquad dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx record the signed projected areas used by a normal vector? Why is the cross product especially convenient for parametrized surfaces? What does forms language clarify about flux? Required examples. Include at least three examples: \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Example} \amp \text{Concept} \\ \hline \mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v \amp \text{Surface normal and area scale}\\[1mm] \mathbf r_v\times\mathbf r_u \amp \text{Orientation reversal}\\[1mm] \mathbf F\cdot(\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v)\,du\,dv \amp \text{Classical flux}\\[1mm] \Phi_{\mathbf F}= F_1\,dy\wedge dz+F_2\,dz\wedge dx+F_3\,dx\wedge dy \amp \text{Forms flux}\\[1mm] (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) \amp \text{Signed projected area} \end{array} What to hand in. Submit a 3- to 5-page essay with: a clear thesis, a diagram of an oriented parallelogram, at least three worked examples, one paragraph defending the cross product, one paragraph criticizing or limiting the cross product, a concluding paragraph explaining what the wedge product changes. The best essays will not treat the cross product as wrong. It is not wrong. It is a brilliant shortcut. But every shortcut hides a path, and forms reveal the path.

chapter.title: Capstone Projects and Extended Explorations

text: Project 3: the many lives of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Single-variable calculus has a central theorem: \boxed{\int_a^b f'(x)\,dx=f(b)-f(a).} This theorem says that adding derivative information over an interval gives boundary information at the endpoints. By the end of this book, the same sentence has grown into \boxed{\int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_Md\omega.} This writing project asks you to tell that story. A seed table. \begin{array}{c|c|c} \text{Object }M \amp \text{Form }\omega \amp \text{Theorem} \\ \hline [a,b] \amp f \amp \displaystyle \int_{\partial[a,b]}f=\int_{[a,b]}df\\[3mm] \text{plane region }R \amp P\,dx+Q\,dy \amp \displaystyle \int_{\partial R}\omega=\int_Rd\omega\\[3mm] \text{surface }S \amp P\,dx+Q\,dy+R\,dz \amp \displaystyle \int_{\partial S}\omega=\int_Sd\omega\\[3mm] \text{solid }E \amp P\,dy\wedge dz+Q\,dz\wedge dx+R\,dx\wedge dy \amp \displaystyle \int_{\partial E}\Phi=\int_Ed\Phi \end{array} In the first row, \partial[a,b]=\{b\}-\{a\}, so \int_{\partial[a,b]}f=f(b)-f(a). In the last row, d\Phi=(P_x+Q_y+R_z)\,dx\wedge dy\wedge dz, so the theorem becomes the divergence theorem. The boundary changes dimension. The form changes degree. But the pattern does not change. Your task. Write an essay explaining how the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus reappears as: \begin{array}{ll} 1. \amp \text{The Fundamental Theorem for line integrals,}\\ 2. \amp \text{Green's theorem,}\\ 3. \amp \text{Stokes' theorem,}\\ 4. \amp \text{The divergence theorem,}\\ 5. \amp \text{The generalized Stokes theorem.} \end{array} You do not need to prove every theorem. Your job is to explain the shared structure. Required examples. Include at least three worked examples, chosen from different dimensions. \begin{array}{c|c} \text{Example} \amp \text{Boundary principle} \\ \hline \displaystyle \int_1^4 d(x^2+1) \amp \text{Endpoints}\\[2mm] \displaystyle \int_C df \amp \text{Potential difference}\\[2mm] \displaystyle \int_{\partial R}x\,dy \amp \text{Area from boundary}\\[2mm] \displaystyle \int_{\partial B} \left(x\,dy\wedge dz+y\,dz\wedge dx+z\,dx\wedge dy\right) \amp \text{Flux from divergence}\\[3mm] \displaystyle \int_{\partial S}\omega \amp \text{Circulation from surface curl} \end{array} Questions to answer. What does boundary mean for an interval, a region, a surface, and a solid? Why do signs and orientations become unavoidable? What changes when d acts on a 0-form, a 1-form, and a 2-form? How do gradient, curl, and divergence fit into one operation? Why is the statement \int_{\partial M}\omega=\int_Md\omega not just shorter, but more revealing? What to hand in. Submit a 4- to 6-page essay with: a central thesis, a translation table, at least three examples, at least one diagram showing an object and its boundary, a paragraph on orientation, a conclusion explaining what the word fundamental means after this course. A strong essay should make the reader feel that the Fundamental Theorem did not disappear after single-variable calculus. It kept changing clothes.
